JOE SIEG. Who are the heroes we hail to-day, And circle their brows with wreaths of bay? Is it the warrior back again, ' To be girt by throngs of his fellow-men? The statesman fighting in keen debate For the laws that will make his country great? r Or the poet, whose spirit in his song WitDers like fire the front of wrong? Yes, these are heroes on whom we m ay call, .;„ But a greater still is behind them all. Who? And we shout, with a ringing cheer, "Joe Sieg' the railway engineer, ' "Who did his duty and never thought Be did any more than a driver ought." E Look at Sieg, I say, as he stands With the levers clutch'd in his oily hands, • And hearing naught but the grind of the wheel ' On the clanking rail underneath his heel; Or, lighting his pipe for a whiff or Cwo, Yet looking ahead as drivers:do. Now, any one seeing him thus would have said, With a very doubtful shake of the head, "Poor stuff after all out of which to plan ,Your hero when action calls for the man." So you would think, but listen and hear The story of Sieg, the engineer. I Down the Pennsylvanian line, In the light of an afternoon's sunshine, Came Sieg with a train of cars behind, • And hundreds of lives that were his to mind. Little thought he of danger near As he watch'd for signals set at clear. • If he thought at all, and that thought could be said, As he stood on the foot-plate looking ahead, It was this: to do what a driver could do— Run sharp to his time, nor be overdue. So along the metals in smoke and glare, With Sieg at his post by the levers there, Engine and cars like a whirlwind tore ; Till, just as the stoker threw open the door Of the furnace, at once through each black flue came i The quick back-draught, bringing with it the flame That, scorching with lightning fingers of pain, Drove Sieg and his stoker back in the train. The:eneine like some wild steed that is free : Shot ailed with a shriek of defiant glee. ; Behind were hundred of lives in a tomb That was hot with the breath of their awful doom. To leap from the train would be certain death, To stay would be food for the flame's wild breath. Now was the time for your hero to plan; : The hour had come, and Sieg was the man. : Not a moment he stood, for at once he saw ; His duty before him, and that was law. Not a single thought of hiimself came near To shake his grand brave spirit with fear. Only there rose, like a flash, in his eye, ; As in those when the last stern moment is nigh, A look that would do all that duty could claim, And with one wild rush Sieg was into the flame. ' The red tongues quiver'd and clutch'd at him They tore the flesh from his arm and limb; They wove, like scarlet demons, between -- , - The engine and him a fiery screen. But he fought his way to his terrible fate' Till he he felt his feet touch the tender plate. Then, blind with the flame and its scorchine breath, And weak from his terrible struggle with death, Be groped for the levers, clutch'd them at length, ; And, with one wild effort of failing strength, 'Mid the hissing of fire and the engine's roar, Threw off the steam, and could do no more. I When the engine at last was brought to a stand, Not a life was lost out of all that band. l No life, did I say? Alas! there was one, But not till his duty was nobly done. For, back in the tender, silent and grim, Blacken'd and scalded in body and limb, ; Lay Siege who had without aid, and alone, Saved hufidreds of lives, and lost his own. That is the story, plain and clear, Of Sieg. the railway engineer. Honour to him, and no stint of praise From the best of hearts in these modern days. Honour to Sieg! I say, and hail This last Jim Bludso of the rail, Who did his duty, and never thought He did any more than a driver ought. —Good If"ords. ALEXANDER ANDERSON.

Humility, sweet as it may be as a trait of character, may degenerate into a vice if not upheld by self-respect. ':Mamma, I want some raisins."" Very well, take a handful." "A handful? Oh, won't you give them to me? Your hand is larger." . The child probably destined to be the greatest of American naturalists is already born. He lives in Ten- nessee, and is the author of the remark that a "Jackass is the only animal that winks with his ears." Husband (reading from Scott: "'Not one woman in twenty marries the first love.' How was it in your case, my dear ?" Wife: "How was it in your case ?" Husband: "You must make the first confession—don't answer like a parrot by asking me the same question." Wife: "Well, here's the truth. If you married your first love, I mar- ried my first. If you didn't, I didn't." A Judge of the Court of Session, well known for speaking his mother tongue in the broadest accent, as well on the bench as in common discourse, on a particu- lar occasion was addressed by a barrister equally noted for the elegance and purity of his style, as his Lordship was the reverse, who opened the case of his client in the following words—" My Lord, the pursuer, my client, is an itinerant violin player." "What's that, said his Lordship; "is that what ye ca' a blin' fiddler ?" " Vul- garly so called," said the lawyer. PRINTER'S GoseEn.—Extract fromla discourse de- livered by Mr. J. Cartwright, of Peckham :—By the pulpit of the newspaper printer we get a larger audience than by that talk-throne that is encompassed by much brick- work and great expansion of temples and tabernacles. Much thought of the pulpit dies with the life-sounds , that gave it utterance. But newspaper or printer's gospel is of large service, spreadeth wide, and renews its freshness a thousand times. The printer he prmteth, and no one giveth him worship. He fills the world with light, and his work pierceth the darkest corners of the earth; yet, with inked fingers and smudged face, he shoulders about in the highways of life, and hath no reverence save his own consciousness of a sweet-smelling savour of honest industry. • _ PARLIAMENTS, PAST AND PRESENT.—The St. James's Gazette says the opening by the Queen of the eleventh Parliament of her reign is a circumstance a parallel to which cannot be found since the times of Henry VI. Twelve Parliaments, it is true, were summoned within the sixty years' reign of George III.; but that Sovereign can only be said to have opened ten of them, for those chosen in 1812 and 1818 were convoked by the Prince Regent. George I. opened two Parliaments; his suc- cessor five; George IV. (as King) two; and William IV. four. Elizabeth summoned eight; but it is when we get back to the early days of Parliaments that the total swells. Edward 11. called sixteen, Richard 11. eighteen,' Henry VI. twenty-one, and Edward 111. no fewer than ! thirty-one. But Parliaments usually lasted only one ! session in those times, and, having be convoked to meet at Westminster, or York, or Northampton, or Salis- bury, or any place which suited the convenience of the King, they were speedily dissolved when their worlewas done. Constituencies had a very direct interest in wish- ing for short sessions, for they had to pay their Mem- bers at the rate of two shillings per day for their ser- vices; and when they were away for forty or sixty days loud grumbles were raised, and boroughs prayed to be relieved from the burden. Perhaps if constituencies in these days had a similar motive for returning Members who were slow to speak and prompt to act, it would re- sult in shorter sessions and better work. OLD FASHIONED WINTERS AND WEATHER P ROPHE'TS.— This is!the time for furbishing up memories of old-fash- ioned winters, when snow and frost were looked for as matters of course, and a green Christmas was held to foretell a full churchyard. And is this to be the beginning of a fresh cycle of hard winters? We may talk of alman- acs, too, and weather prophecies—as King Richard, in his misfortunes, proposed to discuss the question of worms and epitaphs—of excellent shots by the prophets, and equally disastrous failures. Such as that wonderful fluke by Murphy in 1838, when he hit the coldest day of the year, and recorded it three months in advance. That hit made the fortune of the almanac for the year, and Paternoster Row was beseiged with applicants for copies, and Murphy, who was a man with a system a sober minded man too, Who had lights on the subject of meteor- ology, set out to map the weather for the following year with every hope of success. But on every prediction the event ;showed the prophet dismally, hopelessly in the wrong, as he dolefully admitted in the preface to the following year's volume. His excuse was that his cal- culations had been perfectly sound, his predictions com- pounded with accuracy, but that a miserable comet had ' run in from parts unknown, and had spoilt the whole batch. But the next year's almanac was equally a failure, and yet our weather-prophet did not despair. It could be shown that some ot his predictions had been admir- able fulfilled in Russia, while another set corresponded exactly with weather-reports from Mesopotamia. But the British public did not have much faith in weather- prophets after that. They did not care to know what was going to happen in Mesopotamia, and thus poor Murphy sank into oblivion. If Murphy had lived in the present day, with all the abundant materials which are furnished from observatioas all over the world, he might have started some theory about the weather that would have held water a little better than his own. dig it is, scientific meteorologists confine themselves to a forecast ,`-e.. 24 hours, and this morning—it is old Christmas Day on ' which I am writing, by the way—they have .actually got snow on the record—snow or cold rain. Well, it does snow, without suspicion of error; a regular soft, feather- bed kind of snowstorm of the good old-fashioned kind, such as they used to tell us children was caused by the old women plucking geese in Lincolushire.—AU the Year Round.

A parish clerk apologised to a church dignitary who had been summoned to take a service at a small village church. "I am sorry, sir, to have brought such a gentle- man as you to this poor little place. A worse gentleman would have done if we had only known where to find him."

A man in the smoking-car of a railway?train leaned over to a man who sat in front of him, and said, "Have you a match ?" "Yes, but I hain't got any cigar," was the prompt reply," accompanied with a significant wink. " Then you don't want the match," said :the first man

sweetly: The Duke of Wellington was coolness itself. He was one day sitting at his library table, when the door opened, and, without any announcement, in stalked a figure of singular ill-omen. "Who areyou ?" asked the Duke, in his short and dry manner, looking without the slightest change of countenance upon the intruder. "I am Apollyon ;I am sent here to kill you." "Kill me? very odd." "I am Apollyon, and must put you to death." " 'Bliged to do it to-day ?" "I am not told the day or hour, but I must do my mission." "Very incon- venient, very busy, great many letters to write. Call again or write me word—l'll be ready for you." And the Duke went on with his correspondence. The maniac, appalled probably by the stern, immovable old man, backed out of die room, and in half an hour was in an asylum. Colonel Charles Spencer, American counsellor-at-law, some years ago had to defend one Marshall, charged with larceny, against whom there was very strong evidence. Before the trial Spencer went to his client, and told him that his only chance was the plea of insanity, and ad- viced him to play the lunatic, and to answerll ques- tions put to him with the word "spoons." The day of the trial came, and Marshall took his place in the dock, pale, haggard, and wild looking. "Guilty or not guilty ?" asked the clerk. "Spoons !" drawled the prisoner, with a blank stare. "Come, plead guilty or not guilty," the clerk responded. "Spoons !" was the reply. " Prisoner, will you answer the question put to You ra, Spoons !" he bawled. At this point the counsel you the prisoner in- terfered, and told thb Court the prisoner was insane, and not responsible for his actions, Sze. "Do you understand what is said ?" asked the Judge of the prisoner. "Spoons !" was the reply. The Judge discharged hire, as he was evidently insane. .Spencer congratulated him upon his escape, and suggested it, would be a good idea to pay him. His client stared, and moved away with the simple remark, "Spoons "! • - * CHRIOLTS FRENCH-CANADIAN WEDDING CIISTOMS.—A fter the morning marriage service in the church, the bridal party in caleche or cariole make a tour of calls upon re- latives and friends through the day, and then again to church for vespers. Before the evening dance 'at the bride's new home comes the supper. When they rise from the table the bride keeps her. seat, and someone asks in great dignity, "Why does madame wait ?" Is she so soon in bad grace ?" She replies, "Somebody has stolen my slipper. I "can't walk."'"' They carry her, chair and all, into the middle of the room, while a loud knocking announces a grotesque, ragged vendor of boots and shoes. He kneels before the slipperless bride, and tries on a long succession of old boots and shoes of every variety and size till at last he finds her missing shoe. The groom redeems it for a good price, which is spent in treating the company. If the groom is not watchful they steal her hat and cloak, which he redeems in the same way, and they have been known to steal the bride, for whom he must pay most liberally. The church forbids mund dances, so they content them- selves with contra dances. ~.,The event of the evening is

a jig. SMOKY CHIMNEYS IN COLD WHATIIER.—A smoky chimney is an exceedingly great nuisance in a sick room, and even after the well-known method of creating a draught by holding a newspaper against the front of the grate so as to create an up-draught by preventing a down-draught, has been adopted, the chimney will smoke in cold weather. This is because the upper part of the chimney is cold, and the fire in the grate has not power enough to heat the column of air sufficiently. Good may be done by lighting a fire in some room on a higher floor, the flue of which is in contact with the upper part of the chimney from the sick room; but the best plan probably is to create a blaze—if the chimney has been recently swept, and it is safe to do so—by placing on the tip of the fire some sticks and paper, or one of those wheels of firewood which are sold prepared with an in- flammable material. The purpose is to raise the tem- perature of the upper part of the chimney as rapidly as possible, and to keep it well heated. It may not appear worth while to make this self-evident suggestion, but as a matter of fact no one can see much of the sick in private houses without being struck with the relative greatness of the discomfort to which they are exposed by failure to adopt what would seem obvious precau- tions. It is necessary, therefore, to assume that matters so simple as this even are too often forgotten or un- known—Lancet.

Wheerever it's gooin' on th' biziest it's sure to cause bother ' among folk. It's makkin' a wakes o' lots ov us just neaw; an' I've yerd my feyther an' say gronfeyther say it did so i' their day. Thoese et wur th' fast one time will ha' to be thrutehed eaut i' their turn an' flung to th' wall, an' thoose at war th' last Ptia' squeezin' match a bit sin' 11 Ibe pokin' their bite o' *meatus HY front e'en neaw. Theere 'they're at it—little an' big, owd an' youtt, black an' white, l rich as' poor--pell-mell, like wasps in a hustma-bee neat. I icon see it i' ease fowt every day o' my life; an' tle' wo'ld's nobbut a big fowl. Under every thatch it's gooin on, for a heause is 'Anhui a little fowt. When I see two lads agate o' fiusterin' after one wench, an' dooin' ther beet for t' catch her, I know what'll be th' eend on't—hoo'l ha' that ut coons last if he shows th' mooast gam', an th' tother may goo skroikin ; wheam an' tell his mother. His meant hes getten a saltier. When I see a wayver rtra a decent reed o' wark (sammat very skase neaw-a-daya) as' some- b'dy else thinks they could like to have it %horsed', I con yea (guess) what's gooin to happen. Tie' men at has it wishes to do fair by folk—" live au' let live," if anybody con tell him what that meeans ; but th' mon at wants it is quite ready to do a bit lees fair. He goes to th' meethar, an' , says," I'll wayve yon wark so-an'-so's wayvin at is mich less wage, if yo'n let me hey it." Th' meether COR see no furr than his pocket, so let's biro hey is. Well th' tother mon says "I men dive," an' thinks he'll no' be byttes, though he doesno' wish to do wrung, so !goes an' offers hissel for lees wege still; an' so it goes on till one on 'em oomes east o'th' bulls wi' a nose as flat as a peaswad, an' th' tether's fearfully =ult. (I wonder if' th wark wur as went done at th' last as it war at th' fast, or whether it war wo'rth o' that feightin for.) When I see a shop- keeper dein' middlin' weal in a shop, an' givis good satisfaction to his customers, I bet mysel' a wager hie nose is Doane safe, as' I'm sure to win. It'll as' be lung afore sense neighboer mak's his heause-window a bit bigger, an' sticks it full o' lies abeaut beast mich cheaper he eon sell than th' owd 'an con. "A. new bream sweeps dean," an' folk flochen like crows to th' new shop. Things goo on as brisk as n weddia' for a while. Then th' owd shopkeeper dons his window 1' lies. He'll sell cheaper than th' new us; but I know very wed l his nose is doomt. Th' bother . mon intended puttin' it nut at th' fast, °ether by fair , means or feaw, an' what wi' calico at thirty inches to th' . yard; fleaur at eleven peaunds to th' dean ; huller weel , seasoned wi' tallow; as' sugar yo' met mak' sondpapper one, , he manages at th' last. , 1' o conditioss o' life th' slate is gooin' on. Handloom , wayvin's nose wur put eaut by steears, an' steeam's very nee puttin' its own Knife One religion's peggin' away at , another, as if for very life, an' noses are gettin' woefully sqttozzen. Nations at hen had th' lead a tang while ban to . wakken up neaw, an' buckle ther does tight, if they meean to keep i'th' front, for ther noses are i' danger o' beta' put , eaut. Different eons o' folk, too, are grabble' at one • another's throats, an' ksockin' ther heads tigether like a lot , o' skittles on th' spree. They're train' to throat one , another eaut, as if ther wurno' reawm enough for a on NOM. . But as I'm geniis' farr newsy than I con wade, an' swim I . conno'. I'll turn back to eaur fowl, an' show yo' heaw none , hen bin, an' are bein' put eaut theere. When I coom into th' wold my mother said Pre pret- tiest lad ever sun ehoint on, or rain saint on. an' I da'eay I war in her e'en.. As I grew up,wenches used t' 'eight which must nuts me ter a Sunday; en' I da'say some on 'em wished l're a bit owder ; they'd ha' fowten o'er sammat else then. I'd hawpennys, an' tewtty, ding-dong—an' dobby- hoases, an' carts bowl me, an' at last a little wheelbarrow. Thee things fell off o at once, for eaur Ned had 000 m to th' lest, an' nowt could be prettier than he war. Th' wenches fowt for him then, an' nob'dy would look at me. Haw- penays, towlfy, an' dobby hosses went for him, an' I grew up as sulky as a wench nt's foen eaut wi' th' lookiscglaea for makkin' her t' look so feaw. My nose mit put want, an' I reckon eaur Ned's would be in his tarn. Wht.n I fuss get it i' my yesad ut my owd rib—ut is neaw —wry th' nicest wench i' Hazelwo'th, Billy o' Tura' s war partendin' for t' potter after her. I'd seen 'em walkin' eaut t'gether, an' yerd him whistlin' at th' eend o'th' heause wheere boo lived. As ther nob'dy else tryin', Billy took things yessily, an' seemed for t' go comfortably abeaut his cooarsin. , Neaw, then' I thowt, I'd have a turn, an' Billy met look'eant4 for it add be hint an' me for it. So one nest I I went o' seem' heasy th' chances stood, an' fund Billy at th' 1 botiorti o'h' ftry: wtilittill' liko a rellroad, an' wetcMn' for a certain lest to be blown taut. "What art theau after "he said to me. " Whlt art theme after? ' I said to him. Then we began o' shootherin' one anotb!`r, an' elbowin' till we geet to th dur, an' noather on 1-0 ad give up th' tussle. Then we'd a quiet wrote i'th pooarch, at' I laid Billy ov his back in a snifter. " Neaw for it," I thowt, "It's that at shows th' hest pluck stew at 'it win th' day ;" so I °peen% th' jut, en' dashed into th' loom-heeuse; an' afore owd Johnny o'Sammut's could get up fro' his wheel, I'd laid howd o' Sal, an' gam her Bich a squeeste at hoo trent her shuttle, an' broke her treddle-bant. wi' bsin' i' Mott a fluster. Well, neaw, Sher are what I co fair ways an' featv ways o' puttin' noses eawt, an' feaw ways I dunno' like, though ther's less said abeaut 'em than ther met be. Ther's summat at east pa'son coes competition, an' I've es objeetion to it when it's competition i' dam' good; but when a mon sets cant i'th' wo'ld, an' says' "Neaw. Th' yorney doesno' know th' weld wouldno' last ten minutes if everybody wur like him. Neaw for one or two samples OY a very feaw way o' putting noses eawt. Owd Thusten, o' Wanmsley Fowt, is a decent sort ov o • chap. He'd do rest if folk ud let him, or if ther womb' so • mich encouragement to do wrung. He're used to sell his milk at tuppence•hewpinty a quart. But then it tour milk, as' some e' yo'r e'e wayther, at looks as blue reannd th' sides o'th' can as th' rim ofotn owd willow plate. He hadne' larut th' road to th' well yet, an' he happen never would ha' done, if neb'dy had shown him. But ther's aulus some- b'dy ready for t' sharpen folk up, an' put notions i' ther heads ut had better ha' bin kept eine It war so wi' owd Thuston. He're quite satisfied wi' things as they war, an' would be eendway if other folk ad let him. But one day ther a spring cart drove up to th' gate, an' a thin, slankerty chap at favvert he't bin browt up o' promises as' nowt to 'em, began o' sheautin'—"New milk, tuppence a quart !" Th' neighbours ran eaut, an' emptied his cans in a jiffey, an' owd Thuston had to let his go seaur. Th' chap coons again th' day after, an' sowd up another time. Th' milk • looked as good as owd Thuston's at th' fast, but I noticed at he stirred it up a good deal as he messurt it eaut, an' when it had stood awhile it war aulus thicker at th' bottom than it wur at th' top. There snmmat wrung abeaut it, I'm sure, but it wanted flndin' cant, like many a wrung thing. Well, owd Thuston thowt he wouldno' be thratcbt off his own midden wi' sigh a tallow-lookin' wastrel as that; so he'd sell his milk at tuppence, too, if he had to mak' th' difference wi' just t.l smatterin' o' cleean spring wayther ; 80 he offered it up tuppence. Th' tother mon didne sell up th' next time he coons, but took a canful back. Owd Thuston chuckled at this like a lad nt's cheted his feyther cant ov a threshin' ; but he hadno' lung for t' crow, for th' tether mon—he know what ad get th' women ov his side— offered t' give an seance o' tee to oitch ov his customers every month-send, as' his milk went off again like winliin'. When owd Thuston geet to yet o' this, he'd gie tae, too, an' butter i'th' bargain; an' if th' neigh- bours warns' satisfied with that, he'd hood th' keaws o'er to 'em, an' they met milk 'em for thersels' an' he'd charge 'em nowt for Vs' keep. But that wonldno' do, forth' tether mon said he'd give em th' milk ready milked before he'd be byetten ; so owd Thaston had t' give in, an' neaw he churns o he gets, an' sends it away, an' we han to pat up wi' milk at noather oat nor dog 'll tackle; so we'n getten nowt by this sort o' puttin' noses eaut, but quite as mich as we desarven. Neaw then again : one time Pre ware-in a good reed o' wark to "Owd Aaron's." It war o silk when I begun, an' I could ha' getten eleven or twelve shillin' a Week on't' an' no put mysel abeaut. Eaur Sal looked as breet as new pewter, an' said we should build afore lung if we kept on. I'd had it a month or two when Slogger coons one day to th' loom- heause window, as' said he'd getten a reed o'th' same sort to "Slopes," another mesther. 0 th' difference ther wur he'd put a little bit o' cotton up to th' selvedge, for t' mak' it coons in cheper, as he mant for t' undersell owd Aaron. Well, what's sauce for th' goose is sauce for th' totber brid. Owd Aaron must be as wakken as Sloper ; so th' next piece I geet had cotton in it, too; an' booath war sowd for a silk at th' same time. Then Slogger had to chenge to a cooarser reed, an' I had to follow. An we kept changin' every piece, till fro' a thirty-hundert we geet deawn to fifteen, an' put as mich cotton as silk in. When folk fund it cant heaw they'rn bein' cheted, they'd have it no longer; so it went chuck o at once. Every tweets at had bin thrntchin' war put eaut, an' in a feaw way, too. Neaw, ther's a way ce bein' th' meeans o' puttin'one's own nose eaut, an' it's gettin' rayther into fashin neaw-a-days, that is showin' folk heaw t' byet us, an' findin"em summat to do it with. I da'say yo'n yerd th' tale "owd Bobby Walker" tells abeaut a fause sort ov a blacksmith makkin a machine, at he coed " Enoch," for t' strike for him, an' th' fast blow it struck it hit him a crack o'th' top o'th' yead, at welly knockt it cant o' shape. Well, that's summat like taichin' folk heaw to byet us. An' neaw I'll tell yo'summat o'th' sort at happened in eaur neighbourhood.

The Hereford Times has reason to believe that Sir Mas- sey Lopes' 100 guineas prize for the best silo in:England and Wales has been awarded to Mr. John Morris, of Hampton Park, Hereford, whose farm is at ILulliam, Medley. There were 36 entries. The wheat yield of Michigan 25 years ago was 11 bushels to the acre, and the average yield the Past season was about 20 bushels per acre. This improvement is due to systematic rotation and seeding down with clover for two or three years in each course to furnish feed for stock. It is estimated that there are 100,000,000 acres of land on the Pacific coast that are especially adapted to wheat culture- Of this California has 25,000,000; Oregon, 18,000,000; Washington Territory, 16,000,000 acres; Colorado and Idaho, 10,000,000 each; Montana, Utah, and Wyoming, 7,000,000 each. The great bulk of all this wheat land lies yet untouched. Reports from South Australia give a gloomy estimate of the harvest. Wheat in many fields perished before harvest began, while the crops in others were not over 6in. high. Later accounts from Victoria give a more favourable account of the harvest there. It is estimated that the wheat crop will yield 9 bushels per acre, and that 90,000 tons will be a,ailable for export. The numbers of puri. bred cattle sold and the prices paid for them in the Uni:..d States during the year 1885 has been shown, as far as could be ascertained, in a tabular statement by the Breeder's Gazette (Chicago). From this it appears that 7,057 head of Shorthorns avel-- aged £2l 16s. 6d.; 480 Herefords averaged £6O 17s. 6d.; 180 Aberdeen polled cattle averaged £55 17s. 6d.; 105 Galloways averaged £5O 125.; and 1,604 head of Channel Island and Holstein-Frisian (Dutch) cattle averaged £3B 18s. FARMERS As Bt-rcireas.—ln consequence of the unre- munerative prices received for fat stock, a number of farmers in the East Riding of Yorkshire have, like their brethren elsewhere, formed themselves into a "Meat Supply Company," and have announced their intention of at once opening their first shop in Hull. English beef and mutton, it is stated, selected from the company's different farms, will be sold at prices varying from 31d. to TO. per lb. Several landed proprietors have become shareholders in the company. WELSH PONIES.—" Reader" inquired a few weeks ago where he could buy some of the Welsh black mountain , ponies. They are often sold at fairs and markets in the upper part of Carmarthenshire, namely Llandilo, Llan- , gadock, or Llandovery. Those towns are situated near the Black Mountain. Also they can be got in Brecon- shire at any fairs all through the summer; they are ; generally brought down from the mountains in flocks like sheep, all ages, and in a poor condition, but they improve very rapidly when put on good grass, and have often doubled their value in a few months.—R. W. S. CHOKED CATTLE.—It IS not uncommon for farmers to lose cattle from their being choked with pieces of turnip, &c., lodging in their throats, we believe, says Mr. A. P. Ford, of South Carolina. It is generally known that animals may be relieved from such difficulties by an operation so simple that any intelligent boy can perform it without any danger to the animal. Take a common carriage whip, the handle end of which is about an inch or so thick, and quite smooth; grease it well with some melted lard; let an assistant raise the head of the ani- mal so high that the lower jaw will be parallel with the lower part of the neck; thrust the butt of the whip into the mouth, and push boldly and steadily down the ceso- phagus, or passage, to the stomach. We have seen this operation done more than once, and consider it much safer than cutting into the throat to take out the ob- struction. I LABOURER'S ALLOTMENTS.—The Rev. J. A. Timins, vicar of West Mailing, Kent, writes :—When I was appointed to the incumbency of this parish, in 1842, I found that ! a very large number of cottagers had no gardens. I therefore set out six roods of rich glebe land, and offered it at half its agricultural value, in 12 allotments of a rood each. Only 10 working men accepted my offer. After a time, however, the great advantage which the allot- ment-teaants had derived from their gardens became evident, and there was a great demand for more. A working man, speaking at a public meeting a few weeks since, said that he had just paid me his thirty-third year's rent for half an acre, and that he had found much bene- fit from it all that time; but that those who clamoured for allotments of three acres did not understand what they talked about. It would, he said, make the man a slave, and starve his family. SIR HENRY ALLSOPP RELINQUISHING FARMING.—We regret to announce that the declining health of Sir Hy. Allsopp compels him to relinquish that great interest in farming, and in the welfare of the agriculturists in his own county of Worcester, that he has taken during the last quarter of a century. Convinced that well-bred stock in these days- must yield the largest profit to the farmer, lie brought the very best breeds of horses, cattle, and sheep on to his large farm in Worcestershire. As our readers may be aware, his herd of shorthorns was dispersed last year, and brought purchasers together from all parts; now his magnificent stud of Shire stal- lions are to be offered for sale. These comprise the noted horse Enterprise of Cannock (2272). champion stallion at the L9lldOn Show, 1884; Harrold (3703), commended at the same show; and That's the Sort 1 (2924), the well-known black four-year-old. These horses have covered in Worcestershire during the last season, and left remarkably fine stock, one of which took second prize at the Royal Show at Preston last year. If not privately sold, they will be offered at the London Shire Horse Show in February next, PROFESSOR SHELDON Als'D BurTEanm—Professor Shel- don writes :—" I am favoured at some considerable length with the view of one of the leading wholesale pro- vision merchants in London, who is very strongly in- clined to make the sale of butterine as butter a penal offence. This gentleman, a personal friend, deals very extensively in foreign and Irish butter, and also 'very considerably in butterine, and he has caused the makers of the latter article, whose goods he Ails, to clearly mark each package or cask distinctly with the word butterine,' and a trade mark as well; and under this designation he sells to retailers, who may or may not sell the article for what it is. My friend is anxious to see legislative action taken in reference to this matter, for, as he says, he has a desire to protect foreign buttermakers against unfair competition. It will be found, in fact, that all dealers of standing will support the demand for Parliamentaiy interference in this matter, and for a settlement of the question." It is highly satisfactory to learn that those of us who are fighting :against the fraudulent sale of butterine as butter will have the best of the dealers in butter, and even some who deal in butterine, on our side.

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURER AND THE LAND John Greenleaf Whittier, the American poet, rarely writes now; but he has just contributed to the Atlantic Monthly a protest against the migration of the manhood of the country districts to the towns. We are enabled to give some extracts from the poem, which is entitled "The Homestead." Appearing at this time, when the relation of the English farm labourer to the soil is being pressed forward, and in connection with the magnificent speech in the House of Commons, on Tuesday night, by Mr. Joseph Arch, the poem cannot but be greatly appre- ciated. The last four verses represent the condition of the American farm labourer, and the state at which the English labourer aims. Mr. Whittier begins by picturing the deserted and desolate home, and then describes the charms of country life :- 1 Against the wooded hills it stands, Ghost of a dead home, staring through Its broken lights on wasted lands Where old-time harvests grew. Unploughed, unsown, by scythe unshorn, The poor forsaken farm-lands lie, Once rich and rife with golden corn And pale green breadths of rye. Of healthful herb and flower bereft, The garden-plot no housewife keeps; Through weeds and tangles only left, The snake, its tenant, creeps. • . His track, in mould and dust of drouth, On floor and hearth the squirrel leaves ; And in the fireless chimney's mouth . His web the spider weaves.

So sad, so drear ! It seems almost Some haunting presence makes its sign; That down yon shadowy Jane some ghost Might drive its spectral kine. 0 home so desolate and bra! Did all thy memories die with thee? Were any wed, were any born, Beneath this low-roof tree? * * Did rustic lovers hither come? • Did maidens, swaying back and forth In rythmic grace, at wheel and loom, Make light their toil with mirth? Did child-feet patter on the stair? Did boyhood frolic in the snow? Did grey age, in her elbow chair, Knit, rocking to and fro? The murmuring brook, the sighing breeze.' • The pine's slow whisper, cannot tell; Low mounds beneath the hemlock trees - Keep the home secrets well. 0 wanderers from ancestral soil, Leave noisome mill and chattering store; Gird up your loins for sturdier toil, And build the home once more! * * • What matter if the gains are small That life's essential wants supply? -Your homestead's title gives you all That idle wealth can buy. All that the many-dollared crave, The brick-walled slave of Change and mart, Lawns, trees, fresh air, and flowers you have, More dear for lack of art. Your own sole masters, freedom-willed, With none to bid you go or stay, Till the old field your fathers tilled, As manly men as they! With skill that spares your toiling hands,' And chemic aid that science brings, Rfrlaim the waste and outworn lands, And reign thereon as kings!

" Owd Dick Chaddick" wur a feighter. He could ha' leathert "anybody Hazelwo'th, tho' ther mony a bigger an' stranger than he wur. 0' someheaw he'd a knack o' usin' his fists ut nob'dy else abeaut had. He'd larnt it off some chap i' Manchester ut geet his Hein' by feightin', an' what he could mak' eaut o' dark fleets, an' lonely roads. Dick would ha' knockt a chap's yead o' one side, an' put it straight again afore he could ha' felt th' blows, an' nob'dy Hazelwo'th dust cheep to him. He'd ha' gone eaut every Bethurday nest a elearin' tapreawms eaut, an' when he'd done that he'd gone i'th' middle o'th' green an' crow'd like a cock, an' then sung sammat abeaut bein' "Monarch of the deep." Well, he carried on this a while, till one neat "Jack o' Flunters" lest on him, an' Jack offered him a two-tkri pints ov ale for a lesson or two i' this new plan o' faightin'. So Dick gan him a lesson every nee, an' Jack took it up as weal as if he'd bin "born to it," as th' gam' cock said to th' red rag ut it had bin spurrin? at an heaur, thinkia' it wur another cock's yead. Dick said he'd mak' a mon car him if he'd nobbut be hard, for Jack wur strung and limber, if he didne' carry as mony guns as some lads. Ha stuck to his skooin' till his taieher said he thowt he'r larnt up; an' as a wakes-time wur cousin' on, he expected he'd do summat for r give th' skoo a good nante. Th' wakes-time coma ; an' soon after th' rashcart turned cant owd Dick war sees gooin' abeaut in a pair o' red breeches, as' white stockins', an' a white hat. wi' a ribbin reaand as broad as a sash. Folk knew theed be sumreat up afore lung when they seed Dick aailin' abeaut like a war- ship wi' red sides, en th' look eaut for summat o'th' same breed. They warno' far cant on't, for in absent an heanr after that he'd cleared th' "Gowden Ball" eaut, an' knockt a mon o'er a nut stondin', beside duckin' two broom-women in a trough; an' neaw he're gooin' to th' "Owd Bell" for to see what he could de theere, as it war a thrang shop. Well, he'd no sooner gotten i'th' lobby than he flung his hat i'th' middle i'th' tapreaum, an' sheauted mat for th' best mon ther wur to punce it back again. Ti' hat had hardly done rowlin! afore ther a foot went demi through th' creawn, as' jackets were off in a crack. "Well, I'll be summated I" Dick said, when he see'd it war Jack o' Planters at had made his hat into a pump- sacker—" I didno think therm dust ha' challenged thy mestlser, noather; but baize as tbeau has bin so bawd, tak' that, au' goo whows, as' let thy Mother see if hoo'll know tbee maw I've made thee a bit prettier." An' he hit Jack a bat reli' chops ut made one side swell eaut like a red pin- euskin, an' made him lest again th' fire-place as if he'd a notioa o' geohe up th' chirndy in a hurry. " Theigher," Jack said, when he'd getten to his balance, "I'm noane so handeosee ut I need be made feawer ;" an' he lest bouth flats fly like darts eaut of a dartgun. Thor a sheaut set up leand enoogh for t' ha' lifted th' ceilin' eaut ov its place, if ther hadneebin a lot o' women doancia upstairs. Owd Dick had gone (rant o'th seet as sudden as a twinkle o' leetenin, an' folk began o' lookin' for him under th' tables, when at th' same time he lee like a stricken too3d—his e'en gooin up like two owd pits ut han bin o'prrun wi' rushes. Heawever, he getkered bisect up as wed as he could, an' went at Jack agaig, but struck windily, as if he'd fergotten hew. Jack didno' want for t' hit him again, so he doanced rea.und, an' flustered: abeaut like a dandy cock, an' loot owd Dick mow away as lung as he could see, beaut hittin' owt softer than tit' Ewer or th' chissny-piece. At last 'tick geet owd ov his jacket, an' said he're fairly bvetteu ; but There one satisfaction abeau it—he'd taiched someb'dy heave tdo it. So they shook honds, an' ever sin' then they'n gone by th' names ov "Owd England" an' "Young Amerihy," though what's th' meanin' met I dunno know. Happen some wiseakkar con tell me. But ther's another way o' gettin one's own nose thrncht eant than by taichin someb'dy heaw to do it, an' that is by taichin nob'dy nowt. It may seem queer, but it's true for o' that, as I've seen A good sample on't i' one ov eaur neigh- bours, an' this is it. "Owd Square-yead," as we coed him, war a cute sort of a chap. He'd seen th' fruits o' taichin lads heaw to do men's work, an' lettin' other folk know as mich as therser. He're no gooin t' be a foo o' that brun (brand). Let him just get hosed o' summit wo'th keepin' to hissel' an' he'd tak good care nob'dy took it off him. Well, he geet a reed o' wark at wanted a good decal o' gaitin', and he're as fause as a boggart o'er it. Nob'dy must gas into th' loom-heausa, an' he'd vrhitewasht th' windows, so as they couldno' see through. No matter heaw anybody tried to suck him, owd Square-yead wouldna,' be sucked. He goat so at last at he'd hardly snake, for fear o' lettin' a word slip ut he shouldno' do; au' he began aslookin' as reausty as an owd barn-eawl nt's peaarcht by itsel' amung th' rafters till its forgotten what other eawls are like. For two year nob'dy ever poked their yeads i' his loom-heanse nobbut hissel'. If his own wife had tried t' aqueese her cap in, he'd ha' made doll-rags on't afore hoo could ha' batted her eon; an' ash' lads had laft whoam, ther' nob'dy else i'th heause. Well, as he'd show nob'dy nowt, nob'dy would show him nowt, an' one mat be sure th' wo'ld wouldno' stond still for two year. Things changed an' changed, but owd Square- yead wur th' same mon still, if it wurno' at ha geet moore eawlish. Heaw it coom abeaut 1 dunno' know, but o' some- heaw or other wayvia' began a-mendia, an eaur fowl bract- ened up SAMO as if it had been newly sceaured, an' polished wi' tirpitina ate lasere-wax. My owd rib actily brewed, an' for th' fast time sin' we're wed we began o' boxin' clooas. New setae o' werk sprang up at middlia' a' brms could be gotten on. We began a-singin' like birds, an' shuitlee rat- tled as merrily as if they'rn made for doencite. What we must ha' done if we'd o bin like owd fiquare-yead I dean° know, for wi' new aorta o' wark it war avrk'ard for one mon to Re'd eaut iaesi way o) gettin through it; so we helped one another. What one mon didno' know, happen someb'dy else ud find eaut, an' every loent-heause war like a little shoo, wi' one taichin' another. Owd Saware-yead wondered 'what wur up, as' kept cornice to th' dur a-peepin' an' hearkenie, same as if he're feeart snmtnat war gooia' on wrung. In a while we seed moors on him than we'd bin' used to, an' he began o' opperdn' his meanth to folk he hadne' spokken to for two year or moore. If he wondered what had come o'er us, we wondered at what had come o'er him, till one ci,y we see'd th' whitewash wur rubbed off th' Icesna-heause windows, an' his loom wur empty. A week went o'er—a fortnit—ate th' loom war empty still, and th' owd lad did nowt but walk abeawt th' fewt, though everybody else was as busy as "Trap's wife." One day he coom to me at th' side o'th gate, an' said— " Ab, what sort art wayvin' neaw ? " I towd him. " Wheay," he said, " that's same sort as I've bin wayvin', as' neaw I'm stopt. Hew* is it?" "Nay, heaw con I tell ?" I said. "To' should know th' best, for owt yo'n larnt yo'n kept to yorsele so conno' ha' wasted mich." ' e dropt his chin on t' his breast as sudden as if some- b'dy had hit him a seause at th' back o'th yead, an' I could see ut he're powderin' his brains abeaut summat. At last he said— " Heaw mich con thean wayve in a day ? " "Aeant five yard,* I said—"happen six wi' makkin a lung day." "Whey, I never could get through above three," he said; "an' neaw they'n stopt me becose other folk con do it boo ath better an' et:open Heaw is it, I wonder? " Well, it's happen this road," I said. " Yo'n kept yorsel' to Yorsele an' stuck to owd notions, as if ther'd never be any new uns born. We'n gett.n th new uns, an neaw yo 'r owd uns are wo'th nowt to noh'dy. Dunno' yo see?" " Yigh," he said, "I do. But heaw did yo' get hosed o' these new notions?" "By keepin' tk' loom heause windows clean, an' th' dur oppen," I said. "We ha' no bin within taicuin' one another. But as yo'n bin so close an' selfish, yo' wouldno' do for one ov eaur skoo. Yo'r nose is put cant, an' yo' may be con- tent wi' havin' it kept eaut till yo' thowt someb'dy owt to live beside yorsel'. But let me taich yo' this lesson, for it's one ut's bin towt eaur skoo,—a mon war never browt i'th' wo'ld to live by hissel'. If he had bin, he'd ha' had as mony legs an' arms as a earwig, an' as mony e'en as 'Sken- Din' Billy.' If everybody when they set eaut i' life would say--' Which way con Ibe o'th' nwoast use to thoose absent me? '—i'stead o'—' How con I mak thoose abeaut me o'th' moast use to me?"—things ad be different to what they are neaw. If a nose war pat oat then, we could lap it up l' flannel, put it in a glass case, an' lay it nicely by till it war ready for sniftin' th' air ov another an'—let us hope—a better wo'ld than we'n made this.—From Ben Brierley's Journal.

Armour, Free Church Minister, for a breach of the peace at an election meeting addressed by Mr. Dundas, at Sanday, Orkney, on November 24th, was concluded at Kirkwall on Saturday. A sentence of four day's imprisonment was im- posed. After being in prison seven hours he was released. He was followed to the Free Church manse by many hun- dreds of people. FALL OF HODSES.—FIVE PERSONS KILLED.—About 2-30 p.m. on Saturday a serious accident, whereby five persons lost their lives, occurred in Holloway-road, London. Four small dealer's shops were in course of demolition by a con- tractor, and the back part of the buildings bad been taken down. When the men left off work for the day the front walls abutting on the thoroughfare, which re,mained stand- ing, were protected by a hoarding. At half-past two, how- ever, the passers by and neighbouring shopkeepers were startled by the sudden collapse of the whole length of wall, which fell across the footway, carrying the hoarding with it. Five persons passing at the time, three women and two boys, were buried in the ruins. Two other persons, though net buried, were seriously injured by the falling bricks, and were taken to the Great Northern Hospital. AN OPPONENT OF iLICHARD lII.—A very interesting dis- covery has been made in the crypt of Winchester Cathedral, in which excavations are being carried on by the direction of Dr. Kitchen, the dean, to restore the crypts to their an- cient proportiens by removing modern accumulation of of earth. In a miss of masonry just under the ground arch of the fifteenth century Lady Chapel a leaden coffin, enclos- ing a wooden one, was found, and in the latter was the skeleton of Bishop Peter Courtenav, this fact being estab- lished by the coat of arms—three torteaux—at the foot of the cross cast on the coffin lid. This bishop, in the troubles of Richard M.'s reign, was a Lancastrian and an exile with his brother in the cause of Henry Tudor. After the battle of Bosworth they returned, and subsequently the bishop was translated from Oxford to Winchester. He died in 1492. He gave the great bell " Peter " (since re-cast) to Exeter Cathedral, and he was an ancestor of the present Earl of Devon. KAY'S ComPourrp, for Colic and Coughs. The two were indeed both called Lord, but their version honestly showed the difference by employing differ- ent type. The same was done in Psalm ex., "The Lord said unto my Lord," which was literally, "Jehovah said into my master or leader." Judge of his (Mr. Pilcher's) astonishment when he heard the lecturer quote that as Jehovah would come to his holy temple, and justified the false quotation by say- ing that the two words meant the same thing. The two persons mentioned under two differing names (one of which was applied only to Almighty God, the other only sometimes and more often to men; it was indeed the same words as Adonis) were according to that method of interpretation one. The Eternal was the promised master; the Sender was the person sent. That, to his mind, was a contradiction, not a mystery; a thing impossible and not merely unex- plained. A contradiction was that which went against reason; a mystery was that which was above the grasp of reason. It was a mystery how a blade of grass grew. It sprang forth and flourished and died down and in time re-appeared, and they knew no more of it at the end than they did at the begin- , ning. But if he was told that the farmer who plan- ted the grass was the grass, and the grass the man, it would be a contradiction and no mystery; against all reason but not above it. So, to say that Jehovah was to be the Messiah, the leader or master whom they sought, and the Messiah was Jehovah, was to disguise a contradiction in the garb of a mystery and to silence objections, and stay inquiries on false pretences. He cited that example, which came before him the previous Thursday evan- ing, because it exemplified a wrong method of study erising from p, Troll.; eenception of what scripture *AC It Was, however, the method of 81Vodeuborg. Having cited several passages in Swedenborg's own words, Mr. Pileher said it seemed to him that if his words meant anything they meant that the meaning of scripture was not to be taken from the words of scripture, and so attain to the general sense of the whole, bat that they were to take a meaning and put it into the words of scripture. Scripture, Mr. Pitcher want on to say, was the record of man's attempts to realize and to express divine truths, These attempts being human must share in human imperfectness. The seer did not always see clearly, and therefore as prophet did not always prophecy true things. Stu- dents well knew that there were several prophecies in the Old Testament that were never fulfilled. These and similar difficulties arising from the earthiness of the vessel, in which the divine treasure was contained must be allowed for and dismissed from consideration. If untrue they not only need not but ought not to be believed. Most Christians already in practice dealt thus with difficulties in the Bible, though they were shocked, or pretended to be shocked, when others proclaimed adherence to the theory. What educated man now believed in witchcraft, or in anointing with oil instead of sending at once for the doctor? If it be lawful to neglect or deny one portion of scripture it must be lawful, equally just reasons being at hand, to neglect or deny others. That idea of word for word inspiration—whether contradictions he forcibly held together by orthodoxy and labelled mysteries, or they be explained away into meaning something else, often very opposite—was fraught with mischief; opened up scripture to the play of ill-disciplined fancy; created uncertainty in matters which should be of all things most assured; and reduced religion to a thing Which no one could be expected to understand or to trouble with. He, therefore, claimed that scrip- ture be taken for what it was, men speaking to men, the of times speaking in halting human fashion; that men must be taken as having said exactly what they meant, and meant exactly what they said. All that was good in what they said would surely abide a benefit for all for ever. Let all that was not so good because untrue die out of males memories. Godha d witnesses before the Bible was thought of; has His witnesses in hearts and lands which the Bible has never reached, and would have them even if the Bible should ever be lost or destroyed.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

In addressing a cottager, the other evening, who has an extra large garden, which he finds to be a source of pleasure and profit, we remarked that we supposed he was like most gardeners, "frozen out." "Oh, no," was the reply, "for I left my hedge uncut so long as I could do anything on the ground, and before I finished the snow came, which forced me to start making a frame or two for raising such flowers as asters ard stocks and other things we sow in spring. They will also be useful for celery, cauliflowers, annettuce, and then I shall plant them with cucumbers; and I expect by the end of the year to clear enough to pay for the materials from the crops that I shall get out of them." From the ring of this cottager's utterances we feel sure that he has not overrated the value of these simple structures. The in- dividual referred to is but a labouring man, and had been some days out of employment in consequence of the inclemency f the weather, and but for his garden would, like many more, be driven to forced idleness. Men of this stamp are deserving of allotments at reason- able rents, either to supply their own family or to aug- ment their scanty earnings. We are glad to see evidence of willingness on the part of some landowners to concede land in small portions to the working classes. From our experience we find that allotments are turned to better account than those gardens attached to the dwelling- houses. In fact, there are numbers of the latter totally unca,red for, simply because their unwilling owners either have no time or taste to attend to them, and they would rather be without them; but as the locality of the house suits them, the presence of a garden is of little import- ance, and will give no after trouble or anxiety. When the surface of the ground is covered with snow, there are other odd jobs that will pay for attending to as well as frame making. Pea sticks should be secured, trimmed, and pointed; also stakes for different purposes may be made and painted, so as to be ready when required. A few tallies for writing the names of the different seeds that may be sown can be made readily by cutting lathes into about 6in. lengths, pointing one end to enter the ground, and smoothing the surface, which at the time it is required should have a little paint rubbed on with the finger pre- vious to writing upon it. In addition to the name, the date of sowing is frequently written on the labels. THE FRONT GARDEN.— Walk-edgings Continued.—Box was at one time so much in favour for edging;walks that a proposal to introduce any other material would have been scouted, and the demand for it was so great that it readily fetched 3d. per yard, or a few handfuls in bulk; so that any one having a good overgrown box edging found it profitable to take it up, re-plant, and sell the surplus, for one yard will plant several. But now box is scarcely ever asked for, and its use even) in good gardens, where it did not thrive, has been abandoned as too expensive an item. Gardens near towns :land in smoky districts required to have some portioi*of the box edging annually repaired, and when the yearly labour of trimming that which did grow is added to this, we are not surprised that it has lost favour. The method of laying box edging is similar to that described for thrift, only the earth at the back should be made firmer for the box, and the soil covering the roots:should also be firmly pressed with the foot; or, from the loose- ness of the soil, the roots would dry un, and the box would also be soon out of line. After all, when well laid and kept in order, box edging is always admired. Some of the Saxifragias are frequently used for edging walks in conjunction with stones, and have a pretty effect; they are most characteristic when house and garden are olci-fashioned. •If angular stones can be procured, they will answer better than more formal ones, and they neea not be of equal size. TAMA:LIVE, JAN. 13TH (VIA ADEN, JAN. 29TH).—A Con- lerence lasting three days has been held on board the Naiade, lor the purpose of negotiating terms of peace. A basis of lgreernent was arrived at. France waives her claim to a Protectorate, and also to a war indemnity. There is to be a Itrench Resident at the capital to watch external political laatters.. His powers are very clearly defined. Queen Ran- avalona is recognised by the French as Queen of Madagas- ear. The Malagasy Government pays £400,000 which the French agree to accept as a complete release, to cover 3.11 foreion claims before, during, and at the close of the War. France has a right to occupy the Bay of Diego Sau- te; with a three-mile limit ce land round the bay. Tama- tave is to remain in the occupation of the French until the .400,000 are paid. COLLISDN IN NEW YORK HARBOUR. A telegram from New York, dated Thursday, says that during a snowstorm the long boat of the Austrian corvette Donau came into collision with a tug in the North River. The boat capsized, and an Austrian midshipman and four Minors were drowned. WAR INDEMNITY DEMANDED BY BULGARIA, VIENNA, THURSDAY.— The Political Correspondence publishes intelligence from Bucharest to the effect that it is Positively stated there that M. Gueshoff, the Bulgarian delegate, will demand the payment of a war indemnity from Servia, and that Maddid Pacha will support this claim on behalf ef the Porte. DISTURBANCES IN POLAND. WARSAW, TRllRSDAY.—lntelligence received from Lub• lin states that disturbances, in the course of which several excesses were committed by the populace, have occurred at that place in consequence of the police having forced their livay into a Dominican monastery with the object of effect- ing a number of arrests. The military had to be summoned to restore order.

• A BREACH OF PROMISE CASE. £1,600 DAMAGES. At the Manchester Assizes, on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Day and a jury, the case of Howarth a. Taylor was heard. Th'e plaintiff was Maria Howarth, and the defen- dant, Albert Taylor. The action was brou2ht to recover damages for breach of promise of marriage. The defendant formally pleaded, firstly, that he had never agreed to marry the plaintiff; and secondly, that when he did so he believed the plaintiff to be a chaste woman, but found out she was nOt so. Mr. Addison, Q.C., M.P., Mr. Bradbury, and Mr. Sington appeared on behalf of the plaintiff; Mr. Bigham, Q.C., and Mr. Walton for the defendant. Mr. Addison said the real question for the jury to decide would be the amount of compensation which the plain- tiff ought to receive. The circumstances to which he would refer were not only painful to the plaintiff, but were in the ease of the defendant cruel and shabby. The plaintiff was about 25 er 26 years of age, and was the 'daughter of a per- son who for a long time carried on business as a butcher In King-street, Blackburn. She lost her father and mother in 187; and 1876, and after that she kept house for her brother, who continued the business of a butcher. Early in 1880 the defendant began to court her, apparently with a view to marriage. At that time he was a member of a firm of D. and W. Taylor, cotton spinners and manufacturers, Blackburn. but at the end of :the year the partnership was dissolved, and defendant was bought out for £lO,OOO. That money, the defendant afterwards said, he had tett in the business, an income of X.,500 a year being paid to him. The plaintiff's brother objected to the defendant paying his sister attentions, because Taylor was known to be " fast " But notwithstandin.g the brother's objection the defendant continued to pay his addresses to Miss Howarth, Somewhere about October the plaintiff went to Clayton-le- Moors tl fill a position as schoolmistress' for her brother was at that time about to be married. Before she went there, however, they had been on an expedition to Chat- ham, where the defendant seduced her. In January of 1881 ape found herself pregnant, and feeling that she could not retain her position as schoolmistress, she went off with him. They lived as man and wife in many of the watering-places of England, passing sometimes as Mr. and Mrs Howarth, and sometimes as Mr. and Mrs Taylor. After promising the plaintiff marriage he had taken her away from a situa- tion, lived with her as a husband for several years, and now deserted her and the children resulting from the in- timacy.. The defence was that no promise of marriage was given —that, in fact, the plaintiff, during the four years she had lived with the defendant, had never asked him to marry her. He had always been willing to support the chil-
dren. After nearly an hour's deliberation, the jury returned a verdict awarding £1,600 damages, the judge strongly con- demning the conduct of the defendant.

In the Queen's Bench Division, on Monday, Mr. Wyatt recovered £5OO damages from the Rosherville gardens Com- Pany for injuries inflicted upon him by a bear when he was on a visit to the gardens. THE MINISTERIAL CRISk• THE QUEEN SENDS FOR MR. GLADSTONE. A message from the Queen, summoning Mr. Gladstone to Osbotne, reached the right hon. gentleman shortly after midnight on Friday, Sir Henry Ponsimby. the bearer, bay- ing travelled to London by an unusually late train. sir Henry remained with Mr. Gladstone about half an hour. On Saturday afternoon Sir Henry Ponsonby again called at Mr. Gladstone's residence in Carlton House-terrace, and during the day several telegrams in Cypher passed between Mr. Gladstone and her Majesty through Sir Henry Pon- sonby. Mr. Gladstone also communicated with Lord Salisbury at Arlington-street, and later on received a visit from Sir Julian Pauncefort, chief permanent secretary at the Foreign Office, who laid before Mr. Gladstone important information in relation to foreign affairs. Lord Granville visited Mr. Gladstorie a few minutes after ten a.m., and was a constant visitor during the day. Lord Har- tington, to whom a messenger bad been despatched, arrived at half-past eleven, and remained over half an hour. THE JOURNEY TO OSBORNE : ENTHUSIASTIC PROCEEDINGS. Mr. Gladstone left Carlton House-terrace shortly after nine on Monday morning, on his way to Osborne, to have audience of the Queen. The right hon. gentleman, who looked in excellent health and spirits, drove to Waterloo Station, and travelled by the 9-30 ordinary train to Ports- mouth. The hour being early, there was no demonstration at Carlton House-terrace, but at Waterloo there was a con- sidarable gathering of people, who cheered Mr. Gladstone on his arrival and again when the train started. Mr. Her- bert Gladstone accompanied his father to Waterloo. At most of the stations where the train stopped crowds of people had assembled. At Surbiten and Woking there was loud cheering, and at Guildford Mr. Gladstone received a most enthusiastic welcome. He bowed his acknowledg- ments. The train reached Portsmouth soon after mid-day, and Mr. Gladstone was met at the station by a large and enthusiastic crowd. Notice had been posted at the Liberal Club intinuting the time of arrival, and many hundreds of Liberals thronged to the station Alderman Baker (chair- man of the Literal Association) was at the head of the party, and as accompanied by the Mayor and many active workers in the Liberal cause. As soon as the train was sighted running into the station cheering began, and was continued till the steamer left. Earlier in the morning arrangements had been made with the railway sucerinten- dent to facilate a deputation from the Liberal Association waiting on Mr. Gladstone, and accordingly when the passen- gers had left the train, Alderman Baker and his co-workers took up a position on board the steamer Victoria, and there awaited the arrival of Mr. Gladstone, who walked down the gangway accompanied by Flag Captain P. H. Colomb, and hat in hand, bowed his acknowledgements to the cheering crowd. An effort that was partially successful was made to force.the barrier through which the right honourable passed, and, as he neared the boat, Mr. Gladstone shook hands with many of those who crowded around him. On boarding the steamer he at once proceeded to the saloon, looking somewhat excited after such a reception. Here Alderman Baker introduced the Mayor, with whom the right honourable gentleman cordially shook bands, and then asked Mr. Gladstone to allow him (Alderman Baker) to de- tain him a few moment while, on behalf of the Liberals of Portsmouth, he, as their, president, expressed the loyalty to to him as their great leader and their admiration and res- pect for his character. Their hope and prayer for the future was, as it had been in the past, that the blessing of God might rest upon his labours for the commonwealth. Mr. Gladstone, in reply, said : I thank you personally very much, and wish through you to express my thanks tie my friends. My future will be a very short one, but I thank you very much. This is not a political visit, and I need say no more.—Mr. Gladstone was about to sit down in the saloon, when there were loud cries from the crowd for a speech. In response, Mr. Gladstone walked to the saloon door and bowed again and again. The steamer then moved off for Cowes.

div.p: -Ma: GLADSTONE ACCEPTS OFFICE

The Victoria reached Trinity Wharf, or what is popularly known as Her Majesty's landing stage, at East Cowes, at one o'clock, and Mr. Gladstone went ashore at once in a small launch. At Trinity Wharf a considerable crowd had assembled, and the right honourable gentleman was loudly cheered as he entered one of the royal carriages. The drive to Osborne House occupied only a few minutes, and imme- diately on his arrival Mr. Gladstone had an audience of Her Majesty, and undertook the formation of a Ministry. The ri..:ht honourable gentleman remained at Osborne two and a half hours, the greater portion of that time being passed with the Queen. At 3-30 p.m., after lunching, Mr. Gladstone left Osborne, and was driven back to the Queen's landing stage There be again received a cordial greeting, not only from those on shore, but from those who were leav- ing Cowes on board the ordinary steamer. The Qeeen had hoped Mr. Gladstone would have remained at Osborne the night, but he wished to return at once to London after his audience, in order to be present at his daughter's marriage on Tuesday. The passage to Southampton was very pleasant, and on reaching the Royal Pier a large number of persons greeted Mr. Gladstone. The right honourable gentle- man at once entered the train, which moved off towards the town station, where another demonstration awaited him. The platform was crowded to excess, and there was loud cheering, but Mr. Gladstone did not attempt to speak, 'and simply bowed his acknowledgments. He travelled the whole distance to London alone, the only incident being a hostile demonstration at Basingstoke, where another crowd had assembled, and where the groaning was decidedly in the ascendant. Waterloo was reached at a quarter to eight o'clock. Numbers of people had previously gathered on the arrival platform, and Mrs. Gladstone was waiting in a car- riage. As the train drew up, loud cheers were raised, and the cheering was renewed when Mr. Gladstone alighted from his compartment, and, bat in hand, bowed his way through the crowd to his carriage. He at once drove away with Mrs. Gladstone to Carlton House-terrace, and on arriving there received a visit from Earl Granville, who had pre- viously been in consultation with Earl Spencer. STATEMENTS IN PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY.

The House met at 4-15, and shortly afterwards began to fill on both sides as well as in the galleries reserved for ladies until it assumed quite an animated appearance. The Earl of Carnarvon,the Earl of Aberdeen, Lord Tweed- mouth, and Lord Sandhurst took the oath and shook hands with the Lord Chancellor. Shortly before the half-hour the Prince of Wales and the Duke of Cambridge took their accustomed seats on the front cross bench. The Marquis of SALISBURY, amid loud cheers from the Ministerial benches, said: I have simply to state that her Majesty's Government, the late Government—l don't know what to call it—(laughter)—has resigned, and her Majesty had been graciously pleased to accept that resignation. I understand that Mr. Gladstone has gone down to Osborne, and has accepted the task of forming a Government. Under these circumstances I have to move that your lordships do adjourn till Thursday. The motion was at once agreed to, and the House ad- journed at 4-33. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 4-0. Nearly half an hour was occupied by the introduction of private bills, amongst those introduced and read a first time being the Clitheroe Railway Bill and Water Company's Bill, and Ormskirk Railway Bill. On the motion of Sir C. FonsTEE, no noticed of motion were given. DUAL REPRESENTATIvF,s.—As soon as the private busi- ness was disposed of, Mr. J. REDMOND moved that a new writ should issue for the election of a member for the borough of Galway in the room of Mr. T. P. O'Conner, who had also been returned and had elected to sit for the borough of Liverpool (Scotland Division.)—Tbe motion was agreed to, as was also another by the same hon. mem- ber —that a new writ should issue for the Queen's County (Ireland), Ossory Division, for the election of a member in lieu of Mr. A. O'Connor, who had also been returned and had elected to sit for the county of Donegal (Eastern Division.) MR CHILDERS —Mr. Childers, who was introduced by Mr. Trevelyan and Mr. Breston Bruce, then took the oath and his seat. The right hon. gentleman, who was cheered by the Liberal members, at once took his seat on the frent Opposition Bench, where Sir Wm. Harcourt, Mr. Chamber- lain, Mr. Mundella, and Lord R. Grosvenor were now pre- sent. THE RESIGNATION OF MINISTERS.—Tho CHANCELLOR Of the EXCHEQUER said: I have to state to the House tbat her Majesty has been graciously pleased to accept the resigna- tion of her Minister, and consequently we now only hold office until our successors are appointed. lam further in- formed that her Majesty has been pleased to require the at- tention of the right bon. gentleman the member for Midlo- thian at Osborne, and that the right hon. gentleman has kissed hands on receiving her Majesty's commands to form an Administration. At his request I beg to move that the House at its rising do adjourn to Thursday next. —The motion was agreed to, and the House adjourned at 4-35. THE NEW CABINET. On Wednesday night it wae stated that during the day Mr. Gladstone had been occupied in reconciling certain gentlemen designated for his Cabinet to the pests allotted to them, and that early in the evening he had the satisfaction of knowing that he had at length completed an unusually arduous and anxious task. In the course of the evening it was stated "on high authority " that Mr. Chamberlain will appear in the new Cabinet as Secretary of State for the Colonies, that Mr. Mundßlla has accepted the post of Presi- dent of the-Board ef Trade with a seat in the Cabinet, that Mr. Hilbert has accepted office, and that Mr. Arnold Mor- ley will be the new Patrona,e Secretary to the Treasury.
