THE CHANGE OF dt :RNMENT. Shortly before eleven o'clock on Thursday morning Lord Rosebery, the new Foreign Secretary, drove to Earl Gran- ville', and had an interview of 25 micutes' duration with the noble earl. Lord Rosebery subsequently called upon Mr. Gladstone, who at the time was engaged with Lord Richard Grosvenor. Lord Roaebery remain-A at Mr. Gladstone's a quartcr of an hour, and then drove in the direction of Picca- dilly. A few minntes later Sir William Harcourt walked to Mr. Gladstone's, and was followed by Mr. Osborne Morgan, the latter remaining only a very short time. Lord Spencer also bad interviews with Mr. Gladstone and Lord Granville, and Mr. Muudella saw the new Colonial Secretary for a few minutes. Several appointments to minor offices were made on Thursday. They included Mr. J. T. Hibbert to be Parlia- mentary Secretary to the Admiralty, and Mr. H. H. Fowler to be Financial Secretary to the Treasury. Mr 0. Morgan was offered an Under Secretaryship, but he was compelled to decline office at present in consequence of certain per- sonal considerations. It was arranged on Thursday night, that the members of the late Cabinet will proceed to Oshorne to-day (Saturday), to deliver up their seals of office.

CONSTABLE. The Mieroa proposed the adoption of the minutes of the Watch Commintee, which contained the following recom- mendation :—" That the Council be recommended to in- crease the salary of the Chief Constable from £250 to £3OO pelt annum, such increase to take effect from the 25th March, 1886." Councillor BROADBENT seconded the proposition. He wished to say that since the last meeting he had heard complaints with reference to obstructions in Bridge-street. The obstructions were caused sometimes by a cart lead of coa's being upset in the streets, and sometimes by hand- carts being left standing an unreasonable length of time in the street. He had no doubt that attention would he paid to the matter. There was a recommendation in the minutes that the salary of the Chief Constable be raised from £250 to £3OO a year. The subject had been twice considered by the Watch Committee, and the recommendation had been carried unanimously. He had heard that there might be some objection to the proposed increase. He was not, con- sidering the present depressed state of trade, sur- prised at that, but he believed that if an increase of salary was due anywhere it was due to the Chief Constable of Warrington, who had served them so long and so faithfully. If the salary was increased to the amount proposed it would certainly not be above the average rate of salaries paid to Chief Constables in neighbouring boroughs and having command of such large forces as the force. that was under the control of Mr. Hunt. He did not think that it was necessary to say anything as to the value of the services of the Chief Constable, or as to his extremely up- right and conscientious conduct on all occasions (Hear, hear.) If there was any difference of opinion as to the action of the Watch Committee in this particular he was quite sure that any discussion that might follow would be conducted with the feeling that he had expressed—of respect and appreciation for the services of the Chief Con- stable. Alderman TIOLMES proposed an amendment to the effect that the recommendation of the Watch Committee regard- ing the salary of the Chief Constable be not agreed to. He entirely concurred with all that Mr. Broadbent had said with respect to the esteem in which they all held Mr. Hunt, as regarded the services he had rendered, and the manner in which he had conducted the duties of the office that he held. The only ground on which he opposed the recom- mendation was that the state of trade in Warrington, and all over the country, was so bad that the wages of nearly every artizan were now being reduced. It was only that day that they saw that a large manufacturing concern near Warring- ton had imposed a reduction of from 30 to 40 per cent., and other reductions were also mentioned. In the face of that, he asked, how could they go to the ratepayers, who were suffering from reductions, to raise the salaries of officers of the Corporation? For that reason he felt bound to oppose the proposed increase of salary. Councillor JOHN PIESPOINT seconded the amendment. He said that he thought that Alderman Holmes had suffi- ciently explained the reason why salaries should not be in- creased during the present depressed state of trade. He thought that they would not be doing their duty to the ratepayers generally if they granted the increase at a time when every one was endeavouring to meet their require- ments in trade by a reduction in wages not only among the artizans, but among the clerks. He could, as far as his knowledge went, speak of Mr. Hunt as a most worthy and deserving man, and he felt sure that the explanation given by Alderman Holmes would be accepted by the Chief Con- ( stable without the slightest feeling. Councillor SUTTON said that he thought it very improb- able that the recommendation of the Council would he car- ried. He was, under the circumstances, sorry that the Watch Committee proposed it, because it was a very difficult mat- ter, when they respected a man as they did Mr. Hunt, to oppose the resolution, but, at the same time, it was perhaps a more difficult matter to support such a resolution when the trade of the borough was so very bad, and when there were at the time so many suffering people in the town. He hoped that the committee would see their way to withdraw tVt minute and not let it go to the vote. Councillor W. PIERPOINT said thet the recommendation was really one emanating from the committee alone. No application had been made by Mr. Hunt. He believed that Mr. Hunt prided himself upon the fact that from his first connection with the borough to the present time, he had never solicited any advance of salary. That made Mr. Hunt stand very high in his opinion, but he was glad to see that members of the Council were inclined to study econo- my. He would suggest that the money required should be made up by putting an extra cost on the gas bills—(taugh- ter)—and that the Market Committee should not spend so much on an office; thereby, he thought, sufficient money would he saved to allow of the salary of Mr. Hunt being raise& Alderman CROSPIELD said that he should not like any division to take place on the matter. He had a great re- spect for Mr. Hunt. He thought him an admirable man , for his position, and had times been better he should have I been glad to vote for the increased salary. As matters were, ' however, he thought it unfortunate that the proposition should have come before the Council. He did not agree with the last speaker that the amount might be made up by !increasing the price of gas—(laughter and cries of "no ") because he thought that the gas was dear enough as it was, and not 'half good enough. He thought that it would he better for the committee to withdraw the resolution. It would hurt him to vote against it. bct he felt that he should , be bound to do so. Councillor JOLLEY said that, as a member of the commit- tee, seeing that the proposition was uot likely to be carried, he agreed with Councillor Sutton that the wisest course would be to withdraw the resolution. Councillor BROADBENT said that it was gratifying that there was only one opinion amongst the Council of their appreciation of the services and the merits of the chief con- stable. If the matter came to a division they would under- stand that those who voted for and against the increase equally appreciated the services of the chief constable, and that it was only on the ground of depression of trade that some of them did not feel it right to support the resolution. At a future time, if trade was better, they would no doubt be able to do so. Councillor GREENING said that he should have been de- lighted to have the salary of Mr. Hunt increased, but he had made up his mind that the present was not the time to increase the salaries of corporate officials. After a little more discussion it was decided, on tne mo- tion of Alderman HOLMES, seconded by Councillor Frame- ING, that the question be referred back to the committee. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. This committee recoinniended that the follbwing plans be approved :—Of new porch to Mission Chapel. Bank Quay; of alteration to property in Egypt-street for the Co-opera- tive Society. Councillor BROADBENT moved, and Councillor SUTTON seconded, that these minutes be adopted, which was agreed to without discussion. SANITARY COMMITTEE.—SNOW IN THE STREETS. The minutes of the Sanitary Committee only contained recommendations for the payment of certain accounts. Councillor SUTTON moved, and Councillor GuimeiNo seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Alderman Hohatas asked who was responsible for the cleaning away Of the snow in front of houses. He had spoken to the police about it, but he said it was not a police duty. He (Alderman Holmes) understood it was the duty of the inhabitants to see that the snow was cleared away in front of their premises, but it was well that they should know. The MAYOR understood it was the duty of the occupier of a house or shop to see that the footpath in front was clean and passable. The Towle CLERK: That is so. . Alderman CROSFIELD : Supposing they do not do so? The MAYOR: Then they are liable to prosecution. Alderman WEBSTER thought the Corporation were the greatest, offenders. The occupiers did as a rule clean the snow away from the front of their premises, but the Cor- poration did net do anything. Alderman CROSFIELD: Then it is the duty of the police to sue the Corporation. I should like to see that done (Laughter.) The minutes were then adopted, PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.--.TENDERS. This committee recommended the acceptance of the following tenders :—Messrs. Hough and Son, for the labour in forming and paving Arpley-street, Thynne-street, and Jolley-street, and for the forming and tiling of White-street, be accepted; that the tender of Messrs. John Nunnerley and Co., Limited, for 1,200 tons of bur ?tone delivered at Whitecross Wharf, Bank Quay, at 2s 31ed per ton, and 800 lineal yards of curbs at 2s 9d per yard, be accented; that the tender of Messrs. Clare and Ridgway, for 120 tons of Rawtenstall setts at 10e 4d per ton, be accepted; that the tender of Mr. Simnel Cooper, of Newry, Tor 400 tons of granite cubes, at 16s per ton, be accepted; that the tender , of Mr. William Bennett, of Cairo-street, for 50,000 chequered tiles at 72s 6d per 1,000, be accepted. Councillor BROWN moved the adoption of the minutes, and referring to the state of Knntsford-road, said that the deputation had been to Chester to see the County Surveyor, and from what took place, he thought everything would be i done satisfactorily. (Hear, hear.) Councillor ASHTON seconded. Councillor BROADBENT said he thought they must all have remarked the dreadful state of the roads and streets In the town that were macadamised, and he thought they must almost come to the conclusion that the worst possible kind of roads in Warrington were the macadamised. (Hear, hear.) He thought that it was advisable for the committee, wherever practieable, and whenever they had the means, to L as far AS possible replace the macadam with sett paving. (Hear, hear, and "No.") ' Alderman WEBSTER : Except in Bridge-street. Councillor FLEMING said it would be a good job if Fennell-street was paved with setts instead of huge boulders. It was in a disgraceful state. . Councillor DIXON said the Surveyor of one town he had been in told him that they used steam-rolled macadams in their main streets and setts in their side streets. The macadam was better for the horses. 1 The MAYOR said he was satisfied that macadam roads were most expensive. Perhaps it would surprise them that when Bridge-street was rolled by steam the other night it

HOUSE OF LORDS.—THIIRSDXY. The Lord Chancellor (Lord Haisbury) took his seat on ' the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. "there was.a good attendance of peers. The Earl of Milltown and several other noble lords took the oath and subscribed to the roll of Parliament.—The Marquis of SALISBURY: My Lords, I understand it is wished that the House should adjourn until Monday, but there is judicial business which makes it neces- sary that we should meet to-morrow. I move that the House do now adjourn.—The motion was agreed to, and their Lordships adjourned at 25 minutes to five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THIJRSDAY. • The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. To-day the• Liberals occupied the Government side of the House, the Conservatives going over to the OppoAtion Benches. ' MOTIONS POSTPONRD.—Mr. Bradhuigh postponed his motion with reference to labour statistics until the 2nd of March, and Mr. Picton postponed until the same day the motion standing in his name relative to the revenues of the , Established Church. NEW WRITS. • On the motion of Mr. Arnold Morley, who was received with cheers, new writs were issued as follow :—For the county of Edinburgh, in the room of the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, who had accepted the office of First Commis- sioner for executing the office of Treasurer of the Exchequer of Great Britain and Lord High Treasurer of Ireland. (Cheers.) New writs were also obtained on behalf of ether , ministers. ADJOURMIENT.—Mr. A. MOIZLEY moved that the House ' at its rising adjourn until Saturday at three o'clock.—Sir M. HICKS-BEACH: I am anxious to express the hope that the Secretary to the Treasury will on Saturday be able, for the convenience of hon. members, to inform the House on what ; day it is intended to proceed to business. (Hear, ear.)—Mr. ! A. MORLEY: Yes, I will. 1 The House then adjourned.
MR. GLADSTONE'S ADDRESS TO THE ELECTORS OF MIDLOTHIAN.

--- - The Press Association has received- a copy of the fol- lowing address to be issued by the Premier on seeking re- election : Gentlemen,—Having received the commission of Her Majesty to form a Government, and 'having personally accepted the office of First Lord of the Treasury, I have once more to solicit a renewal of the trust which little more than two months ago you confided to me with so marked an expression of the sentiments of the constituency. I need not now, as in September last, trouble you with another lengthened exPosition of my views either on Liberal policy at large or on those grave questions affecting Ire- land, the approach of which it was not difficult to discern, and which have since come into the first rank of political interest. I see no cause to modify any leading declarations of my last address, either on pending subjects of British legislation or on the basis and the necessary limits of a policy for Ireland. I had earnestly hoped that the late Go- vernment might have been enabled to make proposals adequate to the needs of the sister island, but at the moment when an issue altogether separate put an end to the exist- ence of that Ministry it had become evident that this hope must be abandoned. There were three great Irish questions demanding our care —social order, the settlement of tha land questiom, and a widely prevalent desire for self-government, extending be- yond what is felt in great Britain, as to local affairs, but necessarily subject in all respects to the law of Imperial unity. It was made plain last week that while °all ideas of local government for Ireland receded farther and farther into the distance, and while on this very ground it was hardly pos- sible to hope for any enlarged handling of the land question, the one broad proposal with which Parliament was to be in- vited to deal was a renewal of special and restrictive pro- visions for the criminal law of Ireland. This was to be the question of the hour, perhaps the work of the ses- sion. It will be among the very first duties of the new Govern- ment to use its official opportauities for forming such an estimate, as only a Ministry can form, of the social state of Ireland. especially with regard to crime, to the fulfilment of contracts, to the pressure of low prices upon agriculture, and to personal liberty of action. The course of policy, as a whole, cannot be considered without reference to this examination; but, beyond all doubt, the hope and purpose of the new Government in taking office is to 'examine care- fully whether it is sot practicable to try some other method of meeting the present case of Ireland, and ministering Colts wants, both social and political, some method more safe and more effectual, going nearer to the source and seat of the mischief, and offering more promise of stability, than the method of separate and restrictive criminal legislation. To this task we shall address ourselves under a profound sense of the responsibility which in this free country weighs upon the people of the three kingdoms, hut which is es- pecially concentrated upon the advisers of the Crown Where so many risks and obstacles beset the path, we shall not lightly count upon a favourable issue, but we have no eoubt as to the great principles which should guide our course, and we shall draw comfort from the belief that we are engaged in a work of peace. I remain, gentlemen, your faithful and grateful servant, W. E. GLADSTONE. London, February 4th, 188f3.

GOLBORNE- A NEGLIGENT COLLIER.—At the Newton Pet,y Sessions on Saturday, Thomas Broadhurst, a collier at Golborne. was summoned by Mr. Nicholson, relieving officer for the Leigh Union, for neglecting to maintain his wife, at present -con- fined in the lunatic asylum.—The defendant did not appear, and the case was adjourned. TBErr OF JIIGS.—At the Widnes County Police Court, Thomas Carrell, collier, Bamfurlong, was charged with stealing two jugs of the value of 9d, the property of James Acker% landlord of the Bamfurlong Hall Hotel.—The Bench said the prisoner had done a very foolish thing. and he would have to pay a fine of 10s. CHoßax.• SOCIETY'S CONCERT.—The first concert in the Edge Green Primitive Methodist Chapel, Golborne, under the auspices of the Golborne and District Choral Society, was given on Wednesday week. Nothwithstanding most unfavourable weather there was a good attendance, and the various selections were highly appreciated. THROWING SNOWBALLS—At the Newton Town Hall on Saturday, James Bate, a lad, was summoned for throwing snowballs at a man named Davies at Golborne on the 18th January. THE GAS METERS. The Gas Committee reported that during the month prior ; to the 15th January the average illuminating power of the gas had been equal to 19 candles at both works. Alderman flotztEs moved. and Alderman WEBSTER seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Alderman CRosErEDD asked the chairman of the Gas Committee whether the pressure at the gas works was always the same, and said he should also like to ask whether it was possible for any air to get into the pipes and pass through the meters and be charged as gas. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He had great doubt himself about the meters registering gas properly. (Hear, hear.) He thought it was very queer indeed that there should sometimes be an in- creased charge when less gas had been consumed. He wished to know by what method, if there was any method, by which one could test the accuracy of the meter. Hear, hear.) Councillor W. PIEREOINT said that as regarded one of the accounts to which he referred at the last meeting, the party had been threatened that if he did not pay the account a certain surgical operation would be carried out. (Laugh- ter.) If the chairman of the Gas Committee would pro- nounce that that surgical operation would not be carried out he would give notice- The MAYOR: It is for the committee to decide. Councillor W. Pauronrr asked if Aldermar Holmes would give a promise. Alderman Houuss said there was no objection, but they had considered the case referred to very carefully, and they had no doubt that the charge was right. Councillor W. PIERPOINT was proceeding to make some further remarks, when The Tows CLERK said it was entirely irregular; but Councillor Pierpoint could give a personal explanation. Councillor W PIEREOINT said the Council did not quite realise the position he was in. He bad had two accounts I placed in his hands, and had taken up the matter, and if he had not withdrawn his motion at the last meeting there was no doubt he should have carried it, and the parties would have been protected. He considered the Gas Committee had treated him badly. Councillor GREENING said he should like to know in what way the Gas Committee had treated Councillor Pier- point badly. The MAYOR: I am obliged to rule Councillor Greening out of order. Councillor GREENING: I will it down, but Ido not like to hear such statements. The Melon : Mr. Councillor Pierpoint has hispemedy in law against the Gas Committee. Councillor W. PIERPOINT It is the law I object to; I want the law held in suspension for another month. The MAYOR again said the discussion was out of order. Councillor BROADBENT asked whether it was the duty of the Gas Committee or of individual consumers to supply meters with water. The previous night, at his own house, the gas went out at six o'clock for want of water. He also thought more attention should be given to the washing of the gas lamps. He did net know whether the lamps were as dirty in the centre of the borough as they were on the outskirts. Councillor BOLTON asked how it was that Councillor W. Pierpoint was out of order, while Councillor Broadhent and Alderman Crosfi,ld were allowed to speak on matters not on the minutes. (Hear, hear.) (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR wished Councillor Bolton's remarks had not been so general and more specific, so that he might have known in what instances the rule had been departed from.

Alderman HOurns, in replying to questions, explained that the pressure at the gasworks was not so great in the day time as it was towards evening. Respecting the testing of the meters, he said that when any consumer was dissatisfied with his account of the gas consumed, and he thought there was something wrong with his meter, he could take it to the gasworks to be tested. Bupposing,. however, the con- sumer was not satisfied with the decision, he could send the meter to the Government Inspector at Manchester or Liver- pool. If it was found that the meter was not right and registered against the consumer' the expense of the inspec- tion would be borne by the Gas Committee ; but if the ver- dict of the Gas Committee given in first place was found to be correct, then the expense would be borne by the con- sumer. Another question had been asked about air getting into the meters and being charged for as gas. On the gas being turned on in the afternoon a quantity of air rushed through until they came to the gas, and he understood from Mr. Paterson that air was not charged as gas when passing through the meter the time it occupied being so small as to be hardly worth discussing. Mr. Broadbent had asked a question about the gas lamps not being sufficiently cleaned. That was a complaint that had been frequently made in that Council, and he dared to say that the lamps were not always as clean as they should be. A staff of men was kept for the purpose of keeping the lamps clean, but they were not always able to keep up with the lamps as they got dirtied. As to the water in the meters, when, the gas in- spector went round to take the register he generally attended to that matter; but of course there were cases where water might be required in the interval, and the consumers should attend to that. The minutes were then adopted. COUNCILLOR DIXON AND THE GAS METERS. Alderman HOLMES ..called attention to the statement made by Mr. Councilor Dixon at the Council meeting held on the 6th January, 1886, having reference to the accurate

working of gas meters, and to move a resolution thereon. The Council would remember, he said, that at their last meting Councillor Dixon in a speech he then made said : —" A great waste of gas took place in consequence of meters being put in by persons who were not licensed to do so, and it Was his opinion that if the persons who put in meters were licensed to do the work, they would not have ' the large amount of defective fittings they had at the pre- sent time. Only that morning he went into the office at leivet peel where the meters were tested, and he had some conversation with the person in charge, who informed him liteat a great many of the meters which had been brought in registered very heavily against the consumers. He thought he would ask the person in charge that question, as during the last two years a large number of meters had passed out of the hands of the Gas Committee, end when any complaints were made about the consumption of gas they were fetched beck and returned without anything being said. He was sure that he for one was paying more than VI- per cent. for his gas than he ought to do, as a large amount of atmospheric air got into the gas which went through the meter, and was registered as gas, and he had to pay for the atmospheric air which the Gas Committee sent daily through the meter." The Com- mittee felt astonished at that statement, and a letter was sent to Liverpool to inquire whether Mr. Dixen's statement was correct, and the following reply was received :—•• Town Clerk's Office, Municipal Buildings, Live pool, 2nd Febru- ary, 1888. I beg to inform you that I have already made inquiries on this matter, and the facts, as reported to me by my assietant (Mr. Bellamy), are as follows, viz.:-e-That Mr. Dixon (who was directed to Mr. Bellamy from hey office) asked him for the rough percentage of meters rejected, and in reply he was informed that there was scarcely a case on record of a meter submitted to us for examination by the censumer which had been found to register in favour of the Gas Company. It would, therefore, appear that Mr. Dixon was, to say the least of it, under a grave misapprehensien. That was a letter which had come from the Town Clerk's office at Liverpool, and was endorsed by the official signa- ture of the Town Clerk. He (Alderman Holmes) thought that was a sufficient answer to the statement Councillor Dixon made that day month, and he must leave him to ex- plain it away as best he could. If Councillor Dixon could explain it to the satisfaction of the Council he should be very glad, but if be could not he thought they should re- quest Mr. Dixon to withdraw the statement. (Hear, hear.) The Mayon having asked Councillor Dixon if he wished to make an explanation, some discussion took piece as to whether the matter was properly before the Council. Councillor BOLTON asked where was the motion? The MAYOR: There is really no motion. Councillor BOLTON: Then what are we discussing ? Councillor ROBERTS said it seemed that that matter was a personal dispute between the Chairman of the Gas Com- mittee and a member of the Council. He submitted that the whole thing was irregular. Alderman WEBSTER : There is no such thing as a per- sonal feeling between the'Chairman of the Gas Commi:lee and Councillor Dixon.
Councillor ROBERTS: I did not say there was. Alderman WEBSTER : You said it was a personal ques- tion between the two.

Counciller ROBERTS: I did not say so. Alderman HoutEs then proposed that Councillor Dixon be requested to withdraw his staterneut. Alderman WEBSTER seconded. After some further animated discussion, Councillor DIXON said his explanation was that when be went to the gas office at Liverpool he said to the man, "Do von ever find any meters registering against consumers ?" *He replied " Yes." If the members of the Council wanted to go further he would refer them to an article in the Globe newspaper. Some few years ago a discussion took place, and a manager of a London gas works said distinctly to the ratepayers and to the readers of that paper that there were meters which registered against the consumers. He would put it to the chairman of the Gas Committee whether or not he would report the gain made on gas registered as having been consumed over and above what was made. He based that on what he bad been told by a late gas manager, who told him that at St. Helens there was a gain on the quantity registered by meter, after making all allowaßce. (Laughter.) Some raembers were proceeding to further discuss the matter, when The MAYOR said they could not make Councillor Dixon withdraw his statement, and he declared the clisnission closed. The proceedings then terminated.

At the weekly meeting of the American Parnell Fund many fresh contributions were anuounced. The contribu- tions now amount to $48,000. THE CURTIN DasTunamvoes.—About seventy poiiA. pro- ceeded to Fines Chapel, county Kerry, on Sunday, under Mr. McDermott, R.M., in anticipation of a possible disturb- ance. No disturbance occurred, however, and the police were withdrawn about one o'clock. Irina FARMERS AND THEIR LABOURERS.—The relations of farmers and their labourers in some parts of Ireland are becoming as embittered as those of landlord and tenant, be- cause of the efforts which are being made to carry out the provisions of the Labourers Act. Applications made to the Kilrush Board of Guardians for the erection of cJttaees were uniformly opposed by the farmers concerned, and some of the labourers who were in attendance" condemned them- selves for having backed a selfish lot in past years." BOYCOTTING.—At a meeting of the Limerick City Branch of the National League on Saturday night, the Mayor inti- mated that he had received word from the Executive to dis- countenance boycotting. This was no time to boycott any Irish trader.—A resolution of confidence in Mr. Parnell and ' his party was passed, also a resolution calling on the Cor- poration of Limerick to change "the anti-Irish nomencla- ture of the principal thoroughfaies of the city," and another recommending the Corporation to employ no more police pensioners. ADVICE TO IRisHmEN.—The Freeman's Journal expresses the hope that the advice given by Mr. Sexton and other leaders of the National League at Tuesday's meeting will be read throughout the length and breadth of Ireland, and that the determination of the people to abide by that advice will be keen and intelligent. Every word and act that can be distorted into an illegality are, it remarks, greedily caught up and manipulated for English reading, and every foolish threat, every wrongful and criminal proceeding, is SO much harm done to the National cause, and operates by so much in diminishing the influence of the Irish party and the power of their friends in the British Parliament to bring to a peaceful termination the international struggle. MOONLIGHTERS AT WORK.—Reports have been received in Tralee that naoonlighters are nightly abroad in different parts of Kerry. A few nights ago a large armed party visited several houses at Crotta. About eight o'clock in the evening they entered Mr. Fuller's kitchen. Without the slightest protest Mr. Efdler surrendered his arms. They next proceeded to the house of Mr. Barton, when the family were in bed. The party knocked loudly, and at the sum- mons Mr. Barton came downstairs. One of the men de- manded his arms, and threatened him with " the same as Curtin got," if he did not give them up quietly. Mr. Bar- ton refused, and his son took his gun in his hand, which he put at full cock. The click evidently attracted the atten- tion of the men outside, as immediately afterwards one of the men fired a shot through the kitchen door. The shot knocked plaster off the kitchen wall, and fell opposite Mr. Barton on the stairs. The gang then decamped. Next day the police visited the house and found that the Bartons had taken every precaution necessary to defend their lives and protect their property. A party of Moonlighters, number- ing ahout ten, armed with guns and disguised, have also I visited two houses a few miles to the west of Tralee, and succeeded in obtaining firearms and money.

THE WRECK OF THE Hunso's —Captain B. Versey and nine of the survivors of the British ship Hudson, of Glas- goy, were landed on Wednesday at Plymouth. The Hud- son capsized 120 miles south of Blettingburgbs Bay during a terrific gale, and 15 of the crew were drowned. The sur- vivors were pulling about at sea for 60 hours before they were picked up.

ATITYPTED WIFE MMIDER.—A young man named Frederick Meliars has been sentenced at the Lincolnshire Assizes to ten years' penal servitude for attempting to mur- der his wife. The woman was employed at an hotel in Great Grimsby, and the prisoner, after purchasing a revolver and ammunition, went to the hotel and fired point-blank at his wife's head, hut the bullet went too high and only pene- trated her hat. In returning their verdict the jury expressed themselves in strolig terms against the present unrestricted sale of revolvers.

GREAT SNOWSTORMS IN YORKSHIRE. Richmond has experienced a succession of snowstorm, accompanied by boisterous winds. The snoWdrifts are of great depth. On the way to the racecourse from Richmond the drifts are higher than the walls and hedgerows, and on Monday the racehorses were unable to'get near the high training grounds. The teams, however, managed a couple of hours' exercise on a portion of the road which had been partially cleared by a sledge drawn by four horses. The travellers who started from Richmond into the country on Monday were com- pelled to return. DARING BURGLARY.— Early on Saturday morning it was discovered that the residence of Mr. James Francis Grantham, Lorr House, Stilton, had been broken into. The house was thoroughly ransacked. In the library every desk and drawer had been forced. In the drawing•room, after breaking open the different cupboards, the burglars made a desperate attempt to force an iron safe, containing a consi- derable amount of valuable property, but, failing in their attempt, they left, leaving behind them a jimmy, crowbar. sledge hammer, and other housebreaking tools. The pro- perty stolen consisted principally of silver plate, which was valued at between £5,000 and £6,000. DINNER PARTY AT MARLBOROUGH HorsE.—The Princet of Wales gave a dinner party on Wednesday nisht at Marl- borough House. There was a large number of guests, in- cluding the French and German Ambassadors, the Dale of Bedford, the Duke of Westminster, the Belgian and United States Ministers, the Lord Chancellor, the Marquis of Salis- bury, the Marcptis of Hartington, Mr. Gladstone, Lords ißosebery, Granville, Spencer, Iddesleigh, Napier of Mag- i dela. and Randolph Churchill, the Speaker, Mr. Goschen. Mr. Chamberlain, Sir Henry James, Mr. Cecil Raikes, and Mr. Edward Stanhope. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach was un- avoidably prevented from being present. ~.... . LIFE WITHOUT A NEWSPAPER.—Once upon a time a cer- tain man got mad with the editor and stopped his paper. Thebnext week he sold his corn at four cents below the mar- ket price because he wasn't posted. Then his property was sold for taxes, because he didn't read the delinquent notice. He was arrested and fined eight dollars for going hunting an Sunday, simply because he didn't know it was Sunday, and he paid three dollars far a lot of forged notes that had been advertised two weeks and the public cautioned not to nego- tiate for them. He then paid an Irishman with a foot like a forge hammer to kick him all the way to a newspaper of- fice, where he paid three years' sujiscription in advance, and got the editor to sign an agreement to knock him down and rob him if he ever ordered his paper to be stopped again. Such is life without a newspaper. MURDERS AT SEA.—News has reached this country of a terrible series of murders committed on the high seas. A month ago two Manilla seamen on the American ship. Frank N. Thayer, which was then several hundred miles from St. Helena, armed themselves with knives aud stabbed to death the first and second mates. The captain was dan- geronsly wounded, but locked himself in his cabin and got out his revolvers. Other members of the crew barricaded themselves in the fprecastle, but the carpenter, helmsman, ad a third coolie aman were murdered The assassins , remained masters of the deck for thirty-six hours, and then Captain Clarke succeeded in shooting one dead and wound- ing the other, who leaped overboard. It was then found that the shin was on tire, and the survivers were obliged to leave 1 her in a boat, in which, after a week's exposure, they reached Et. Helena. RON. WISS. TAYLOR. at the building in Bold-street can have the. not loan of books free of charge; but this is what is wanted, except as applying to books - kept in stock for reference purposes. What is wanted is that boy or girl, or man 01 woman, should be able to obtain a book and. take it home and read it at convenience and at leisure. Minutes saved are minutes gained, and the minutes saved in reading are a double gain—often enough in a life-time bringing in compound interest. It should be remem- bered, too, that the habit of reading is an I acquired habit, and in order that it may be acquired books should be at arm's 1410 -- not in the next street, or half a mile away. There are scores, nay, hundreds, of our young men and young women drifting into the habit of spending idle and often IniS- chievous hours, and all because they have not found the unexhaustible source of delight which comes of reading good books. Whr, they have not touched "the Pierian spring is a question to which various answers ruio,t be given; but unquestionably one substantial answer is because the cup has been too far removed from them. This is a defect which is being remedied all over the country, and it is time that Warrington should let it be seen that, if it is too late to lead, it is not unwil'' ling to follow on the right road. We cannot believe that want of means blocks the waY.; it is rather want of determination. There ls a certain amount of inertia which requires tn be overcome, and if our readers will express, themselves fully and freely they will in all likelihood supply the determining force. the present moment, the subscribers to tue Library number less than .700 all told, so that the 5s annually which they each pay brings inf about 2150 per year. It is for the sake 0 this sum that we stand still---that we are be- ing left behind, notwithstanding a contribtv, tion from the rates of between L'soo and 26n0 a year. For a mucti less subsidy out cy. the corporate exchequer, towns less than Warrington can have a iree Library, and We' think it therefore pertinent to ask, as we cl,o. ask, why Warrington Library cannot be mule free?

THE Runcorn Improvement Commissioners have had a big wrangle over what on the face of it is a little matter and Mr. SHAW, til,e,t; chairman, has felt it his duty to resign. It,' much to be regretted in the interests of tne public that matters should have come to this pass, and we cannot but think that the tni,:. jority of the Board would have done well 1` they had refused to accept Mr. SHAW'S resig* nation. The chief point at issue .between, the chairman and some of the members °' the Board has arisen out of the action of the Highway and Sanitary Committee in making a recommendation as to an appointment on the Upper Mersey Conservancy Board whet' they had no power to do so. The chairman, knowing the business of the Commissioners better than the committee, struck out the minute, when he saw what had been done, lfl order to save the time of the members. A" the next meeting of the Commissioners, a protest was made against what some of theta regarded as a high-hand proceeding 011; the part of the chairman; and, as is usual , in such cases, things were said that had better I have been left unsaid. The chairman is a Liberal and he could not fail to note that the recommendation, which it is admitted ought never to have been made, related to the ar pointment on the Conservancy Board of chairman of the Conservative Association, and that, singular to say, the matter was in: troduced after he had left the meeting at which it was considered. When he fenny' that the recommendation was out of place—" ! Was really no part of the business of the corn- ' mittee—he.acted within what he still believes ! to be the rights of a chairman in ending the mat' I ter by striking out the minute. Such things are done by chairmen, and time is thereby saved, but, nevertheless, we believe that, technically' speaking, the chairman put himself in the ! wrong. The strict course would have been to let the minute come before the Board of I Commissioners, arid leave it for them to send it back to the committee to be rescinded. it would have come to the same thing in the end, after the loss of, perhaps, • not a little time, and making the committee look not a little ridiculous. The sqnabble has been as to the power of the chairman to sum/nal-11r set the committee right; but the matter at issue was really so small that the Commis- sioners ought not to have allowed it to result in the chairman's resignation. Runcorn can ill spare men like Mr. —HAW, who are able, zealous, and thoroughly upright in their dealings. The mistake should be rectified at the earliest possible opportunity.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

- - Let boys beware! Fines have been in- flicted by the magistrates for snowballing at Golborne, and at Farnworth. So long as lads confine themselves to pelting each other, the matter is one scarcely worthy of the notice of the police; but it is time to in terfere when snowballing becomes a brutal assault upon passers by.

And why shouldn't boys and young men behave themselves at football matches? Players who go from home to another town are visitors ; but hooting and throwing at in- dividual players, as has been done at War- rington, is not such a welcome as they have _a right to expect. This is not the way to help .Warrington players; they are ashamed of it

Our " neutral " contemporary reports a sPeaker at the shareholders meeting of the Ship Canal Company as saying that the stars in their courses fought against Cicero. This Was certainly hard on "Cicero," but it will be news to the admirers of the ancient orator. There is something in the old book about the stars fighting against Si:era. Can it be that somebody has been napping?

--- There is a good deal said by Home Rulers about the Old Parliament in College Green. Alacauley hadn't a very good opinion of it, for he describes it, in his essay on William Pitt, as "the most tyrannical and the most corrupt ssetnbly that ever sat in Europe." It is to ?e hoped, if a fresh start be made, we shall Iraprone on that. The Irish Nationalists of Widnes have had 4.4 Meeting and put on record their "great 'isglist and disappointment at the insuffici erlcY of the measures" proposed by Lord ?alisbury's Government for the benefit of itreland. It is a pity they were not wise in They have sent Mr. T. C. Edwards- Nloss to represent them, and now they must !hake the best of him. They sowed wind and nave reaped a whirlwind.

The Rev. T. R. Matthews, of "the Earles- town church scandal," was under discussion at the meeting, on Monday, of the Newton Commissioners. Ttiey want to find him some trustees for the day school, so that oper steps may be taken for enlarging it; Jilt he prefers one-man government, and a ki)(3llcY of masterly inactivity. Ah, could they uut remove the vicar! The school would soon be enlarged.

At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, .Witness, giving evidence in a drunk-and- disorderly case, said the defendant was not drunk and then, as if to correct himself, added—" and he was not sober." The wit- Was thinking perhaps of the Scotch- 'llan who insisted that a man was not drunk B°lcing as he could lie on the floor. (N.B. Some men will •" lie " whether drunk or Ober—on the floor or anywhere else)

The Town Council of Accrington have entered oa formal protest against the way in which magistrates are appointed. It seems that there have recently been two batches ttlade, ore of four and the other of three—all „Conservative. As Accrington is out-and-out ,Liberal, this is hard to bear; but what are l'OrieS to do? The sun shines but little for them, and they must make hay whilst it 'hines,

there is a movement on foot to obtain ;.arthing stamps for the postage of newspapers 't would enormously increase the sale of newspapers in country places, for newspaper proDrietors could then ser,d a penny paper uY post for a penny. A postal charge of so Per cent for the carriage of a penny paper is Fertainly high; but the question is—Would It, Pay the Post Office to adopt the farthing Stamp ?

,At St. Helens, as at Warrington, the Coffee tavern Companies pay a dividend of zo per cent. This is very satisfactory to the share- 41ders, who, starting with a philanthropic Motive, can have no objection to finding that the movement' pays its way. At St. Helens. the company has, in addition to the dividend, decided to pay a bonus of one shilling per share. It would be better if this extra shil- ling were devoted to giving "the British Workman" a bigger and better supply.

Mr. T. M. Pattison is making headway as ' a composer. Referring to a Garden Bazaar held last week in t. James's Hall, "The Manchester Guardian " says—'• During the • afternoon the band of the g_th Dragoon Guards played selections, and visitors had the pleasure of listening to an operetta writ- t..ll by Mr. T. M. Pattison, entitled "John bull and His Trades." Our townsman though lost to the eye in this part of the Country is not likely, we are glad to know, to °e lost to the ear. His cantata, "A Day with 'o,ely Lord," is about to be performed at wycliffe Church, Warrington.

. Sir Gilbert is fond of conundrums. Here °ne which he may "let off" at his next T eeting :—Why are the Sankey wire-drawers like the leaders of the Tory party? "Give it up?" Because they are "down i'th' mouth," and "a good cry" now would be a great relief to them.

"Vote for Greenall and Good Wages" was the master-placard of the Tories.,. It was regarded as a good cry; the Sankey wire- drawers rallied to it; and went in a body to Ifote for Sir Gilbert, What do they think of It now when they are out on strike against "Paddy's rise ?" But three months gone— "ay not so much—and this is the reward.

Durimg this period the interior oi ;:tle structure will be beautified at a cost of about .E5OO. r• George Yarwood, Church-street, is the contractor. .14.17NPRAL OF A VOLUNTEER AT RUNCORN.—The tuners t George Shaw, formerly assistsint clerk to the Widnts ~„ehool Board, took plAce OR Sunday afternoon at Runcorn _‘'ernetery. IRUNCJRN BOARD OP GUARDIANS.—There was 110 busi- ness of public interest transacted at the meeting on Tuesday. IVIDNIs C.E.T.S.—At the monthly meeting on Thursday the Rev. C. Rumutt lectured to a good audience on the sub- ject of "Sunbeams." A COUNTY COURT AT WIDNES.—To the petition asking for a county court to be held at Widnes, 570 signatures have been obtained, and it has been forwarded to Mr. T. C. Edwa-ds Moss, M.P., for presentation. SONS OF TEMPERANCE, WesroN.—This society held its anniversary en Wednesday, in the Wesleyan school- room, Weston, when the members and friends sat down to a substtntial tea. Afterwards Mr. John Wesley Kirkham was called to the chair. Songs, dz.c., were indulged in, and the usual vote of thanks to the chairman and ladies for their services brought a pleasant evening's entertainment to a

close. DIE WESTON POINT STEAM TOWING COMPANV.—The balance sheet of this company showed a balance of £515 41 7d, and on the recommendation of the directors a dividend of 5s per share on the original shares, and 3a 101 per share on the new issue has been declared. The retiring directors were Mr. Jamas. Handley, J.P., and Mr. E. Fin- lay were re-elected. This company now possess five Steamers. CHuRcH OF ENGLAND TEMPSRANCE SOCIETY, HALTON. —On Monday night a meeting convened by the Vicar was held in the Girls' Schoolroom. Halton, for the purpose of forming a branch of the Church of England Temperance Society. There was a large attendance. Mr. Thomas Miller, organieing secretary for the diocese of Chester, was in attendance, and gave an interesting and instructive ex- position of the aims and objects of the society. Some 400 persons afterwards joined the society in the two sections, the majority connecting themselves with the total abstin- ence section. ROBBERY FROM A WIDNES 11AR.—JOhn Smith, Of Bold, was charged at Widnes Petty Sessioss on Thursdey with having stolen en the Ist inst a bottle of whiskey, valiae 3e, the propetty of Jonathan Wade, from the Railway Hotel, Page-lane, Appleton.—Serah Ann Wade said about one o'clock on Monday the prisoner and another man went into her father's house, the Railway Hotel, and had some beer. She had occasion to go out for about ten minntes, leaving the prisoner and the other man by themselves. When she returned they were not there, and on looking round she missed a bottle of whiskey which was there before she went out. Tbe whiskey would be worth about 3e.—P.o Bruce proved apprehending the prisoner, who acknowledged having taken arid drank it, and than thrown the bottle away.—He was sent to prison for one month with hard la- bour. Ruercortte GAS COMPANY.—The annual meeting of share- holders was held yesterday, under the presidency of Mr. F. Rigby, J.P., and the usual dividend .of 10 per cent was declared. The revenue account showed that by the sale of cannel as £3 713 6a id had been received, by public lighting and under contract £302 12s, making a total of £4,015 18e ld, The rental of meters amounted to £2OO 85 hi, and the residual products had realised £897 1.68 81. Other items brought up the receipts to £5,247 21 61. The total expenditure was £3,388 78 3d, leaving a balance of £1.860 15s 3d. The total share capital paid up was £37,600, and there remained to be borrowed £18,333. From the capital account it appeared that the cost for new mains and service was £1,343 4s sd, and that the cost of the special Act was £645 Os 7d. The balance sheet was adopted on the motion of the chairman, and the directors were thanked for their steryieee en the enntion et Mr. Pritchard, eaeoected by Mr. W. islaedley. RU/iCoRtI CO-OPERATIVE OCIETY. The half-yearly meeting took place on Tuesday evening, in, the Co-opera- tive Hall. There was a crowned attendance of members, and Mr. D. Worthington presided. In their report the di,ectrs said the total sales for the half-year amounted to £34,365 18s 11d, being an increase of £2,595 15s 2d on the corresponding period last year. The net disposable profit was £5.162 5s I'l. The directors recommended a dividend of 2a 10d in thee on grocery, drapery, and boots and shoes, which would amount to £4,933 Sc lid and 91 in the 4on butchery. The £lll us taken from the reserve fund last half-year was to be replaced, and £l9O 9e 74 to be added. Numerous questions were asked upon the balance sheet and satisfactorily answered by the chairman. The report and balance sheet were ultimately adopted. It was decided that a competent, gentleman should value the property of the society. Mr. Fitzpatrick gave notice that at the next meet- ing he should move that in consequence of th.e growing trade of Widnes the meetings of shareholders be held alter- nately in that town and Runcorn. ELOPEMSNT Me/ SiteeCiet.—i circumstance of an ex- traordinary character which has just occurred in the his- toric villnge of Halton, near Runcorn is affording the gos- sips of that rural locality a subject of conversation prolific with incident and sensationalism. It appears that a work- ing-man. who has a wife and numerous family, and who has lived in the village for a number of years, was recently induced to receive "a nice young man lodger" into his house. Things went smoothly for a time, but at last the husband began to suspect that the lodger was paying too much attention to his wife, and being taxed with insinua- ting himself into the affections of his landlady, a quarrel ensued, and the lodger left the village. He retired to a dis- tance, whence lie continued to lay seige to the female's heart. An evening or two since he paid a surreptitious visit to Hat tor, and having had a conversation with the " ficisle fair one," he took train for Chester. The following morning. after the tmehend had gone to work, the wife pro- ceeded to Halton station, taking with her two of the child- ren and a quantity of luggage. On discovering what had occurred the husband's grief was great; he set off in sAreh of the guilty couple and discovered them in the WeBh town of Newport. He gave them " e piece of his mind," and, deciding to leave them for ever In. file undisturbed enjoyment of their illicit love, he raurned to Halton. BRUTAL DOG FIGHT AT RlniffOßN.—Before Captain C. W. Hazlehurst and Mr. Jelnea Handley, at Runcorn Police Court, JozAlph Bailey and Richard Done, labourers at Runcorn, were charged with causing or permitting to be 111-treated two dogs at Clifton. James Done was charged with aiding and abetting. On Tuesday the fight between the dogs. one of which was a bull terrier, and the other a bull dog, was arranged to take place at Clifton, near Run- corn. The terms were that the combat WAS to continue one of the animals "gave in" or was killed. By means of the usual hissing and other encouraging noises, the dogs were made to attack each other in a very ferocious fashion, and both sustained very shocking injuries. At the end of half an hour the spectators saw a man In the vicinity, whom they took for a policeman, and the docts were separated. On the same afternoon in- formation of the occurrence wes conveyed to Runcorn Police Station, and P.S. Neild and P.C. Hammersley went towards the spot. On the way they met the prisoners, Accompanied by the bull terrier, which was limping on three legs. The dog was taken charge of, and en Thursday the prisoners were apprehended. Proof of the charge was given by George William Nicholls and William Percival Ceaseain Hazleburst considered the case one of gross cruelty, Battey and Richard Done 40s and costs, 18a 7d each, or a month. James Done was discharged with a caution. PovERTY AND CRIME AT WIDNES. Before Mr. Hol- brook Gaskell, junr., and Mr. T. S. Tinimis. at Widnes Police Court, on Monday Eliza Roberts, a married woman, was brought up on remand charged with stealing five eggs. valued at 61, from a shop in Mersev-road, the property of Joeeph Routiedge.—Mr. Knowles appeared for the defence. —Ann Routledge, wife of Thomas Routledge, 35, Mersey- road, Widnes, said she carried on the business of a confee. tiener there. Between nine and ten o'clock on the 28th nit, the prisoner came ieto her shop and asked her for a pennyworth of petatoe pie. She told her she had none ready, and the prisoner left her basin and went away. Wit- ness went into the kitchen, leaving nobody in charge of the shop. About ten minutes afterwards P.C. Holbrooke cam. in with the prisoner and the egos. Tke prisoner said, " I took those eggs. I'm very sorry; I hepe you'll forgive me." —Mr. Knowles pleaded for the defence that that week the prisoner had heel nothing to eat but bread and butter, and seeing the eggs in the shop she let her hunger get the better of her reason and took them. She was a married woman and had two children. Her husband had been out of work since Christmes, and their poverty had been so great that they had pawned everything they possibly could. The pri- soner was suffering from a diseased leg, and for some weeks had been in the hospitels of Chester and Liverpool. From What her husband told him unless her leg was taken off she would'very likely die. He thought the time she had been In prison—five devs—was sufficient punishment for the , ()three she had committed. He remarked that the only money the family bad was 5., and this would have to pro- viii' the family for a week. Mr. Gaskett seid the Bench conld not recognize that poverty was any excuse for theft, and they must, therefore. inflict a penalty on her. Teey had taken into consideration everything Mr. Knowles hid said, and would fine the prisoner ss, or seven days. CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN PUBLICAN. -- Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. James Reynolds at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Samuel Worrall,of the Navigation Inn, Canal-street, was summoned for permitting, drunken- ness. Mr. W. H Linaker defencled.—P.C. Smith stated that about five o'clock on the 19th January he entered the defendant's house and In the parlour he saw Mr. Middleton, farmer, Moore, and Mr. Field, of the Norton Aram, Hilton, at one table. At another table there were three other men. Mr. Middleton had a glass of beer before him, and before Mr. Field was an empty spirit glass. Mr. Field was very drunk and was leaning his head on his bands en the table. The other men were quite sober. He left the house and in. a few minutes he saw Mr. Field come staggering forth, to a trap which was standing at the door. With some difficulty he got into the trap. He then got out of the conveyance and again entered the house. Shortly afterwerds witness ang Police-Clerk Wallace went into the house and found Mr. Field leaning against the bar parlour door. The de- fendant was staanding there and saying "It's no use you coming here; I shan't supply you." He also told witness he had not supplied him with any drink and should n•t do so.—PoliCe-clerk Wallace corroborated.—Mr. Linaker called Peter Onto, a labourer, who deposed that Field sent him to Mr. Peek's for a trap. When he returned he saw Field be- ing pushed out of the house by the defendant, and he bad no drink whilst witness was there.—The defendant also gave evidence. Mr. Field mem only waiting in the parlour until the trap came. He had no drink there.—By Mr. Leah : Mr. Field had been in the house before on the same afternoon. He had not heard of him having had a fight that afternoon.—This closed the case for the defence, but after some discussion, Mr. 'Middleton who was sum- moned for the defence, was called on the application of Su- peentendent Leah. He deposed that the defendant refused to supply Mr. Field with anything. Witness had a small lcincroscle.—The Bench considered there was no evidence to convict, but jus:ified the police in bringing the case into court.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY. 6, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY. 6, 1886.

THE WIDNES WOUNDING CASE.—At Widnes Petty See- sins, on Thursday , Michael Carr, a labourer, was brought up on remand, charged with I,aving, on the 14th January, unlawfully wounded John Kelly. at the Widnes Alkali Works, by striking him bliind the ear with a piece of brick, inflicting a wound about four inches in length.—Dr. Mc- Cambridge stated that he was attending Kelly, who was suffering from a fracture of the skull. He was not in a fit state to appear in court.—The case was accordingly further remanded for a week. SNOWBALLING AN OLD MAN AT WIDNES.-011 Thursday, r Widnes, Samuel Fenny, David Tnrigge, and Henry Har- rison, boys, were charged with snowballing an old man, named Edward Atherton, on the 19th ult.—Complainant stated that he was working near Farnworth Church gates on the day in question, when he was set upon by a gang of lads, who snowballed him so severely that he could not net on with his work. He was hit on one of hie eyes and
blinded for two days. He recognised the Vine defendants among the gang young man named Frederick Lee car- roborated.—Each defendant WAS ordered to pAy the costs, 103.

Hove THE PUBLIC ARE SWINDLED. Mary Hulse, oF Northwich, was charged at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, with having attempteal to obtain a ticket for a night's lodgings by making a false statement.—Superinten- dent Leah and Inspector alillington preyed the case. The Inspector gave the woman a bad character and Mr. Leah said be had bean very much annoyed by the woman. She was very abusive in the police ottice. She took three chit- dren about the country with her in order to excite public charity. Her hueband had refused to live with her on ac- count ef her loose habits. The Bench sentenced the woman to a moath's hard labour. ' A DISHONEST ERRAND BOY AT WIDNES —At Widnes , Police Court, on Monday, William Joseph Henry Platt (12), was charged with having on the 26th January. stolen 2s from Mrs Heyes, wife of John Heyes, Farrant-street, Wid- nes. About tea o'clock on that morning Mrs Heyes haneled the prisoner a 2s piece, and asked-him to go and fetch some provisions. He went away with the money, but did not re- tura with the provisions or the money. He left Widnes, and last Thursday WAS apprehended and brought to the police station. On being charged with the theft he said , " Yes ; I did take it, and spent the money." MN Heyea was usable to appear, and he did not expect that she would be able to be present until that day five weeks. The prisoner ' was remanded until March 11th. RUNCORN CASES AT CHESTER ASSIEBS. At Chester Winter Assizes, en Saturday, Moss Williams (35), labourer, for an attempted assault on a little girl named Ann Bostock, twelve years of age. at Runcorn, on the 31st October, was sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment with bard labour.— George Wilsoe (20), sailor, was indicted for unlarefttlly weunding John Wyatt with intent to do him grievous bodily bent, St Runcorn, on the 27th November. From the opening statement of Mr. J. E. Bankes, who prosecuted, it appeared that the parties were employed on board the schooner Agnes Ellen, which was lying in dock at Runcorn. They had ben drinking together, and on their return prisoner went to sleep. All hands being sum- moned on deck, prisoner was roused from his sleep by Wyatt, whereupon, saying " Here is KoVtling 1 share paned this morning for some of you, and I 'can we it," the prisoner stabbed prosecutor in the left side, inticting a dangerous wound, which nearly penetrated to the heart. Prisoner was elkntence!l to five years' penal servitude. A RUNCORN PIGEON FANCIER'S GRIEVANCE. John Morris, keeper of the Commercial Hotel, Bridge-street, was summoned before the Runcorn nagistrates on Monday. to answer a charge of cruelly illtreating a tame pigeon. Thos. ' Bas.kerville, the complainant, stated that he li.-ed at 6, , Ellesmere-street, and his premises adjoined the defendant's. On Sunday, the 17th January, be saw one of his pigeons caught by the beak in a trap on the defendant's window-sill. He climbed to the place and released the pigeon. It was bleeding very much. There were two traps on the window- sill. which was spread with Indian corn. The defendant was inside the room.—P.C. Wallace stated that the pigeon and traps were brought to the police station, and he went to the Commercial Hotel. The defendant after some hesita- tion said the traps did not belong to him, and took the offi- cer up into the bedroom where he found corn both inside and outside the window.—Th defendant held that it had not been proved he set the traps, and he argued that even if lie had, he had a right to do so to catch vermin He had been very much annoyed by the complainant's pigeons. Upon one occasion a pigeon got into a roOn't and he bad to kill it.—The case was diemiesed. _

• THE HISTORY OF 11/LL CLIFFE BAPTIST CHA.PEL cal be obtained from Mr. John S. Green, 34, Bridge- -street, Warrington. Price 6d.—Advt. PENWORTHAM BRIDGE.—Sir Henry James, re- plying to a letter of the Clerk, to the Bury Guar- dians, says the .questiOr. of building Penworthana Bridge is wit:nin the discretion of the county jus- tices, with whom it would be out of place for him to attempt to interfere. OREA.T SANKEY SCHOOL BO.A.RD.—A monthly meeting of this Board was held at Mr. Sutton s Office, Bewsey Chambers, Warrington, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Messrs. Turner (chairman), J. C. Ridgway, W. B. Kerfoot, W. D. Houghton, J. Cook, and Mr. S. Sutton (clerk.)— _Finance: The Clerk reported that the treasurer's balance in favour of the Board was -£1,667 17s fid.— The Schools: A letter was read from the Rev. E. S. Jackson acknowledging the receipt of the notice to quit the school buildings at the expiration of the present quarter. He also requested the Clerk to in- form the Board not to inconvenience themselves as the present schools were at their disposal as long as Ithey might require them.—The Chairman: That is very satisfactory.—The Mastership: The Chairman said there had been a very large number of applica- tions—spinewhere about '2so—for the post of head- master of the schools vacant by the resignation of Mr. Minton. Some of the members of the Board had sifted five of the applications from the others, and that number of applicants were in attendance on the Board that day.—After a somewhat pro- longed Consideration of these five applications, each applicant being in turn called into the room, it was unanimously decided to appoint Mr. Clarke, assis- tant master at Heath Side Schools, to the vacant post.—This was all the business of public interest. THE QUEEN V. JUSTICES OF CHESHIRE.—In the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Jus- tice, on Tuesday, before Sir James Hannen and Mr. Justice Mathew, sitting as a Divisional Court, Mr. Asquith, on behalf of Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co., chemical manufacturers, carrying on business at Beckton, in the Congleton Division of Cheshire, moved for a certiorari to bring up an order of the justices for the purpose of its being quashed. The learned counsel said the order in questidn directed the applicants to abate a certain nuisance, consist- ing in the emission of smoke from a chimney in con- nection with the applicants' works. It appeared that on the 22nd of October last year the Congleton Sani- tary Authority served on the applicants a notice un- der the 94th section of the Public Health Act, 1875, to the effect that the Authority had been satisfied of the existence of a nuisance at the applicant's works, arising from the chimneys sending forth black smoke in large quantities, and that the appli- cants were required in twenty-one days to abate ' the same. Subsequently, on the 7th December, a summons was served on the applicants, and on the , 9th the magistrates made an order directing the lapplicants, within three calendar months from the 'date of the service of the order, to abate the nui- sance, and for that purpose to make up and con- struct all things necessary so that the same should be no longer a nuisance. He (the learned counsel) maintained that the order was invalid, on the ground that there were no specific works directed to be executed, . either in the notice originally served upon the applicants, or in the order of the justices founded upon the notice, and that the justices had exceeded their jurisdiction.—Their lord- ships granted a rule n. - -

it was not the custom of the Commissioners to fill the vacancy when there was one, and asked where was the " high-handed work "of Mr. Lake, and the "drastic con- duct '' of Mr. Lightburn. If there was anything like this it was done by the committee in taking upon themselves work which had never been performed by toe c.rmmittee before. That was where the evil was. When he undertook the office of chairman of that Board his aim was that the business of the Board should be done so as to he a credit to all concerned. He had spared no time and veins to make it so, and until recently they had assisted him to secure this desirable result. But whetter it was because of the Liberal victory in to is division, which had been such a great trouble to some of them. (Cries of " No," no.") Whether this recommenda- tion was that the chairman of the Conservative Associa- tion should be put into this particular office, or whether it was considering the source from whence this information came about the vacancy that they were obliged to pass it without inquiry, he knew not, but it aid appear that unless some of them were allowed to bring the Board into discredit by passing a recommendation which had never received a moment's consideration, and to publicly discuss with wrangling and evil speaking and wilfully misconstrue words and actions, they were net satisfied. He had no ambition to preside at a Board that seemed inclined to take a course like that. He would never preside at a Board where wrangling and evil speaking seemed to be the desire of the majority of its members. He therefore resigned his position as chairman. The Law Clerk said they must accept Mr. Shaw's resig- nation before proceeding to the appointment of a chair- man.

Mr. Lake said that as Mr. Shaw seemed to make a some- what personal attack upon himself he would move that the resignation be accepted. He went on to say that his only contention was, not that filling up the vacancy was right, nor whether there was any vacany in existence, but that the Chairman of the Beard had no right to strike out a minute without the consent of the Com- mittee, however foolish that minute might be The chairman wanted to make himself a judge over the rest of the Board, and that was what a chairman was not and what the gentlemen of that Board would not knuckle down to if they had a spark of the manliness he gave them credit for. If Mr. Shaw would not admit that he had no right to strike out the minute, there was no other course but to accept his resignation. Mr. Taylor seconded Mr. Lake's motion. Mr. Lightburn thought no party politics or party motives should be introduced in matters of this kind. (Hear, hear.) They might have made some deep laid scheme to attack the chairman, who, he thought, had no right to take up their time by making them listen to such a rigmarole as he had addressed to them that morning; imputing motives that' no one had any idea of. Mr. Grice said the way in which the Board had b2en talked to showed a little vindictiveness, and if there was any party feeling it was not on the Conservative side. He thought they ought to accept the resignation. Mr. Speakman remarked that the chairman had no power to veto anything that took place at a committee meeting. It would have been more straightforward, business-like, and manly if Mr. Shaw had allowed the minute ta have come before the Board and given them the information in his pos- session. There had been a mistake all round with regard to this minute, and he did not think it would be remedied by the chairman vacating his position in the way he had done that merning.

' Mr. Meadowcroft did not see how a gentleman with a spark of self-respect and manliness could have adopted any other course than that which the chairman had adopted. Mr. Meadowcroft challenged the gentlemen who made the appointment to show their right to du o. When gentlemen ckarged the chairman right and left with high handed con- duct, it was desirable that they should at least come into the businrss with clean hands, and not attempt to ride roughshod over the chairmae on an assumption that a minute passed by the Sanitary Committee was a minute of the whole Board. ("No, no.") 11-4erritg to the School Board incident, Mr. Meadowcroft said Mr. Shaw three times denied that the statement published in one of the news- papers was correct, and yet Mr. Lake pteree ded in his remarks. He then fell back upon a rule of the Finance Committee, which stated that that committee had control over the offices of the Board. He could not conceive of any- thing more absurd than an argument of that kind in order, in his opinion, to found an attack upon the chairman altogether undeserved. He pointed out that when he was chairman of the Board he granted or refused the use of the Board-room at pleasure. But on the occasion in question it was not refused. The chairman explained to the School Board that they had used the Commissioners' mem on two occasions without permission, and the School Board thanked him for his courtesy, and yet he was attacked in a most ferocious manner for doing that which the School Board complimented him on.—Mr. Meadowcroft spoke in high terms of Mr. Shaw's capabilities, wide experience of the Board's business, and his independent and conscientious character, and said it was because he declined to cringe to one section or the other section th,o; be had been asseiled both inside and outside that Board-room.

Mr. Dol,son said that lae accepted Mr. Shaw's explanation at the last me:44;g, and if the Board had done the same, there would, haYo ban an end of this unpleasantness. A Umoit St!aighifor ward, able chairman had never occupied the Cliair than Mr. Shaw—(hear, hear)—and he hoped he would see his way to retain the psitien, Mr. Pritchard explained th 6 dburse that the charman took on the occasion when the School Board had tire use of the boardroom for the third occasion. The chairman came to the School Board office inirnediately before half- past ten. There were present Father Fennelly, M sere. Hazlehurst, L? 1, the clerk, and himself. The chairman explained that they bad used the boardroom on two previ- ous occasions without permission, and the caretaker had had instructions to keep the room locked, as had been the custom. He understood they were to meet that morning, and he would take upon himself to lend them the use of the room without their making application that morning. The members present thanked the chairman for his courtesy in attending, and for his readiness in granting the requisite permission without asking his consent. As soon as tne chairman had left the room the members of the School Board came downstairs and the room was open for them to walk straight into the room. He really did not know what other course any gentleman could pursue and show more courtesy and kindly feeling towards the School Board. The statements of Mr. Lake at the last meeting were founded upon error. (Hear, hear.) These unseemly attacks upon the cbairman were unexpected, and if the chairman sat down under all the indignities heaped upon him, he should con- sider he had lost all self respect. Mr. Shaw, in a speech of some length, said if he were placed in the same position again he shoulel strike out the minute. Under the circumstances he could not alter he decision, and he should be pleased it they would accept Ifle resignation. Mr. Lake said the only thing he objected to was the toil- ing of the door. The Chairman: Which I did not do. Mr. Meadowcroft : Perfect right to do it. Mr. Pritchard: We knew nothing about the locking of the doors whatever. The room was open. • Mr. Lake said Mr. Shaw denied that the statement in the newspaper was correct, but he would give nothing but shuffing replies to his (Mr. Lake's) questions. Mr. Dobson moved an amendment that Mr. Shaw be re- quested to occupy the chair until June, when his term of office would expire. Mr. Shaw declined, and the motion was not seconded.. The resignation was accepted without dissent. Mr. W. Fisher was appointed chairman pro tem. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. The Medical Officer reported that the number' of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 30. One of these was registered on a coroner's certificate, and of the re- maining 20 deaths rive were due to scarlet fever, six to bronchitis, three to consumption, two to cancer of various ofgans, two to premature birth, two to inflammation of the lungs, two to intestinal diseases, two to natural decay, one to croup, one to measles, one to inflammation of the liver, and one to spinal deformity. The abwe show an ay.raae death rate for the twelve =no of a little over 21 per 1000 of the estimated population. In answer to the Chairman, the Medical Officer said dar- ing the previous month the deaths from scarlet fever were nine, this month fiver so that there was a reduction. The fever was more or loss spreading over the town.

The General Purposes Commi.tee recommended that the offer of the Runcorn Gas Company be accepted, viz.:— " That the four large lamps be purchased by toe Commis- sioners for the sum of £25• and that the Commissioners should also pay for eleven additional lamps. as payment for the gas consumed by the said four lamps." The minutes were confirmed. THE CHADOR AGAINST A SCHOOL BOARD VISITOR. Mr. Lightbarn. in moving the adoption of the Health Committee, said the School Board had inquired into the case of the child Martha Walton, and had exonerated their officers from all blame. The Commissioners, therefore, ought to be satisfied, too. All he knew was that the child went to school in an unfit state, and then she jeopardised the lives of all she came in contact with. If the inquiry led to greater care being exercised on the part of parents and others in the future, the Board would have done wise in the course they adopted. The medical officer was quite within his duty in making the report he did. Mr. Dobson seconded the motion, which was carried. There was no other business.

FEMALE BRUTALITY AT WIDNES. On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. Hol- brook Gaekell, jour., Mary Ellen Devine was brought up on remand charged with unlawfully wounding Elizabeth Burns, by striking her on the beadwith a poker. Mr. Knowles appeared for the defence.—Elizabeth Burns, 21, Railway-street, Widnes, said the prisoner had beet lodging at her house several weeks previous to the 17th January. She left the house on the night of the 16th, and returned on the following morning at 1-30. Prisoner commenced to use bad language because there was no fire in the kitchen. Witness and her sister left the house and went next door. The reason they left was on account of the prisoner's violent language to their mother. After being in the next house for five or ten minutes, they heard a noise and wit- ness, her sister, and Mrs. Dowd came running into the house. They there found the prisoner holding their mother by the hair. Witness teld the prisoner she ought to be ashamed of herself pulling an old woman's hair like that. Prisoner told her to "go oat." Witness tben hit her once In the face with the open hand, whereupon prisoner got hold of her by the hair and hit her a violent blow with the poker on the top of her head. She was rendered senseless.
