The first business was the consideration of tenders for carrying out the new sewerage scheme for Weston Point.— Mr. Aaron said it had been agreed that the Mersey Salt and Brine Company should put in one length of sewer under the supervision of the Authority. On going down to Weston Point some time ago he found that the length of sewer had been laid in a bed of quicksand, and surely the Authority would not pass that. He suggested that the engineer of the Brine Company should see the Authority's engineer on the matter, and if he passeel the sewer in that state he (Mr. Aaron) should propose that the Authority get another engineer. (Laughter.)—The Rev. J. J. Bryant said the company were responsible for the proper constriction of the sewer, and he thought that took all responsihility from the Authority.—The Deputy Clerk stated that two months ago ate Authority decided to enter Imo an , agreement with the Brine Company. One condi- tion was that the company should put in a length of sewer from the proposed junction of the Runcorn Commissioners' sewer to the company's dock, and that the sewer should be laid to the entire satisfaction of the en- gineer of the Autho;i,v. He afterwards found that not only was that portion of the sewer cut open, but the pipes put in and covered. This was 'clearly a breach of the agreement, and on that ground he (Mr. Lineker) had de- clined to submit the agreement between the Anthority and the company until the sewer was in a satisfactory condition, and the reason that he had brought an action on the part of the Authority, which was now standing against the com- pany, for interfering with the Authority's drainage, and if he were to advise the Authority to conclude the agreement it might prejudice their position. He advised the Authority not to put their seal to the agreement until the conditions of the Beard were thoreughly satisfied. He suggested that the tenders for the ether parts of the sewer be accepted provisio •ally upon satisfac'ory terms be- ing completed nth the Heresy 13 ine and Salt Company,— Mr. AartAi g4T,I 0 ieng to impr v !relents in the sewer of Lent's-row, Weston Point, it was not neces- sary to include that portion in the scheme. He thought if the doctor and inspector would do duty a little bit mere there would be less sickuess.—The Inspector (Mr. Farrington) was of opinion the sewer was now adequate.—The Rev J. J. Bryant drew attention to the serious nuisance that would be caused by the open sewer from Lunt'.s-row passing behind habitations. He did not think it was consistent with the dignity of the Board that a teacher skould be per- mitted to write such impertinent letters.—The Chairman said he had a letter from Mr. Annett containing some kind of an apology for that. div.head: RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.
div.p: RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.

The annual meeting of .this Association took place on Monday evening in the room of the Association, Westminster Cocoa Room Buildings. Toe proceed- ings commenced with an excellent tea provided by Mr Plevin' manager of the Cocoa Company, of which a good ntanber of members partook. The public meeting subsequently held was presided over by Mr S C Beckett, and 'here were present the Rev T M A.rmson, Messrs J Simpson. F A Lake, F J Norman. H Fitton, J Le Couteur, S Coventry, J A. Smith, T Cooke, J K Digges, J E Meredith, W Shaw, G Howard, W Pownall, jun. (hon. sec.), &c. At the outset the Chairman called upon The Secretary to read the annual report. It stated that the year had been in many ways very prosperous for the /association, though the coancittee deplored very deeply the death of their late esteemed president. Mr. Norman had always had the welfare of the Association at heart, and supported it liberally, his last thoughts being brightened by the recollection of his connection with the Association and its useful labours. Mr. Beckett, who had succeeded • Mr. Norman as president, by his sound advice and co operation rendered great assistance to the committee at a very tryine tine, and they took that oppor- tunity of thanking him for the same. Through the agency of the gymnasium, which undertaking from the first had the late president's sympetey and support, there had been an increased membership Of 30 to the association. This circumstance wag doubtless due to the formation of the rounders club in the summer, which proved on the whOle a success, giving to maoy of the younger members a means of obtaining wood healthy outdoor recreation, a want which had long bees felt by the committee. The committee ex- pressed their thanks to Mr. J. C.tristie, secretary of the club, for the efficient manner in which he had conducted the affairs of the club,aand to Mr. Hivey, secretary of the Rounders Association, for the ready way in which he res- ponded to a request to initiate the inernbe,s into the laws of the game. The reading-room continued to be fairly well patronised, and the committee hoped its ad- vantages would not be neglected for the lighter pastimes of the AssoCation. The o flirraittee expressed thanks to those who had contributed periodicals to the room. Thanks were elso expressed t ) Captain Le Couteur for several acts of kindness n ndered to the :teseciation. Al. lotting to the recent treat to the aged people, the committee tendered sincere therrks to all who sepia! fed the undertak- ing so liberally, either by gifts of money, gifts in kind, or by labour as well as to the nameroue ladies and gentlemen, who worked so heertil7 for its success. The past year had seen the lebours of many monttis cglminate successfully in the opening of the gynanaeiien id a style worthy of the association and of the town. Terough the kindness of Cap- ' tein Hazleherst and the officers of the Volunteer Corps the Drill Hall was placed at the dispese! .f the committee. The hall had been fitted up by Mr. Alexander, of the Liver- ! pool Gymnasium, on which account there was yet owing a sum of £3O. This the committee hoped to reduce shortly by giving assaults at arms. The membership of the gymnasium now reached 85, and was still increasing, showing that the latest effort of tee associa- tion for the bsnetit of the young men was being suitably appreciated. Toe report went on to state that the balance of £6 153 from the Aged Persons' Fund had been expended in provisling soup dinners to 200 persons on Friday, Satur- day, and Monday, the 29th, 30th January, and February Ist, Mr. Shaw having placed his mission room at toe dis- posal of the Committee. (Applause.) Mr. J. E. Meredith read the statement of acconnte, which showed the receipte to be as follows :—Balance, £2 14s 10d; subsc iptions from honorary members, £26 15s; subscrip- tions from ordinary members, £lB 4s : re-sale of papers, £5 Os 3d. Donations : Mr. Joseph Verdin, £10; Mr. 3. T. Brunner, £5; his Grace the Duke of 'Westmins- ter, £3 ; proceeds of concert, £lB 18s ; balance from Rounders' Club, Os; total, £99 fie 9d. Shaw secoudeel, aud Mr. J E Meredith supported the motion with great pleasure.— The motion was carried unanimously, and Mr. Lake then took the chair, and said it was pleasant to feel that one had the confidence and respect of his fellow- men ; and it was still more gratifying when the men whose confidence he Lad were of such a character as the members of an association of that de- scription. He thanked them most heartily for the compliment they had paid him He felt that the president should be one who had taken a mare aetive part in the work of the association than he had done, but haying chosen him, he trusted they would make the best of rather a lame horse. He congratulated the associa- tion upon having gone in for the cultivation of the physi• cal as well as the mental and spiritual parts of their nature. Be must confess that at one time he shared the opinions of other young men that Young Men's Christian Associations were rather " goody goody" concerns, where only one part of the nature was cultivated; but he was glad to say that his connection with that association had dispelled any such views. (Applause.) Captain Le Couteur proposed that Mr. Meredith be ap- pointed treasurer, aud that a hearty vote of thanks be accorded to him for the efficient and able manner in which he had managed the finance during the past year. (Ap- plause )—Mr. Howard seconded the proposition, which was carried by acclamation.—Mr. Meredith responded.—Mr. T. Cooke proposed the re-election of Mr. Pownall as bon. secre- tary. The plaintiff denied this ptarement Mr. Carrot! in answer to questions, admit- t,d that the plaintiff was a servant in Mr. Speakman's ^m- ploy and liable to be dismissed at a trip's notice. div.p: WORK AND WAGES IN WARRINGTON.

The strike which has resulted from the notices of reduction of wages given to their employes by the proprietors of the Sankey Wire Mills still con- tinues with no indications of an early, settlement being arrived at. About forty wiredrawers and a number of labourers are out on strike, but the music wiredrawers at the Sankey Mills still re- main at work, owing to their wages not being affected by the notices of reduction. We have it on good authority that the statement which has been made public to the effect that the wages which have been paid to the men who have struck work were fifty per cent in excess of the regular trade list paid by the Whitecross Company, . Messrs, Rylands Brothers, and other firms is wholly incorrect. It appears that in October last the wiredrawers throughout the country, with the view of meeting the depressed state of trade, drew up a patent steel rope list of prices, which was a ten per cent, re- duction on the then prevailing list. The new list has been accepted by all the masters with the exception of a Sheffield firm, whose employes are now out on strike, and Messrs. Houghton, of the SankeY Wire Mills. The strikers allege that if they accept the reduction Messrs. Houghton. seek to enforce, their wages would be reduced from twenty to sixty per cent, beneath the re- vised list which has been adopted by other firms. We find w 4 were in error last week in stating that the Whitecross Company were making a reduction in the wages of their wire drawers. The men have received no intimation that a re- duction is about to take place, and they give a direct contradiction to the statement that .Mr. W. D. Houghton, who is seeking to enforce a reduction. at the Sankey Wire Mills, has been paying "fifty per cent, in excess of the regular trade list of prices."

THE As.sinsmEts-r OF LAND.—Mr DARBTSHIRE again brought forward the question of the assessment of land and agricultu- ral land and houses, and argued that the present eeduction of 5 per cent, on the assessment of land and 7.12- per cent, on that of land and houses was inadequate and ought to be increased. He suggested that the deductioas should be 10 and 15 per cent. respectivcly.—Tbe CHAIR- MAN was of opinion that so large a deduction would never do. They would then be dealing with landed properly more liberally than in almost any other Union.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE said Chester and Wirrall Unions were quite as liberal as that.—The CHAIRMAN inquired en what ground Mr. Derby- shire thought the present deductions too smell.—Mr. DAR- EySHIRE said the reason why he thought the deduct.ons too small was that while on a hundred pound's worth of land they only allowed a deduction of 5 per cent, on heuse pro- perty of equal value they allowed 15 per cent. The reason why 13 per cent, was taken off houses was that it needed that much to keep a house up ro its letting rtlue, and the reason why they took 5 per cent, off land was, he presumed, that that amount would keep the land up to its letting value. He, however, considered that land needed as much expenditure as houses to keep it up to its letting value.—The CHAIRMAN asked what was re- quired to keep land up to its setting value —Mr. DARBY- SHIRE referred to fencing, ditching, keeping op,en the drains,. and manure.—The CHAIRMAN said manure would be the heaviest item, but he thought that could not be nate) into account. An ironworker might as well argue that he should have a deduction because of the price of the cal he used. Manure was the raw material of the farmer just as much as coal .vast of the manufacturer—Mr. DARBY.SHIRE thought that manure ought to have some consideration ; it was one of the means of keeping the land up to its letting value.—The CHAIRMAN said that was a question between the landlord and tenant. div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY—Before Vie Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- man Davies, Councillor Greening, and Mr. John Fair-

raion.gh. MISCELLANBOUS.—James Thompson. charged with beg- ging in Wilderepool-road, was dismissed with a caution, and William Boyle, charged with begging in Horsemarkeastreet, was similarly dealt with.—Josepb Elton was fined 103 and coats for being drunk and disorderly in Market-rt.—Annie Mahar, for being drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road on Baturday night, was sent to prison for a mouth.—Robert Scanlon was fined 5s Ind costs for being drunk and disor- derly in Foundry-etreet.—John Kearns, for being disorderly in Winwick-st. on the 25th Janaary, was ordered to find a surety in £5 to keep the peace for six month. Thaler BY A Grna.—Mary Ann Wright (16), daughter of a tanner residing at Latchford, was charged with stealing a black coth jacket, value ss, the property of Mary Elizabeth Snape, and with stealing by means of a trick from Messrs. Roberts, shoe dealers, Bridge-street, two pairs of boots, value 21s. Prisoner, who had been a domestic servant, went to I lodge at a Cocoa-house in Winwick-street. She made the acquaintance of Snape, who set out with her to look for a situation for the latter. Snape lent her the jacket so that she should present a good appearance. Toe two got into an omnibus, and when leaving prisoner went away, ostensi• bly to change a half sovereing, and decamped with the jacket. Afterwards, in consequence of a complaint made to a constable to the effect that she had been indecently as- saulted, she was, taken to the police station, when the jacket which she was wearing was at once identified as the one stolen from Snape. Inquiries regarding the girl were insti- tuted, and it subsequently transpired that she had been to the shop of Messrs. Roberts and obtained two pairs of boots under the pretence of being a servant employed at Mount School e.—The Mayor said that the prisoner had given her father—a very respectable man—great trouble,and the mode in which she bad effected these robberies showed consider- able ingenuity. She would have to go to prison for two months, which would afford her time for reflection. Hui-manses —Patrick Doneghue was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Saturday evening, and with as- saulting P.C.s Bell and Caldwell. Evidence was given to the effect that prisoner was drunk and creating a disturb- ance in Winwick-street. On the appearance of the officers he kicked them. In connection with the case three men named Phcenix, Downs, and Bowen were charged with as- saulting Lance-Corporal O'Hare, and Privates Devine and Raguley. The soldiers went to the assistance of the police, and were assaulted by the prisoners named. Donoghue was sent to prison for a month, PhamiX and Downs were each fined 108 and costa, and Bowen was fined 20s and costs.— The Mayor warmly complimented the soldiers on rendering Atich prompt assistance. . - Worrapsev Rasum.—Margaret Mort was charged begging is Wilderspool-rcad. She said that she came : Golborne, but on the magistrates asking her if she lisa., 'Valid go that place if dismissed, she replied that perhaps they bad better eena her to prison for seven daps. One of the magistrates said that perhaps it would be as well to send her to gaol for a month, and prisoner smilingly replied that "she wouldn't refuse."—The Bench thereupon committed her for that period. TITESDAY.—Before Councillors Broadbent and Greening. lIISCELLANBOUB.—WiIIiam Williamson was fined 5s and coats for being drunk in charge of a horse and vehicle near the Central Station.—A man named Cummings was fined Se. including costs, for being drank in Sankev-street.--Jas. Harriam, described as a clerk out of employment, was Charged with being drunk and disorderly in Cloth Hall Yard on the previous evening, and breaking five windows at the lodging-house of Ann Farrell, doing damage to the extent of 4s 21. Prisoner said that he had been robbed of ss, and broke the windows out of revenge.—He was fined 5s and coats, and ordered to pay the damage, or go to prison for 14 days.

Richards, a young man, was brought up in custody on a charge of refusing to perform his task of work whilst an inmate of the casual ward of the Workhouse.—He was sent to priaon for seven days. A BAD CHARACTER —Martha Com, for indecency, was sent to gaol for 14 days. RxmovAn To Avon) DisTuAlNT.—George Daniels was summoned for removing goods from premises rented by him under John Houghton, at a weekly rental, for the purpose of avoiding distress, there being then the sum of £2 15s 8d due from him.—The case was adjourned until Monday for complainant to tering direct evidence of the removal of the goods.

ALLEGED ASSAULT BY A WOMAN. Mary Griffiths a respectable-looking woman, was charged with assaulting William Deinnett on Saturday night last. Complainant said that he went to a public-house at about ten o'clock on the evening in question and entered into a little " chaff " with an elderly lady, with whom he frequently had a little "gammon." The defendant, with her husband was present, and told him (complainant) that he was nothing but" trash." She then, he alleged, picked up a glass, with which she struck him behind the ear. In answer to Mr. P. Davies, who defended, witness denied that he was not sober at the time, but admitted being tamed out ; that, was, he said, because he got excited when he was struck. Mr. Davies said that his instructions were that the complainant grossly insulted the defendant and she pushed him away while she had a glass in her hangl. Mr. Davies ealled wit- nesses who said that complainant was not sober and was the agressor. The summons was dismissed on payment of costs.

A SINGULAR SURCHARGE. The CLERK stated that Mr. U. Hazlehurst, district audi- tor, when auditing the accounts of the Guardians for the half-year ended at Michaelmas, had disallowed 7s 61 out of Is 6d, the cost of what he termed an" elaborat3 pocket knife with corkscrew, cfcc., attached, supplied to the master of the Workhouse. He had made the surcharge on the following grounds :—" Ist. Because there was no necessity in my opinion for such an excessive expenditure being incurred by the said Guardians at the cost of the poor rate, and fur- ther because the sum paid in respect of the cost of such knife is excessive, unreasonable, and improper, and there- fore illegal to the extent of the sum disallowed by me. 2nd. Because in allowing the sum of Is as the reasonable cost of a penknife for the use of the master's office I have allowed in my opinion a sufficient sum for the purchase of an ordinary office penknife and as much as ought reason- ably to have been defrayed at the cost of the poor rate by the Guardians of the said. Union. 3rd. Be-cause the said payment is not authorised by statute or other competent authority." The Clerk added that the gentleman who had been surcharged had appealed to the Local Government Board and no doubt the surcaarge would be remitted.— Mr. HARRISON: Who is the unhappy individual who signed the cheque ? (Laughter.)—The CLERIC said there were three gentlemen who signed thi cheque, the chairman being one.

Mr. HENLEY, the Local Government Board Inspector, who was present, stived that he had recently been over the work- house and schools, but he had nothing very special to bring before their notice. Having made several suggestions as to the furnishing of the vagrant wards, /sc., he said that with regard to the Infirmary he found it clean and in good or- der. The nurses evidently did their duty well, and he re- ceived no complaints, the people appearing to him to be well taken care of. Still he could not shut his eves to the fact that they seemed to be getting overcrowded in the Infir- mary. It would be for the Guardians to consider whether the present state of things was normal, or whethn it was caused by disturbance in the different trades in the district. If the present condition was normal, it was perfectly clear that they would have to make, sooner or later, some new provision for their sick. He should advise them to consi- der very carefully what number they would be required to accommodate, 90 as not to build in excess of that numbsr. There was a tendency in the present day to build is excess of requirements, as it was very easy to borrow money, and he thought Boards of Guardians and other public bodies ought to be very chary of borrowing money—(hear, hear)— but wLo.n the necessity arose the money should be borrowed. In the male department of the infirmary they had 57 beds and 57 inmates, so that they were full up, and in the female department they had 134 beds and 13 occupants, so that they were more than full. Mr. Hen- ley next referred to the crowded state of the children's quer- tere, and he advised that the children should, as far as possi- ble, not be accommodated in double beds, as that WAS often a cause of the spread of disease. With regard to the man- agement of the workhouse, he had nothing to complain of. He found it in aood order, clean,and received no complaints. (Hear, hear.) Referring to Padgate Schools, he said he also found them in a satisfactory condition, but suggested some improvements as to the dietary tables. In conclusion, he said he was glad there were so few things he had to speak about, but he feared that that question of building at the workhouse must force itself upon them.—The CHAIRMAN asked if the difficulty would be met by reducing the number of children.—Mr. HENLEY said he was afraid not. He would advise them, however, that if they built at all they should build proper wards for the sick. They need not put up an expensive building, but they should so build Oat at a future time there could be no question of their sick not being properly treated.—ln answer to Mr. Derbyshire, who said that the workhouse was certified to accommodate 407 persons, Mr. HENLEY stated that when he visited it there were 422 inmates —The CHAIRMAN and a few other mem- bers having referred to the favourable report and valuable suggestions by Mr. Henley, the discussion dropped. This was all the business of public interest.

RUGBY RULES.

WIDNES V. MR. LYCRTT'S (LITHB—RLAND) TRAIL—This match was played at Widnes, on Saturday, and a one-sided game ended in favour of Widnes lay two goals, two tries, wad ten minor points to one minor point. RUNCORN RECREATION (2ND) V. ST. PAUL'S, Y.M.F.S. (Livsapoot.)—A matcn was played between the above teams on Saturday, on the ground of the former, resulting in a victory for the borne team; Recreation three tries and six minors, St. Paul's one try and one miner. Abrams, Massey, and Grounds obtained tries for Runcorn. WESTON SIIANTERS V. FRODSHAII ROVERS.—ThiS match was played on Saturday on the ground of the latter, and an evenly contested game ended in favour of the Shanters by one goal, one try, and six minor points to one minor. The tries were got by peakman and Walford. Hughes kicked the goal. For the Shanters, Moores and Brooks at three-quarters and Tudor and Webster at half played well, as did also all the forwards, their dribbling at times being splendid. For Frodsbam, Owen at back and T. and W. Rogers at three-quarters played a very good game, while Pendlebury at half did a lot of work, his tackling at times being very good. The forwards played up pluckily, especially Darlington and Thomas.

'RUNCORN v. BooTLll.—The return match of these teams was played at Runcorn, on Saturday, when ;he frequenters to the ground of the home club witnessed a very amusing game. The state of the ground, owing to the re- cent weather, was in a wretched condition, the players presenting sorry figures. The Runcorn team were vela unfortunate in not haying two of their usual Mree-quarter backs viz., H. C. Speakman and T. Johnson, while two of the home second team filled vacancies in the Bootle team. The game ended in Runcorn scoring one goal, three tries, and eleven touchdowns to one touch-in-goal. The Bootle team played a plucky up-bill game, Ridock, the full back, saving in capital style. For Runcorn, Wood, the full back, was in good form, making himself generally useful all over the job •, Wainwright played a good tbree-quarter game, in fact all the members of ; the team played well. Teams :—Runcorn: T. Wood, back; G. Wainwright, W. A. Riley, and E. Lunt, three-quarter backs; H. Hughes and H. Andrews; half-backs; W. Wright, W. Hughes, J. Lewis, W. H. Broady, J. Dean, J. Barns, W. Faulkner, J. Gatley, and F. J. Joule, forwards. Bootle S. Ridock, back; W. Pendleton, S. Layfield, and J. Wil- liams, three-quarter backs; Shiogler and D. Quigg, half- backs; G. Page, T. Cox, Graham, J. liidock, C. Drew Fisher, Walker, Kay, and Spedding. Referee: Mr. F. Parry, Liverpool. WARRINGTON V. OLDHAM.

The return match between these clubs was played off here on Saturday in the presence of about 3.000 spectators. Great interest was manifested In the game, each bit of good play being warmly applauded. The Warrington captain, Mr. Warren, was unfortunately hurt in the first halt of the game, and was afterwards unable to take his usual place at " half," although, after a short rest, he pluckily returned and made a fourth "three-quarter." Barnes was the re- cipient of an ovation when he appeared on the field in his jersey, and it is to be hoped he will soon regain his form. Considering the slippery state of the ground, a good exhibit- bition of football was shown, and Oldham were very lecky to win. The hnme team had the bet of the game, both for- wards and back, although the visitors' forwards worked grandly in the loose. Warren won the spin and Barlow started the leather, play commencing in neutral ground. Davies was next prominent in the scrimmage. Stott and Farrell were each conceded a free risk, and aided by a run by Ballow, the home territory was for a moment invaded. A strong run by Jolley reversed matters, and some good work was here put in by Barnes, Massey, and Gilbert. A

rush of the Oldham forwards was nicely stopped by Buxton. 1 Barnes next missed a pass from Jolley, which let up Woods, but Buxton nicely picked up and kicked into touch. A nice bit of passing was next put in between Farrell, Stott, and Barlow, but Rigby, from a line up, secured the ball, and, after a strong run, kisked into touch in the Oldham 25. Hough next came with the leather well at his toes, but, kieking too hard when close on the Oldham line, the ball roiled dead. Barlow kicking out. Jolley, Ashton, and Fair. Turner were soon busy; but the frequent objections of i the Oldham umpire kept play in neutral ground. The home forwards showed themselves superior in the tight packs, but the visiting int wards were equally effective in the loose. Both full backs were called upon in turn to defend their lines, which they were quite equal to. Povey next showed up with a dribble, and Barnes with a screw kick, Rigby and Dillon also thing good work, but the Oldham forwards rushed the ball over the line, and Ripley dropping on it gained a try, which Farrell safely piloted over the bar, and • this, the only point secured by Oldharn, won them the game. Half time was shortly afterwards called, no other point be- ing scored. Ashton started the second half, and with Davies was soon busy. Gilbert next made a good run, and Rigby and Turner put in some useful collaring. A line up was formed in mid-field, from which Povey came through and dribbled beautifully, passed the Oldham backs, and over the line. Here Speakman rushed up and dropped on the ball, secur- ing a try. Jolley took the place, and made a good attempt, but failed to land a goal. Barlow kicked out, and Turner returned into touch in the Oldham 2:5. Some good work was done by Speakman, Barnes and Massey, the visitors' goal being threatened. Kent relieved by a long kick. Warren passed nicely to Massey, who was playing well, and the latter again invaded the 25. W. H. Wood next made a dribble, which Speakman pluckily stopped. Buxton was soon afterwards called on, but had not time to return. A long kick by Mass-v, which was well followed up, agaia in- vaded the Oldham 25. Speakman was next unfortunate in not getting over. Jolley now secured possession, and had a drop, the bill rolling dead. Time was called witheut any other point being secured, which left Oldham the win- ners by one goal to one try and two miner points. For the winners Barlow, Farrell, Stott, Wood, and Ripley played a good game. The whole of the home team played well. Each did his allotted work in fine style, and if the I same team could only be kept together it would soon find itself at the head of Rugby football. TRAMS :—Oldham: Back, Butterworth; three quarters, Barlow (capta;n), Stott, and Armstrong ; half, Farrell and Mills ; forwards, Court, E. Wood, W. H. Woods, J. S. Taylor, T. Taylor, J. D. Kent, Woolstencroft, White, and Ripley; umpire, Mr. Hulme. Warrington: Back, Bux- ton ; three quarters, Jolley, Barnes, and Massey ; half, Warren (capta;n), and Gilbert ; forwards, Ashton, Fair- field Turner, Pavey, Rigby, Dillon, Speakman,. Hayes, Davies, and S. Hough; umpire, Mr. T. Barnes; referee, Mr. R. Wilcox.

- Lord Randolph being a constant guest at Mr. Chamberlain's table. This is as it should be, and forms a pleasant incident in political life. The Prince of Wales's dinner party, by the way, spoiled a good many social arrangements. In Lon- don it is the custom to issue dinner invitations at least three weeks in advance. Some people, to make sure of the guest make it three weeks and two or three days. Many of the guests at Marlborough House last night had made earlier engagements, several having arranged for dinner parties at their own house. The Prince of Wales, who does not in- vite, but, like the disappointed host of the New Testament commands people "to come in," is not under the necessity of issuing such prolonged in- vitations, thinks a week's notice sufficient. The invitations for last night's dinner were issued on the 26th of January, being just eight days notice, the consequence being a notable dislocation of social arrangements in London. The season has not yd set in with full ferocity, and the uncertainty of Parliamentary arrangements further disturb its progress. Nevertheless, London society has applied itself with renewed vigour to the occupation of giv- ing dinners and accepting invitations.

St. Thomas's played an excellent game throughout, the captain and centre forward being most con- spicuous. Delaney (goal), the centre forward, and J. Toubey played well for the home team.

WIGAN V. GOLBOTINS.—The return match was played On he Wigan ground on Saturday, in Ow Presence of 400 spectators. In the firet match Go'borne won by two goals to one, but on Saturday that teselt was exactly reversed. The game was of a rather rough nature. For the visitors Clarke, Clegg, Morris, and Flynn were best, and Jenkinson in ;pal did well. Golborne team : Jenkinson, goal; Clare and Clegg, backs; Unsworth, Clarke (captain), and Lowe, half backs; Flynn, Morris, Cottom, Hemborough, and Kay, forwards. EABLINITOWN WINDMIHRS v. STANLEY.—These teams met at Liverpool, on Saturday. The visitors had to play two second team men and Stanley one, owing to the ens- pension of Culkie. The result of the match was a great surprise, for it was expected that a team that had passed successfully through two rounds of the elist-ict cup during the present season, and which twice defeated Stanley last season, would at least have given a good game, instead of which they were completely routed. The game ended in favour of Stanley by fifteen goals to nil. Stanley :—G. Wright, goal ; A. Dick and R. Stevenson, backs; H. 'Pollock. G. Kerr, and A. M'Callum, half backs; R. M'Neil, W. Wil- son, W. Macgregor. T. Highet, and W. Brown, forwards. Earlestown Wanderers: T. Champion. goal; H. Selby and J. Plant, backs; J. Lowe, W. Allison, and R. Johnson, half backs ; A. Allen, W. Limond, W. Thompson, W. Shaw, and J. Shaw, forwards. EARLESTOWN V. BOOTLE.—These rival clubs met at the Hawthorn-road ground, Bootle, on Saturday, when about 1,000 spectator lined the enelesteres. Both organisations; were represented by strong teams, eat up ara Italf-ittrosi rho result was equal. At a quarter-past three Roberts kteied off for the home team, who were playing against a moderate breeze The visitors immediately put their opponents on the defensive, but Bootle, bringing the ball down on the left wing, secured a corner, which was of no avail, however. The globe travelled backwards and forwards several times, the home team at length getting a splendid chance of scor- ing by Anderson and Eyton-Jones, the latter making a good shot, which struck the post. Bootle now made a furious onslaught on the visitors' goal, but Appleton, the custodian, was too many for them, and, being ably assisted by Dux- bury, the impending danger was averted, and the ball found its way to the opposite end, where Rich, with a splendid shot, scored the only goal for the visitors. Bootle directly afterwards secured a free kick in front of Earlestown's goal from a foul, but Appleton threw the ball away. The home team, however, claimed that the leather had been through the goal, and the referee allowed the claim. This decision occasioned considerable dissatisfaction to the visitors, some of whom left the field. After a stoppage of about ten minutes the game was resumed by Dagnall, but up to half time no other point was registered—the teams changing ends with one goal each. The home team, with the wind in their favour, which had now freshened very much, at once assailed the visitors' quarters, securing several corners. Anderson put in a shot registering a second goal for Bootle. The home team from this juncture bad by far the best of the game, but the visitors defended splendidly, Appleton, between the uprights, fisting out time after time in a miracu- lous manner. The final result was—Bootle five goals, Earlestown one goal. The brothers Green' Duxbury, and Simm played well for the visitors, whilst Roberts, Eyton- Jones, the brothers Veitch, and Anderson distinguished themselves for the home team. Teams:—Bootle: G. Gal- braith, goal; T. Veitch and W. Veitcb, backs; It. Devlin, A. Gibson, and F. Woods, half backs ; W. H. Routledge and T. Morris, right wing ; W. Roberts, centre; R. Anderson and J. A. Eyton-Jones, left wing. Earlestown ;J. Appleton, goal; R. Green and J. Green backs; J. Whalley, J. Duxbury, and R. Bowker, half backs; W. Rich and J. Ellison, right wing; A. W. Dagnall, centre; J. W. Sims and T. Siddeley, left wing.

A splendid =itch was the result of the meeting of Swin- ton and Rochdale Hornets on the ground of the insects, a grand game ending in a draw—Swinton one try and five minors to the Hornets one try and one minor. Tottington stole a march upon the Broughton Rutgers, as the Rangers were without four of their best men, which will account for their defeat. Oldham paid a visit to Warrington, a splendid game re- sulting in favour of Oldham by one goal to one try and two minors. Warrington had by far the best of the game, though two of their men, Messrs. Warren and Barnes, had received slight injuries and were not of much use to their team.

Runcorn had for their opponents Bootle, but at no'stap of the game were the Bootlites dangerous, Runcorn even- tually winning by one goal, three tries. and eleven minors ' to one minor.

St. Helens Recreation have every reason to be proud of their victory over Southport Olympic, whom they defeated by two tries and six minors, to one try and, one minor. Newton bad to submit to defeat at the hands of Newton Heath by three tries to one try. This result should have been reversed.

St. Helens met Aspull, on the ground of the latter, a pleasantly-corrested game ending in favour of Aspull by one goal, four tries, and eleven minors to one minor. Mere combination is vranted for St. Helens.

S3IOIIT TINE A. 4 Tuz VILDUCT Woaas.—The con- tinued depression in trade has seriously affected the wagon works of the London and North-Western Railway Company at Earlestown. For some time past portions of the men have been working only four and five days per week; but as there was no improvement the whole of the works ceased operations on Friday evening last until Monday at 9 a.m., and this will continue until further notice. Thus the men are working less than five days per week,

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. It would be interesting to know, as if we live long enough we doubtless shall, the secret history of English politics during the past week. To begin with there was the mysterious delay in sending for Mr. Gladstone after Lord Salisbury had resigned. The late premier, it will be remembered, went down to Osborne on Thursday, and had plenty of time to coniplete his business before night. As a matter of fact this was done, for he left Osborne at eight o'clock in the morning without a renewed in- terview with her Majesty. Naturally enough it might have been expected that on Thursday night Mr. Gladstone would have been communicated with by telegraph and prepared for a journey to Osborne on the following day. No message, how- ever, reached him till half-past twelve on Friday night. How was the interval employed? On this point there is no necessity for conjecture. Mr. Frederick Greenwood, the editor of the St. James's Gazette, is on intimate terms with the leaders of the Conservative party. The St. James's Gazette whilst scolding the Daily News for commenting upon this strange episode, ingenuously admits that Lord Salisbury was sent back from Osborne with com- mand to make a last desperate effott to keep Mr. Gladstone out. There had been earlier negotiations with Lord Hartington, whom the Conservatives have madly desired to set up in opposition to Mr. Gladstone. On Friday Lord Salisbury returned to town with a command to use the Queen's personal influence with Lord Hartington to induce him to reconsider his determination. But Lord:Hartington, as might be expected of him, stood loyal to his party and his old leader. Neither Royal influence thus exceptionally exerted, nor pique nor personal ambition availed. Lord Salisbury, baffled in his last attempt, was obliged to telegraph to Osborne an account of his failure, and then, there being no other resource,. Mr. Gladstone was roused up half an hour after midnight on Friday and commanded to make a long journey to Osborne to have an audience with the Queen, who might as well—in- deed much better—have been at Buckingham Palace.

On Monday Mr. Gladstone felt that he had pretty well succeeded in forming his Ministry. I had on Monday night the opportunity of seeing the list of the principal offices as they were then disposed. First, and most emphatically settled, was Mr. Glad- stone's. acceptance of the Chancellorship of the Exchequer. Ile had entered upon this new depar- ture with more than youthful energy. Ile desires his new and perhaps greatest work to crown a long and glorious career. No effort on his. part should be spared to make the Ministry strong, popular, and successful. In olden times his assiimp- tion of the Chancellorship of the Exchequer was sufficient of itself to establish this character, and therefore, whilst having on his mind the Herculean task of grappling with the Irish problem, he, was prepared also to direct the finance of the country at a particularly difficult epoch. Earl Spencer was to take charge of the India Office, Sir William Harcourt to be home Secretary, Lord Rosebe7 Secretary for the Colonies, Lord Kimberley Foreign Secretary, Mr. Childers at the War Office, Mr. Chamberlain First, Lord of the Admiralty, Mr. Trevelyan President of , the Local Government Board, Mr. Mundella Presi- dent of the Board of Trade, and Mr. John Morley Chief Secretary for Ireland. It will be seen that the list as finally settled varies in almost every ap- pointment. It was Mr. Chamberlain who upset the apple cart. There had at first been some difficulty with Sir Wm. Harcourt who wanted to go to the Woolsack. Mr. Gladstone had., however, succeeded in overruling this desire, flattering Sir William with the declara- tion that he really could not be spared from the House of Commons. But Mr. Chamberlain was ob- durate on the question of the Admiralty. The statement current yesterday that being a Radical he thought it would damage him in the country if he were associated w_ith one of the fighting depart- ments is pure nonsense. When the time comes Mr. Chamberlain will surprise people inclined to that belief. During the discussion in the Cabinet, at the time of the Penjdeli incident, there was no voice more warlike than that of Mr. .Chamberlain, who was insistent that at whatever cost anything like a slight upon the British flag must be vindicated. The fact is Mr. Chamberlain desired to be one of the secretaries of State. Failing that, he has accepted the presidency of the Local Government- Board 'where he will find much to his taste. The second object of Sir William Harconrt's ambition, the Woolsack being out of the question,. was the Chancellorship of the Exchequer, and this ' he has obtained, leaving the Home Office for Mr. Childers, 'Mr. Campbell-Bannerman becoming Sec- retary of State for War, a distinct promotion. • Lord Rosebery goes to the Foreign Office, an appointment universally approved. Conservatives, not less than , Liberals, hailing it.with delight. Another appoint- ment, the announcement of which has met with a reception that must be eminently gratifying to the person concerned, is the accession of Sir Farrar Herschel to the Woolsack, whence Sir Hardinge Giffard retires after the brief labour of seven months with a peerage, a snug pension of £5,000 a year, and the satisfaction of knowing that he has provided for as many of his friends and relations as there were openings for. The most important and significant appointment is that of Mr. John Morley to the Irish Secretary- ship. This is remarkable in itself as being the pro- motion at a single bound of an unofficial member to a seat in the Cabinet, and the direction of what is, perhaps, the most difficult and delicate post in the Government. But, beyond that, the appoint- ment is recognised as a pledge of the policy Mr. Gladstone intends to pursue towards Ireland. It will be a policy just in its conception, generous in its extension, and sternly loyal to Imperial interests. Everybody knows Mr. Gladstone's view on the Irish question. I have quoted more than once the sen- tence in his speech at Edinburgh, in which he de- clares that he would extend the widest measure of local government to Ireland, but only after he had in the first place safeguarded the interests of the Empire. We read a good deal in Tory newspapers of Mr. 'Morley's desire to extend local government But nothing is said of the qualifying sentence which appears wherever he has dealt with the sub- ject, and in which he, too, puts in the forefront the maintenance of Imperial interests. Looking at it , altogether, and taking due note of the exclusion of Lord Hartington and Sir Charles Dilke, it must be admitted, even by the adversary, as in truth it is, that Mr. Gladstone has formed an exceptionally strong Government. If his own health be spared, we shall see great things done for Ireland before the year is out. Members change sides in the House of Commons to-day for the second time within a year. The attendance was not very large, and the empty front benches gave the assembly a peculiarly unfinished appearance.. At the present moment Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Chamberlain, Sir Wm. Harcourt, Mr. John Morley, and half a dozen other prominent members of the last Parliament are members no longer, and would be liable to arrest by the Sergeant-at-Arms if they presumed to enter the House. They will be back again in ten days, and then the real struggle will commence. In the meantime there is one decidental circumstance which is matter for general congratulation. The Irish members loftily ignoring the change of parties, remain in their old position on the left of the Speaker. Liberals may come and Conservatives may go, or vice versa, but they remain for ever. Though not originally intended to meet the convenience of the House, the dermination has that effect. The Opposition are naturally fewer in number, and in the last Parliament the Par- nellites succeeded in nearly averaging the seat accommodation. In the present parliament, as far as it has gone, their national and instructive desire to be in Opposition greatly embarrassed the House. In 1880 the combined forces of Conserva- tives and Parnellites reached 298 as against 3541 Liberals. That was scarcely a fair division of ac- ' commodation, but it did well enough. In the pre- sent Parliament, whilst Liberals and Parnellites sat in Opposition, the division was 419 on one side of the House and 251 on the other. The 251 found some difficulty in settling themselves down. As for the 419 their condition may be imagined. The composition of guests at the Prince of Wales' dinner party last night is significant of the happy position his Royal Highness occupies in politics. It is presumed that he has political views, and it is said they tend in a Conservative direction. But no one by any overt or covert act of the Prince would be able to guess. It will be remembered how in 1880 when to the consternation of the Conserva- tives Mr. Gladstone was triumphantly returned to power, one of the first to call upon him was the'. Prince of Wales. Sir Charles Dilke and Mr. Cham- berlain are frequent and favoured guests at Marl- borough House, where, as ,last night, they meet some of the chiefs of the Conservative party. Side by side at the Prince's hospitable table last night sat Mr. Gladstone,,and Lord Salisbury; Lord Hals- bury and Lord Rosebery ; Lord Hartington and the Earl of Iddesleigh ; Sir Lyon Playfair and Mr. Raikes •, Mr. Chamberlain and Lord Randolph Churchill—this last a by no means unusual thing,

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL, MEETING 01 SHAREHOLDERS.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL, MEETING 01 SHAREHOLDERS.

The tint ordinary meeting of this company was held at the Concert Hall, Peter-street, Manchester, on Monday. The chairman of the board (Mr. Daniel Adamson) presided, and there was a very large attendance of shareholders, the number who gave up tickets at the door being 1,117, includ- ing many ladies. The Creeettneer, on rising to move the adoption of the report, was received with cheers. He said the total amount spent by the Provisional Committee during its existence was £146.003 8s sd; of that sum they had actually paid £126,796 Os I'd, having in hand atl the end of last year £1,886 14s 2d towards payment of the debts remaining through the Parliamentary operations. Towards the total sum he had mentioned they had actually received £128,682 14e. After the bill had been passed the Provisional Com- mittee retired, and the directors as appointed by the Act took their place. They did not think it necessary to make further calls on the subscriptions, because that would have given rise to considerable bookkeeping, but each subscriber becoming a shareholder was credited with an equivalent sum. That, however, left the Provisional Committee in an indebtedness of £27,122 Os 9cl in respect of unpaid accounts. The gross expenditure to secure the bill in every way was £150,000 in round figures. At the beginning of last year representations had been made by the directors to the Pro- fessional gentlemen who had been engaged in the course of the Parliamentary fight with a view to their taking a charitable view and reducing the amount of their fees ; he was happy to say that many of the engineers and other professional men had met the directors by dividing their accounts into two and accepting half of what they were entitled to. (Cheers.) The committee had been careful from the commencement to over rather than under estimate the cost of the undertaking, and they had the satisfaction of being told by Mr. Leader Williams that there was no doubt that responsible contrac- tors would be found to execute the works for as little as, if not less, than the parliamentary estimates. (Cheers.) Be- fore going into the Committee of the House of Lords, Lord Redesdale struck his pea through the clause in the bill giv- ing power to pay interest during construction, and the pro- moters were then unable to alter his lordship's opinion upon that matter, sad the Act which was obtained did not contain that power. He thought it was only right that he should ' make known exactly what had taken place with reference to the arrangement with the Messrs. Rothschild. All that Messrs. Rothschild asked was 1 per cent, for negotiating the whole busineris,*provided that the interest bill was passed. About £750,000 bad already been subscribed, and the pass- ing of this Interest Bill would enable large numbers of the investors to take up shares proportionate to their means. On the whole, the company ROW occupied a better position than they had done before, and their prospects of getting the money required were morally certain. He and the Board had received communications from Germany, France, and other countries which led him to the conclusion that the three years' fight they bad had was three years of great national advertisement, and that the canal was now as well known throughout Europe as the London and North-Western Rail w<y, and better apereciated. (Cheers.) The directors had coaled° the conclusion that in a large undertaking like this it WAS desirable to strengthen the Board by the addition of citizens who would accept such responsible positions, and the gentlemen suggested were Mr. W. H. Elouldsworth, M.P., seir Jos. Cocksey Lee, Mr. John Rogerson, and Alder- man William Henry Bailey. There was one name that should eever be lost sight of; and although the directors had not always had the pleasure of his presence, they had had his support and heartfelt good wishes, and he would like him to feel that the shareholders appreciated the great assistance he had rendered them—he referred to John Rylands—(loud cheers) who bdd already subscribed £50,000, and who would doubtless be ready, if it be- came necessary, to subscribe £25,000 or £50,000 more. ' (Cheers.) It being now 12 o'clock, the meeting was adjourned for the purpose of holthng an extraordinary meeting convened at that hour for the despatch of special business, viz., th 9 approval of a bill now before Parliament. The CHAIRM&N, amongst other things, stated that the object of the bill was to enable the directors to pay interest during the period of construction at the rate of 4 per cent. per annum, but sot exceeding in all £752,000. The Chair- man concluded by moving a resolution approving of the bill. Mr. SAMUEL Prarr seconded the motion, which was unanimously carried. The ordinary meeting was then resumed. The CHAIRMAN having moved the adoption of the report, the motion was seconded by Mr. JAMES PLATT, and carried unanimously. Mr. REUBEN SPENCER moved—" That Daniel Adamson, Henry Boddington, jun., Jacob Bright, William Fletcher, Richard Husband, Charles Paton Henderson, jun., Richard James, Joseph Leigh, James Edward Platt, Samuel Rad- cliffe Platt, and John Rylands, being 11 of the first directors of the compeny, be and they are hereby continued in office as directors of the company." (Cheers.) Mr. W. H. Jos:more seconded the resolution, which was carried by a unanimous vote. Mr. W. H. Houldsworth, M.P., was elected a member of the board, in the place of Mr. Greaves. Messrs. Besdin, T. Leech. and George Hicks were elected shareholders' auditors, and tide concluded the business of the ordinary meeting. The meeting then proceeded to the transaction of special business. It was resolved that the number of directors be increased from twelve to fifteen, and Sir Joseph Cocksey Lee, Mr. John Rogerson (Durham), and Mr. Wm. Henry Bailey (Salford) were elected directors. Dr. Mecxen proposed that the remuneration of the direc- tors be £2,000 a year. He urged their getting to work. If needed, they would send them directors from Runcorn and Warrington, who would push them on. Warrington would it due, goof atthi et and ne de n faol rt tt hethde?VliCn e - toria." Cheers.) that tofiwndn tihf etinheyawsotua Mak)! STOTT seconded the resolution, which was carried. The auditors salary was fixed at £lOO each per annum. the remuneration of the secretary being left to the discre- tion of the directors. Sir JOSEPH LEE moved, "That the remainder of the s 1885 hare, caanpdi tnaol taanl thre ao dr iyz ecdr ebayt etdh, eblSe I carnecaht eeds t,earnSd htihpa tCtahnea dl iAr ecct., atsuthanodrizmedanntoeri,stsouesutlaceh sax., a torst subceh atni es, theyin aresuc hh earn% buyn n lens, on such terms, and subject to such conditions as they think advantageous to the Company." Dr. PARKHURST seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. The common seal of the company having been affixed to the register of shareholders, Mr. J. T. W. MITCHELL, president of the Co-operative Wholesale Society, proposed a vote of thanks to the chair- man. The services which Mr. Adamson had rendered would be recorded on a page which time itself could net wipe out. (Cheers). Alderman BURGESS (Warrington) seconded the vote, and said he thought the company had been wonderfully fortu- nate in having Mr. Adamson as their guide in obtaining the Act. No man could have more patiently waited and exer- cised more forbearance. Having brought the Manchester Ship Canal to its present stage, Mr. Adamson was unques- tionably better adapted than any man present to carry the matter to completion. (Cheers.) Sir JOSEPH LEE put the resolution, which was carried with three times three and a profuse waving of hats. Ihe CHAIRMAN, in reply, said that after the kind recep- tion which the meeting had afforded him, he would feel abundantly encouraged to continue the work until the ships of all nations floated in their midst. (Loud cheers.) The proceedings then terminated.
The Manchester ship Canal Company, on Tuesday, paid into the Bank of England the sum of £2090 on account of the purchase of the Bridgewater Navigation Company's undertakings.

AN •ANNOYLNCII AT WABORANT. At the Newton Town Hall, on Monday, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, David Pennington, of Burtonwood, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Wargrave, on Sunday. P.C. McMullen deposed that the prisoner was" staggering" about the foot- patb, jostling people and insulting them as they passed along. A. fine of 5s and costs was imposed. POLITICS AND DRINIL—James Killelea, of Earles- town, was summened at the Newton Petty Sessions on Satur- day for being drunk and disorderly at Earlestown on the 2nd ult. After Constable Lloyd had given evidence in sup- port of the charge, the defendant said he was not drunk, be bad only been speaking about Liberals and Tories. He had slid there were more Irish and Welsh Liberals than Tories, but his friend bad said it was the other way about. He called a witness to support bin assertion. The witness said the defendant had had only two glasses of beer, but on be- ing pressed by Superintendent Weir be admitted that the de- fendant was not sober, adding "and he was not drunk."-- The defendant was fined 5s and costs. MEDICINES, ELASTIC BTOCKINGS. CHEMICALS, DRUGS, Ice., by rarcels post, under lib.. 3d. Kay, Brothers, Stockport.— Advt.

PRFSCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting was held on Thursday forenoon at the Workhouse, Whiston, when there were present Mr. J. Leatherbarrow (in the chair), Rey. J. Barnacle, Messrs. J. T. H.ll, W. Birchall, James Buckley, Williim G. Ash- ton, William Tyrer, James Fisher T. Dubell, T. Eatock, J. Lowe, J. Griffiths, J. KenwriglA, E. Sythr, W. Swift, J. Ellison, J. Agnew, R.. Leigh, 11. Hulme. W. New- some, T. Sadler, W. Gerrard, F. Hill, Joseph Jackson, and S. H. Hartley (clerk).

WORXHOUSE MASTER'S RRIPORT. The Workhouse Master reported there were 496 inmates of the workhouse this week, 498 last week, and 481 in the corresponding week last year. Thirty-six vagrants had been relieved, against 37 in the corresponding week last year. He further reported the gift of a large number of periodicals for the use of the inmates of the orkhouse from Mrs. Gerald Rawlins, of Laurel Bank, Rainhill. The thanks of the Guardians were tendered to the donor. MEDICAL ornmaas AND THEIR DUTIBS: STRICTURES ON DR. COOPER. The Clerk read a communication from the Local Govern- ment Board enclosing an extract from the report of Mr. Haslehurst, district auditor, with regard to omissions from the list of "necessaries ordered to 4e given to patients" in the medical relief books furnished to the medical Officers of St. Helens, Sutton, and Widnes. Upon the receipt of that communication he wrote to the medical officers in question, and had received their replies —Dr. McNic )11 (St. Helens) said if his assistant had not copied the orders, as he ought to have done, be would see that it was done in the future. Dr. Casey (Sutton) replied that he hasi no explanation to affix, las he had not thought the matter so important. He could I only remember two cases of omission for the past two years.. IDr. Cooper (Widnes) was sorry to learn that there were some omissions. He took every care in keeping a correct record, and was at a loss to know on what date such omis- sions bad occurred. Daring his holidays his deputy might not have been particular in putting down necessities ordered as he was not used to he work. In future he would take every care to carry out the instructions of the Board cor- rectly.—During a discussion which ensued, the Clerk explained that it was very important the books should be properly kept, and that the lists supplied by the medical officers correspondt d with the books. At present the medical officers sent be returns, and it was for the Guardians to say whether they would con- tinue to receive the returas, or whether the books must be produced. He thought the Guardians ought to have the books before them. They received the returns as a matter of convenience to the medical officers.—Mr. Doball : Their own irregularities have brought this about. There was a great discrepancy in Dr. Cooper's book and his sheet —Mr. Hall moved that they receive the sheets as usual; but the Clerk said that did not need a resolution.—Mr. Dobell said it was a good suggestion that they should have the books before than for the purposes of comparison.—Mr. Kenwright subsequently moved that Dr. Cooper be called upon to resign, as he thought he was unfitted for the post. —The Chairman: There are other doctors mentioned as well.—The Clerk explained that in September Dr. Cooper's appointment would lapse, and tbey might then consider whether to re-appoint him.--Mr. Kenwright said he was aware of that, but he would move that Dr. Cooper be asked to resign. If a man was not doirsg his work they did not want him any longer.—Mr. J. T. Hall seconded the mo- tion.—The Chairman said that that matter could be con- sidered after they had dealt ,vith the other question.—Mr. Dobell then moved, 11r. Longton seconded, and it was resolved, that the medical officers of the Union be requested to forward their relief books to the Guardians' meetings instead of their re- turn sheets as hitherte.—'rhe motion of Mr. Kenwright was next discuseed, Mr. Hill asking if they had power to summarily dismiss any officer.—The Clerk said it would rest with Dr. Cooper if they called upon hint to resign. He could either do so or he could refuse to do so.—Mr.bDobell said he had been engaged for twelve menths and he thoueht the matter might rest in abeyance until them—This course was agreed to and the motion was withdrawn.

THB ROMAN CATHOLIC BURIAL DIFFICULTY. The Clerk said the burial difficulty had been settled, and read the following letter from the Rev. Father Winkler : "Portico, 23rd January, 1886. Dear air,—l hereby beg to inform you that I have artan;ed the matter with Father Brindle and that the burial service will be continued in the Catholic Church, at Prescot, the same way as before.— Yours, ttc., B. M. WINKLER." (Hear, hear.) He reported that he had received a lengthy letter from the Rev. Father Brindle explaining his reasons why he had taken the course he'had adopted, and the Board decided to take the letter as read.

THE DEATH OF DR. MILLNER. A letter was read from the Rev. J. Barnacle, Rainford Vicarave, stating that Mrs. Millner wished him to intimate that Dr. Millner, union medical officer for the Rainford district, died on Wednesday, the 27th ult. The doctor had been .a great. sufferer for a long time, but persevered in order to fulfil his duties.—The Clerk pointed out that the offices of medical officer and vaccination officer for the Rainford district had just become vacant, and as there was no duly qualified medical practitioner residing in that district, he suggested that the matter should remain in abeyance until such time as the Guardians could make a permanent ap- pointment. He had communicated with Dr. Casey, of the Sutton district, and that gentleman bad expressed his wil- lingness to do anything to oblige the Guardians.—The Rev. J. Barnacle moved, Mr. hill seconded, and it was resolved, that the appointment of a successor to Dr. Millner should re- main in abeyance, and that Dr. Casey be asked to perform the duties for the present.—The Clerk slid he had received a letter from Dr. Anderson, of Billings, in reference to the question, but as there was not a duly qualified medical man in the district, it could not be entertained.

A PREMIUM FOR DESERTION. The Clerk read a letter from one of the relieving officers stating that two batches of men had recently been sent to America from the Widnes district, and in many cases the men were married and had left their families in a destitute condition. He was afraid there would be a large influx of women and children into the Workhouse in consequence. —Mr. Hall said there were six cases, including twenty peo- ple, before the Relief Committee that morning, and the relieving officer had told him that there would probably be twenty-five more cases at the next meeting. It would be a very serious matter for the Union to have to maintain the families of the men sent to America, and he thought it should be publicly known that when an appeal was made for contributions towards paying the fares of working-men they were assisting men to leave their families to be main- tained by the Union.—Mr. Hill thought it was offering a premium for desertion.—Mr. Hall said it was the case of taking away the head of the family and bread-winner, and leaving their families chargeable to the rates. If the whole family was taken away they would have no reason to corn- nlain.—The Clerk said if they knew the time when the men intended to start for America they might be stopped under warrant as they would be in the act of deserting their families. Mr. Fisher asked if a comrnunicatien from that Board would do any geod.—The Clerk suggested that the American Consul be seen on the matter, and then it might be possible to stop the landing of any man in America who had deserted his family.—lt was decided on the motion of Mr. Dobell, seconded by the Rev. J. Barnacle, that that course should be adopted.— Mr. Newsome said it was rumoured that the men— chemical labourers—were required to fill the places of men oat on strike at Philadelphia.—:11r. Tyrer : They will find it a very hot shop.

COUNTY RATES. . The Clerk reported the receipt of 'a precept from the de- puty clerk of the peace for the county requiring the Guar- dians to pay the sum of £7,299 103, the proportion due to- wards the county rates. It was decided to leave the payment until it was due, THE OFFICERS' SECURITIES, The Clerk suggested that the question of the securities of the Union officers should be taken into consideration by the Guardians.—After some conversation the matter was referred to the Finance Committee.

THE IJISCONDING OVERSEER. The Clerk said he had received a letter • from Mr. Henry Anderson, secretary tl the London Guarantee and Accident Society, who wrote under date January 25th— "Re Wood.—ln reply to your letter of the 22nd inst., we scarcely see how our offer to pay in advance part of a pos- sible claim can be so twisted as to justify a demand for pay- ment of the whole amount, and if the Gulrdians are not disposed to adopt our proposition,.there is an end to the matter so far, which must stand over in the ordinary course for the usual proofs." He (the clerk) explained that " proofs " meant the certificate of the district auditor that there were certain sums due from the overseer.—Mr. New- some afterwards asked if they bad any further information respecting the absconding overseer.—Mr. Hartley (clerk) said he had heard nothing of Mr. Wood, and it would be impossible to ascertain the exact amount deficient until the accounts had been certified by the district auditor. He had reason to believe that the amount would not vary much from the amount he had previously stated—namely, about £1,200 As the 'assistant overseer, he was desirous of closing all the current rates by the 25th March, so that the new overseer might start with a clean book, and have everything 'straightforward. He afterwards asked the Guardians to allow him something on account of the expenses incurred while acting as assis- tant overseer for the Woolton district. He remarked that he had clerks working for him..—On the motion of Mr. Dobell, seconded by Mr. Newsome, it was resolved to allow the Clerk £3O on account.—Mr. Newsome gays notice that at the next meeting he would move that the remuneration to be paid to the assistant overseer for the Woolton district be 5d in the pound instead of 6d in the pound on the amount collected.

RELIEF CASES. Mr. Rail moved that a return be furnished to the next meeting showlng the number of cases sent to the Workhouse during the oast year by their medical officers, and also the population of each medical officer's district.—Mr. Tyrer seconded the motion, which was casriod. This concluded the business.
COAGVLINE.—Cement for Braken Articles, 6d. Is, 2s postage 2nd. everywhere. Kay, Bros., Btockporc.—Advt.

FATALITY AT PEWFALL COLLIEEY.—On Friday, Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at Garwood on the body of John Birchall, thirty-eight years of age, who lived at Haydock. On the previous Monday he was at work in No. 2 pit, Pewfall Colliery, when a fall of roof occurred, and, being struck .with a large stone, fatal in- juries were inflicted.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

A reserveir at Roberta Island, California, has burst, caus- ing the inundation of 35,000 acres of land. The damage is estimated at 600,000 dollars. MUTINY ON REFORMATORY SHIF.—A mutiny of an alarming character took place on Monday on the ship Clarence, the Roman Catholic reformatory ship lying in the Mersey. On Sunday evening about eight of the lads refused to attend mass on board the vessel, and although little or nothing had been said to them, their discontent developed on Monday morning into direct disobedience of orders. They then became uproarious, and being joined by five others, went about the ship possessing themselves of any Weapons they could lap their hands on. Belaying pins, and several iron bars about four feet long, fell into their hands. They then made towards the boats lying in the vessel's davits, bat were followed by several other lads who are known as quartermasters, and also the officials. The mu- tineers kept the quartermasteru and others off, and cut the boats adrift, but they themselves were prevented getting into them. Three of the quartermasters were wounded in the head, and a fourth received injury to his shoulder. Mr. Potter, the schoolmaster, was also wounded. The scene whilst it lasted was most alarming, but fortunately the re- mainder of the boys did not join in the disturbance. The thitteen lads, each aged about 17 or 18 years, were charged before the Liverpool maaistrates on Tuesday morning with riotous conduct on board the Clarence, and also pith assaulting and wounding some of the officers. The case if as not gone into, a remand being grantee' until Thursday, owing to the serious condition of Instructor Connolly. Statements from the boys were read, in which they alleged that they had been brutally treated by the officers of the vessel. _ _

POVERTY." The opportunity has lately been afforded me of visittig the estates of Col. Edwards, in Shropshire, who desires it to be known that he is of Conservative politics' and who made use (-)f the words at the head of these remarks, as the corn- pthe etttat justification of his adherence to the system of tabtaurers' Smell Holdings, which has long prevailed on elal ate of which he is the present owner. The facts 1 rae izindly enabled to glean from occupiers of the holdings n cluptien are in many ways of deep interest, and should en- e"rtge all those who believe that in this direction is to be "3,1211° a solution of the difficulties arising from the flocking °II the rural population to the towns, and the labour starving 0... thelt_land, to say nothing of she large area of tenantless "'`fr„es this emeetry. On the estate in question, as I had the opportunity of nesting, j there are, besidA the large farm tenancies, twenty holdinB of 13 acres and under, occupied by labourers, or ernalltalaaesmen, embracing almost every vocation of the n ccu • t side. The rent roll for eight years past showed so arrears, and the occupiers themselves assured me they bad made nr) claim for deductions, because they had needed none. The owleer's verdict was that he found the route of his small holdings as safe as consols. On intleriting the property he had been urged to do away with the small holdings and throw them into adjoining farms, belt had declined to do so; and the gratitude of the thriving and contented occupiers must in itself be a reward for a deei Ilion which in its results should widely commend the exathEple of 001. Edwards to other landowners, as it will certa inly strengthen the hands of those who are urging its adopti. an on public grounds. In my ireeaad through the village I was accompanied by a man in Cealonel Edwards's employ, who was a warnatsuppor- ter, naturally, of a policy which allowed of his renting a small farmi of four and three-quarter acres. What his wages were'l I did not learn, but the average agricultural wages were twelve shillings per week. The people visited answered hay questions with the greatest readiness and intel- ligence, wh.en their first fears, that they were being inter- viswed by (•-ine who desired to take away their land and add it to the larree farms, were allayed. Taking a few of the cases of PeoPle visited—No. 1 had a holding, as stated above, of four and three-quarter acres, for which he paid a rent of £l4, including his house. One cow was kept, which I saw comfortably ' hewed and feeding with a floe calf by her side. Grazing mute were two nice yearling heifers, worth e,er- tainly £8 eat ,h, which were shortly to be sold. Two pigs were in the s4y, and a geed number of poultry were kept besides. Tht'. little farm was divided into three well-kept fields, and, as its tenant proudly said, he didn't think there was a prettierf little home in England. The house-mother said, truly en ough, what : help the milk had been in the rearing of her family of eleven children. Answering the question, consi antly put as to how the cow was first get on a waggoner's yi .ages, she replied—" If e saved a bit of money in younger day s, before we were married, and laid it out on a cow, and I feincy most do that way." The wife milks and makes the butter; the husband, as it was explained, in winter time sorlietimes not seeing his farm and stock by day- light from Sane.jay to Sunday. The produce from the farm c consumed every the bacon and Pt.ark of two large pigs, a constant Supply of year at home was 11Ias. of butter per week, skim milk, bead, taa eggs and an occasional fowl. Two calves were reared annt•tally and the butter would bring in £l2 a year. Altogethei the sales would not be less than £35 a year, besides the t'aome consumption, which would be worth little, if anything,'.' short of ten shillings per week Purchases of meal for the pik.o, of bran • aad some roots for the cow, . would be the ehie, items of outlay beyond the rent. The tenant paid some c.eie else to get in his hay, helped by the

wife. did the live stock; and surely a system which enables a bereaved woman to stay on in her little farm and pay her way is to be preferred to one whose first thought was parish relief in some shape, and which, it the best, would have forced her into some uncongenial occupation. The last case, No. 4, which I would shortly allude to, is perhaps the most striking of all. The farm was one of 13 acres, and the tenant as usual was absent at his work. He was a farm labourer earning thirteen shillings per week, and had boon at the same place for 30 years. He had a stock of three cows, three yearling heifers, and aix sheep, the lambs from which were usually sold in August for alsont 355. each. The wife was dead, and the little farm was looked after by a daughter. Abundance of provisions were consumed in the, ' house from the farm. The man had begun with a smaller farm of three acres, and had gradually saved enough to stock a larger one. The capital on this farm would considerably exceed £lOO, and that the man was not spoiled as a labourer was proved by his long continuance under the same em- ployer. Such facts as the foregoing would suggest that Colonel Edwards's statement, that the village was one without poverty, would be true of countless other villages were the plan iatroduced into them which has proved so good and wholesome in its results in this Shrobekire parish. Is a matter of fact, out of a population of 000 people, the follow- ing is the pauper list, viz.: one lunatic, two over 80 years of age, one cripple, and one person of bad character who had recently arrived. It is not contended that the presence of 4ve-and-twenty email holdings alone produced the bene- ficial results, but the prospect of occupying similar farms in due time. The hope of saving suffieient to stock a farm and gain a profit on the savings against old age, must every- where form the most powerful incentive to thrift. ' Of the sordid economy which we are told characterises the small occupier there was no trace. Of happiness and contentment, , of abundant food and health, of prosperous and thriving little farmsteads there was every proof. Surely the efforts of those who by every means desire to extend the system of Labourers' Holdings throughout the country find abundant justification in this village, where, broadly speaking, as compared with other parts of the coun- try, "there is no poverty."—From "Three Acres and a Cow," by Frederick Impey.
