&THREE ACRES AND A COW."

- Sir,—The question asked by" Ignorant" in your last issue is one that troubles many. He is not alone in his ignorance. Leoking over a Newcastle paper, I dad that several correspondents give various versions of the origin of the term. One haz irds a rather ctrious theory that the phrase has a c-innectisn with one frequently used in America, on toe occesion of the first election after the War. Democratic candidates for the Southern States, he says, during that election, offered to every negro who would vote the Democratic ticket " forty acres and a mule." The elements in each ca=e, land and live stock, are, as he claims, the same, but I think we shall have to look nearer home for the correct solution. Anot,teer correspondent attributes the phrase to Sir M. Hicks-Beach, and a third to Mr. Chamber- lain, who, he says, popularised it by making use of it in one or two of his public utterances. This correspondent gives a quotation that may explain the true origin. At least, it is as good a one as I- have vet seen. He quotes from John Stuart Mill's work on "The Principles of Political Economy," people's edition, publ'shed in 1369, where the author deals with the question of small agricultural holdings ,and refers more particularly to the system of cultivation adopted by the peasants of Flanders. The words are, 4. When the land is cultivated entirely by the spade, and no horses are kept, a cow is kept for every three acres' of land, and entirely fed on artiflcial grasses and roots. This wide of cultivation is principally adopted in the Waes district, where the properties are very small." It is quite possible that whoever brought the words "Three acres and a cow" into such notoriety may have read the above pas- sage.—Yours, dtc., H. S.

SOCIAL EQUALITY. Sir,—Mr. Chapman is not an exacting catechist. Were he a school inspector there would be very little complaint in his district of over-pressure of the juvenile brain. He is evidently too benevolent to set questions which would have the effect of raising in any one who had to answer them the unpleasant feeling that they were "in a corner." I will deal with the list of queries he has put to me in the order in which I can do so most briefly. He asks, "Will 'Jacques' explain the difference between a capitalist land- lord and a capitalist trader? " Wetl, there is a slight difference. It le the difference that exists between a thing that is and a thing that is not. There is such a thing as a "capitalist trader," hut there is no such thing as a "capi- talist landlord." The landowner is a monopolist, the capitaliet is not; and therefore there is as much difference between them as there can be between two things which are in their very nature different. This, of course, is a piece of very elementary political economy; but as Mr. Chapman , appears to have overlooked it, I may perhaps give an illus- tration of *hat it means. Let us suppose in the case of one of the factories or workshops in Warrington that the buildings and machinery belonged to a "capitalist trader," and the land upon which they stand belongs to what Mr. Chapman improperly calls a "capitalist landlord." The trader has no monopoly of buildings and machinery of that description; a huadrd, or any number of other similar factories or workshop, might be erected, and, and would be if they were found to be unusually remunerative. But as for the site upon which the factory stands that is a mono- poly, and cannot be reduplicated. If the site afford any peculiar facility for production, the landlord will obtain all the extra profit. The manufactarer, who has no monopoly of buildings or machinery, can expect nothing more than the cerrent returns upon the kind of capital he possesses. If he obtained more than this others would embark in the name business, and by competition quickly bring down his profite. Mr. Chapman is again thirsting after very elementary in- formation whets he inquires, "Will 'Jaques' also show how fortunes are or can be made by one or more individuals without a corresponding loss to a larger number of other individuals? " The answer is that if a man creates his own fortune he takes nothing from anybody else. If by the exetrien of his own talent, skill, or industry, he adds as much or more to the aggregate wealth of the country in which he resides as his own fortune consists of, there is no corresponding loss to other individuals. Let a capitalist in- troduce a new industry into Warrington which increases the annual wealth produced in the town by £20,000, would anyone be the poorer? Certainly not, but many would be the better off, because although the capitalist might secure a very comfortable income out of the £20,000, far the "larger part of ft would have to be distributed amongst a larger number of other individuals" in the shape of work- men. But introduce a landlord, a man who "toils not neither does he spin," and then the case is different. He does nothing to augment the annual wealth of the town, and the more his income is increased, the greater is the "corresponding loss" to a larger number of other in- dividuals.

As Mr. Chapman says, the question of Communism is a wide one, and I shook! have liked to give my definition of what I cell " the unnatural equality of Communism" at greater lergth than, I am afraid, your correspondence column will allow of. The ideal commonwealth of the Communist is one in which men are to work according to their capacity, and to receive of the produce of the commu- nity accend'n,g to their wants. Thie is an arbitrery and artificial mekhod of rewarding labour which will inevitably tend to reduce men to a common standard. Men labour be- cause they have desires to gratify, and if in the communal state the desires of the man who labours little, or is capable of only inferior work, be as amply gratified as those of a man who is capable of extraordinary achievements, you take away the incentives of the latter. The equality of Commu- nism iS unnatural, because it is contrary to the great natural Jaw of evolution which asserts that human progress is due to the elimination of the feebler and least capable, and the preservation cf the superior types of human beings. if men receive according to their wants the incapable and the capable are alike preserved, and therefore a communal state would almost certainly fall behind in the race of progress, and ultimately he extinguished by some more developed community, whose progress had been less impeded by artifi- cial fetters.

Ia conclusion, sir, may I venture to advise Mr. Chapman that whn, he comes to make the farther remarks he has promised, and which I am sure will be valuable and inter- esting, he will clearly keep In mind the difference between landlordism and capitalism. Unless he does this, I am afraid his conclusions will be as unreliable as those of an arithmetician. who dealt with the figures three and six as if they meant the szme thing.
JAQUES.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRADES COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TRADES COUNCIL.
Sir.—A very few words will satisfy me in noticing Mr. Will's kind and gentlemanly letter published in your last bane.

The Council numbers more members than I was aware of, 1 and their meetings must be of a most exciti .g and interest- I ing character, seeing that sue society, the Thick Iron and Steel Wire Drawers' Society, " is already represented by 200 members on the Council." If the other societies in the town manage to send as many delegates. Mr. Wild's position as secretary will be no sinecure. I think "a guiding star" may be required if the sugges- tion contained in Mr. Wild's letter is based on fact. How do your readers interpret the following P—" Vonbtless a short sketch of their proceedings would have been interest- ing to your readers, especially to Mr. Whitham." Reading between the line,, to me this is a simple confession that the Warrington Trades Council has no more important businese than listening to slander. If so, the sooner it ceases to exist the better. There would then be room for a modern, and not an antideluvian Trades Council. Speaking seriously. I want to know what the Council has done to benefit trade, or to secure better wages I' It bus now been in existence a ;umber of years, and all that I can learn of its doings is that it his always been willing to endorse the decision arrived at by trades represented on the Council to strike. So much for Mr. Wild's letter, but I have yet another document before me, for which I am indebted tO. his kind- ness. This is the balance sheet of the Warrington Trades Council for the year 1885. I find that five trade societies , are represented on the Council, whose contributions, dating from October 7th, 1884, to April 7th, 1885, amount to 12 12s 4d. In addition to these is the Wiredrawers' Society, whose contributions for the same period amount to £2 is Bd. Clearly, from this. it would never do for the Council to offend the delegates of the Wireirawers' Society, or they would, to use Mr. Wild's elegant language, "se snuffed cut." With this balance sheet is tacked on a report, in which reference is made to "prejudiced and bigoted minds," and a hearty wish is expressed against " conciliating " such like, as none but "observing and thrugbtful men " are required. lam interested in these passages. "An honest tale epeeds best, being plainly told." The passages I quote are not plainly told; they are fall of ambiguity. The writer of the report having unfortunately commenced by making ridicu- lous charges, is forced to go on with them. He says : "We regret that evil influences oil:weld be at work ceasing wrong impressions to be made regarding the objects of Trade Unionism." I should be very sorry if Buch a charge as this was laid at my door. Yet I have a strong impres- sion the cap was intended for me. I therefore propose to notice the whole of the paragraphs relating to wiredrawers. I take the first, which reads :—" We notice with satisfaction an improvement of the wiredrawing trade of the town, and generally throughout the country during the last few month's." Rather a rich bit that, Mr. Editor, to set before men who; for the last twelve months, have been working three and four days a week. It is only equalled for stu- pidity by a further statement that the "men are now work- ing fall time." I don't know a time when, during the past ten years, they would have been justified in making such a statement. True, there has been occasional spurts, but a sustained trade is indeed a thing of the past. The tit-bit of the report is the following :—" A most special feature in the wire trade of the town being that one large firm has now ceased to import German wire for netting, thereby admitting that they can compete success- fully with the Germans ra result most gratifying to us as workmen)." Would it be fair to ask these wiseacres to whom these " most gratifying " results are due P Was it due to their foresight, when during the first strike they, at the bidding of blind guides, walked about the streets of Warrington far six months rather than do what they could to enceurage 5 trade that, to use their own words," has found work for a•larger bpdy of men I"' I ask do these men who always

promise, panso, prepare, p,stpone And end by letting things alone; take praise to thr,mselves for bringing about this " reeult most gratifying?' Was it during the second strike that these so-called Trade Unionists betrayed any keenness of perception? Did they not try their utmost to give the lie to their employers when told that better machinery and a better class of mate- rial would be provided for them P The fact la, tdr, they
have been mistaken in their conclusions all through, and do not like to confess it.

Could these men look at trade questions from a purely historic point of view, they vreuld know that there are forces at work over which they have no control ; and all they can do is to so bend and mould circumstances that they shall not be its victims. I have no wish to pile up the agony, but it may be that a bad future is before us. Bel- gians. Frenchmen, and Germans are closely insitating us and building up large trade centres. The markets that are open to Us are open to them, and the industrial aupreinacy of England is threatened. What are workmen going to do? Are they going to wait for capitalists to take the nutter into their own hands and then cum capital instead of blaming their own supineness? In many trades now a grand oppor- tunity exists for workmen reclaiming their lost position : will they use it ?—Yours, kc., H. WHITHAM. , Feb let, 188 G.

div.head: PEACE SOCIETY.
div.p: THE PEACE SOCIETY.

Sir,—An old proverb tall us " There are none so blind as those who won't see," arad I feel I must include " Hodge" in that category. He seems to act en the principle that " Where ignorance le bliss, 'tis folly to be wise." Yet his affected ignorance of one class of circumstances is made too transparent to deceive anyone by his evident acquaint- ance with other collateral circumstances. He has evidently considerable skill in the use of that commodity which he calls sophistry; and by which he manages to twist and dis- tort the meaning of an opponent, and to explain away the blunders of his political chief. But even in this be lacks inish, and will require a let of practice before he manages to convince anyone not blinded by prejudice that a false statement, made to deceive, is strictly and " absolutely true," but more of that anon. " If," says lodge," it be Mr. itathbonee purpose to prove that the Peace Society metes out equal treatment to Tories and Liberals when they engage in war he has undertaken a hopeless task." Ale! "there be much virtue in an if;" but where will he find any expression of mine that bears out such an assumption. I certainly never had any such intention. To do so would be as manifestly unjust as for a judge to mete out equal treatment to one men convicted of manslaughter, and ano- ther of wilful murder. To say that the Peace Society had condoned the offences of Liberal Governments against their principles is one thing, but to say that it has not meted equal treatment to Tory and Liberal for those offences is entirely another. It must ever be borne in mind that although the Peace Society bits persistently condemned and protested againit the wars of the Liberal Governments, it has had to recognise the fact that whatever support and encomegement it has ever rebeived from either party as ' such has come from the Liberal,and not from the I Conserva- tive petty. That the members of the society in the House of Commons have opposed the Liberal wars by every means in their power, as well as those in the country, history will testify, as in the case of the Crimean war, and the Chinese war of the lorcha Arrow, ay! and every other war of the last half century. It was in consequence of their opposi- tion to the two wars above named that several prominent members of the society lost their seats in Parliament, nota- bly tleoee of Cobden at Huddersfield, and Milner Gibson and Bright at Manchester (but which Manchester afterwards bitterly repented), which called forth that address of char- acteristic outspoken honesty from Mr. John Bright when taking leave of the representation; wherein he declared it te be an honour to suffer in the cause of peace, and on be- half of what he considered is be the true interests of the country. As I said in my last letter the springs of their ac- tion have been from diametrically opposite motives when- ever the peace party and tae Conservatives appeared to be acting conjointly in opposition to the Liberal Government. Bearing all this mind, it is not difficult to account for the apparent difference in the strength of the opposition offered by the Peace Society to the late Liberal Government and their Tory predecessors. In the case of the Tories, the op- position was backed up by the whole strength of the Liberal party both in and out of Parliament ; and the, to 6, not because the Tory Government had not blustered enough, or had not been sufficiently aggressive; but because it had blusiered at all; because the Tories had adopted an ag- gressive policy in place of the peaceful policy of their pre- decessors ; because by this aggressive policy they had changed as by a magician's wand, a period of peace and prosperity into a period of turmoil and adversity, a sense of security and confidence into a sense of insecurity and danger; a condition of goodwill between ourselves and other nations into a condition of ill-will, bickerings, and actual strife ; a belief in our honour and integrity into a distrust of our ill-concealed devices, chicanery, and subterfuge; in short, the establised order of six years was reduced in a very short space of time to chaos. It must also be borne in mind that those difficulties which "crowded like waves upon them" were of their own creating, as the distinct outcome of that spirited foreign policy which they so loudly trum- peted forth on their accession to office. But can the same be said of the difficulties which beset their 'successors ? Aseuredlv not. It has been said, " The evil which men do In their lives, lives after them ; whilst the good is oft in- terred with their bones." And so it was that the evils of this sorry Administration lived after them, as a legacy be- queathed to their successors, and on which the Tories had been condemned and compelled to surrender the seals of office before the tribunal of the nation. Hence it was the crowning blunder of the late Liberal Government that it did not renounce at once and entirely, instead of tardily and partially, this policy of meddling and muddling ; and it was the inevitable consequence of this blunder that all their subsequent difficulties—so far as foreign policy is concerned—sprang. The peace party foresaw this, anal re- peatedly warned the Government that such would be the case. Were these warnings seconded by the Tories ? Cer- tainly not. On the contrary, they laughed them to deri- sion. But the time came for the fulfilment of these warn- ings, and with that the time for protest. Then the Tories In opposition took council among themselves, and concluded that there was an opportunity net to be lost, for, knewhag the consistency of the peace party, they saw that it would do all in its power to restrain any development of a bellicose tendency, and oppose to the utmost any actual warfare. They thereupon determined to act in apparent concert with the peace party in their opposition, and thus, without committing themselves to their principles, effect the overthrow of the Liberals. But if " Hodge " and the Tory party imagined Mr. H. Richard and his followers such a set of noodles as to fall into such a trap, they were most grievously mistaken. The cunning device was clearly seen through, and it was for this reason, and not because they were Tories merely, that Mr. Richard found it necessary to repudiate any alliance with them to overturn the late Gov- ernment. To have done so would have been jumping out of the frying pan into the fire ; and I contend there was nothing inconsistent in all this, nothing which lays thew' open to the implied charge by" lodge" of condoning the offences in one party which they condemn in the ether party. They are, generally, peace mere first and Liberals after. But if the Tory party will avow itself ready to honestly co-operate with them in carrying their principles to a practical issue, then, I will answer for it, that Henry Richard, ivith his colleagues at his beck, will most readily step forward and shake bands upon the compact. With regard to the second part of " Hodge's " last letter, I can easily understand the feeling of soreness which has been occasioned by recalling to his mind the distinguishing feature of Lord Salisbury's previous term of office ; but if he is wise he will drop the subject as he would a hot potatoe, for I assure him the more it is probed the more it will stink. He tells us that it is a calumny, based entirely On what has been called the " Salisbury-Schouvaloff episode," and also that what his lordship said on that memorable oc- casion was " absolutely true." Was it ? Well, let us see. First of all, however, we will see what his lordship's own idea of the truth may be, for if he has a different code of morals to our own, there may be some difficulty in substan- tiating the charge. 'lbis is what he says :—" He who em- ploys a less accurate term, when a more accurate term is available, is guilty of tampering with the purity of truth." Now, I am willing to accept that as the basis upon which to found the charge. It will be remembered that in June, Is7B, the country was startled beyond precedent by the publication of what purported to be a draft of a conveetion between Lord Salisbury and the Russian censul, Count Sehouvaloff. Lord Salisbury was questioned as to its ac- curacy, not authenticity, mind. His reply was that it was "wholly unauthentic," and "not worthy of confidence ;" but it turned out to be absolutely true in every particular. Was this reply, as " Hodge " says, " absolutely true ?" or was it, to put it mildly, " tampering with the parity of truth ?" " lodge" had better be careful, or he may find the stigma of his chief eticking to him, as well as the con- tagion of bis spirit. But that was not all ; otherwise such stigma would never have attached itself to his lordship's name. It is on record that after trying by threats and cajol- ing to compel the Ameer of Afghanistan to receive a resi- dent envoy, be declared to the House of Lords that they had not tried to force an envoy on the Ameer. There is also the unfortunate record of. both Lords Carnarvon and Derby giving him the " lie i'the mouth " for declaring that there had been no dissensions in the Cabinet, the sounds of which must have been still ringing in his ears when he compared Lord Derby to Titus Oates.

If " Hoage's " thirst for useful knowledge is not yet sat- isfied, I shall not object to indulge him a little further, al- though I have very little time at my disposal for this sort of thing. There are one or two other matters that I should like to have touched upon, such as the success and spread of the adoption of the Peace Society's principles, and the estima- tion in which its advocates are held, as opposed to the scorn and contempt alleged by' Hodge ;" but I find it difficult to crowd into the limits of one letter all one would wish to say, and must now draw this a'ready too long letter to a close. Thanking you for your past courtesy, I remain, yours, A. RATHBONE. 43, Arpley-strset, Warrington, January 27th, 1886. [With this letter, we must bring the correspondence on this topic to a close.—ED., Ex.]

Mrs. Fraser has intimated her intention of building, at a cost of £l,OOO, a chapel in the Manchester Cathedral as a site for the diocesan monument to her late husband, Bishop Fraser. WIFE MURDER—At Chester Assizes on Wednesday, be- fore Lord Chief Justice Coleridge, Owen aged 39 wears, was indicted for the murder of his wife. at Landican, near Birkenhead. The evidence showed that the accused, when under the influence of drink, beat his wife to death. He was found guilty, and sentenced to death. There was a very unusual scene at Knutsford when Owen M'Gill arrived by train from Chester. A great crowd had assembled and accompanied the convict and his guards to the gaol, indulg- ing in booting and yelling until M'Grill bad entered the building.

A GENEROUS OPFER. Mr. DEwitunsT said they were all aware that there had been a good deal of distress in Lymrn owing to the want of work, both out of door and in the fustian cutting. He be- lieved that in the fustian cutting there had been more work during the last two months, but it had been indifferently paid, the cutters dot having had much more than would keep body and soul together.—Mr • FORSTER said the trade had not been worse during the last 20 years.—Mr. DEWHURsT said be had been wondering if they do anything to alleviate the distress, and he thought they might do so by repairing some of the roads. He then enumerated cer- tain portions of the road which might be repaired. Tbe material for these repairs would, he said. cost about £25, and the manual labour £75. and if the Board would pro- vide for the former sum he would provide for the remainder. He thought they might in this way engage for two or three months twelve men, choosing men with tbe largest fami- lies. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. GIBBON moved that this generous offer of Mr. Dewhurst be accepted.—Mr. HALL, who said the offer of Mr. Dewburst would do a great deal of good, seconded the proposal, which was unanimously agreed to. This was all the business of public interest.

A DAIRY SCHOOL TOR CHESHIRE. Arrangements are now being entered into for the establishment of a dairy school for Cheshire. It is probable that buildings will be secured somewhere near Ctlester. The Duke of Westmin- ster, Lord Tollemache, and other leading landlords are sup- porting the echeral, and circumstances are now favourable to carrying it out.

SUSPECTED MURDER OF AN IRISH FARMER.—The body of a farmer named Michael Creggan, who resided at Fork- hill. hear Newry, where the recent agrarian murder occurred, and who disappeared on Christmas evening, was found in the Newry Canal on Friday morning. The body is much disfigured, and there is a vary deep wound on the top of the head which leads to the belief that the deceaLz.d was. murdered.

KILLBD BY A GOLF BALL.—At Hoylake on Friday morn- ing Dr. Churton, of Chester, coroner, held an inquest en the body of Edward Eccles, 16 years of age, who died from the effects of injuries sustained by being struck by a golf 13,111. In the course of a match at Hoylake one of the balls struck him on the back of the head and knocked him down. He died from the injury on Thursday. A verdict of acci- dental death was returned. WELSH LAND LBAGUB.—It is stated that Mr. Michael Davitt, who is at present in London with Mr. Parnell, will make a stay of some days in North Wales before his return to Ireland for the purpose of establishing the Welsh Land League. The objects of the proposed league will be to se- cure fair rents, security of tenure, abolition of the game laws, facilities for farmers and labourers to buy farms and holdings at fair rents on similar lines to the Irish land laws, freedom of Welsh rivers, and disestablishment and disen- dowment of the Church in Wales.

M‘Kane (C), 4.178; Mr. Leamy (N), 2,667. The vacancy was caused by the death of M. M‘Kane. DEATH OF MR. lit Tall MASON.—Mr. Hugh Mason, ex- member for Ashton-under-Lyne, and the defeated Liberal candidate for the constituency at the late election, died at eight o'clock on Tuesday evening. During the cotton famine Mr. Mason was the only manufacturer who kept his mills going at full time throughout. In the centre of the model cottages which he built near his mills he erected a building at the cost of £lO.OOO, containing a lecture-hall, baths, and workmen's club, attached to which was a cricket ground and a gymnasium. •
WARRINGTON.

THE REV. R. PILCHER, 8.A., will preach to- morrow (Sunday) evening in Cairo-street Chapel on "The true method of Bible study." OPENING SERVICES will be held to-morrow in the Working Men's Mission Chapel, Bank Quay. The preachers will be Mr. R. Johnson, of Manchester, and the Rev. Howell Jones.

COCKHEDGE MISSION MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT' SOCIETY.—On Monday evening Mr. Wm. Hocken- hull, jun., read a paper on "Perseverance." In the debate which ensued Messrs. Green, Roger, Blease, Broadhurst, Atherton, and Muskett took part. Mr. Matthew Hunt, vice-president of the society, occu- pied the chair.

"CHINA AND THE CHINESE."—A meeting of the Warrington Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Society was held on Wednesday evening, the Rev. J. H. Jones presiding. Mr. W. H. Bayley read an excel- lent paper on "China and the Chinese." The essayist gave a graphic description of the habits of the celes- tials, and their modes of government; the essay throughout was .of great interest. The following took part in the debate which followed :—Me§srs. J. Dixon, C. Plinston, J. Swift, W. J.. Dunn, and the Chairman.

KINDERGARTEN LECTURES.—Last evening Miss Warmington, head mistress of the Edge Hill Practising School, commenced a course of lectures on the kindergarten system of teaching, at the War- rington Training College. The success of similar lectures gi.ven previously was so marked that this year it was decided to offer teachers and students not connected with the college the opportunity of attending the course on stated terms, and about nineteen ladies living in and near Warrington took advantage of the offer, and will attend the lectures in conjunction with the second year students. The course is to be continued until the latter part of April, and the students will be weekly instructed in the various subjects now required in the attainment of a thorough knowledge of kindergarten. The I students are provided with books and material { necessary to the teaching of the system, which is one of the best methods of instructing the young. By means of it children are taught in the elementary stages to count numbers by means of beads, &c., and to derive a knowledge of formation by the placing of sticks in various positions; this is gradually developed into a knowledge of geometry. The children are not simply told how to count num- bers or form objects, but the value of their instruc- tion lies in their doing it themselves in a practical way, at first in simple ways until knowledge is surely obtained and higher branches of study are undertaken. Last evening was devoted to stage one , of drawing, which was ably explained and illus- trated by Miss Warmington, who secured the close attention of her pupils. The lectures give promise of being very successful. "Tin?: MIKADO."—On Monday and Tuesday Mr. D'Oyly Carte's celebrated opera company gave two performances of the new Japanese opera t` The Mikado," the joint production of Mr. W. S. Gilbert and Sir Arthur Sullivan. There was a very good at- tendance, especially in the better class seats, many of the .elite of the town and neighbourhood being present. The opera was both well mounted and well performed, the leading characters in the piece being each and all in the hands of thoroughly competent artistes. 7:-Though the most recent work of its joint authors, "The Alikado " is not the least interesting. The change of venue, though it does not affect the conventionality of much of the humour of the dia- logue, serves to give a refreshing newness to the conditions leading up to the various tableaux, and also —as a foil for many of Mr. Gilberts witty sallies. Just as Mr. Gilberts librettos may be said to be all of a piece, the music is but a continuation of the string of sparkling and often quaint melody which the composer has run off during the past decade; and in the line which he and his collaborateur have

during that period made peculiarly their own, it would be hard to say that either shows signs of poverty of resource. The characters of Nanki-Poo, Ko-Ko, and Pooh-Bah were cleverly undertaken by Messrs. Walter Gilbert, Albert James, and E. Clowes, and to the first and second of these fell the lot of sing- ing many of the more exacting numbers. The Misses Wilkinson, Young, and Taylor, as the three sisters of Ko-Ko played and sung their parts ad- mirably; and in the somewhat thankless part of Katisha Miss Millie Vero proved her- self a conscientious and painstaking artiste. As the Mikado, Mr. It. Fairbanks made up very well and sang with ability, but in the ex- igencies of the opera he had comparatively little to do. Many of the ear-catching songs and ditties, and one or two of the concerted pieces, were en- thusiastically encored on both nights of perfor- mance, the partially unaccompanied " Madrigal" after the opening of the second act being specially singled out for favour. The scenery and dresses were much admired, the locale of the opera giving wide scope for effect in this direction. Altogether the visit of Mr. D'Oyley Carte's company has been a great treat—a welcome relief to the entertainments we have had in the town during the winter season.

TILE Nsw JERUSALEM CHURCIL—On Thursday evening Mr. Gunton, of London, one of the mission- aries of the New Jerusalem Church, gave a third lecture in Cairo-street schoolroom. The subject on this occasion was "The two advents of the Lord, the nature and purpose of each." There was a fair attendance. In the course of • the lecture, which was attentively listened to, he referred to the be- lief held by a large number of people that the Lord at his second coming would appear in person. They, he said, did not expect anything of the kind because they could see that there would be no use in such a coming and they could see insuperable difficulties connected with such a supposition as that. If the Lord came in a material body where would he come to? Would he come to Warrington? If he did then people in Manchester and Liverpool, to say nothing of such places as America and China would not see Him. Some thought He would come to. Jerusalem, but if He did would all the millions Of people on the earth go to JeruSalem ? In truth this assumption of the Lord's coming in a material person was absurd and ridiculous. He (Mr., Gun- ton) and those who believed as he did thought it was the increase of understanding of the spiritual lessons contained in the divine word that constitu- ted the second coming of the Lord. That had been going on now for nearly a century. The ministers of all denominations had at the present day clearer perceptions of the divine word than they had forty or even twenty years ago.—At the con- clusion of the lecture, the Rev. R. Pilcher, 8.A., said he did not think they should let that course of lectures be brought to a close without their acknow- ledging the instruction they had all received, and the kindly Christian way in which the lectures had been given. Not that he agreed with a great deal Mr. Gunton had. said, but Ile did not think that was necessary in this world. He was of opinion that it would do them all good if they were to sit down about once a month and hear something they did not agree with. They all were apt to get into 2. certain rut :or manner of thinking, and it would do them good if they could be shaken out of it. But- ler, the famous ethical writer, had a very wonderful passage which he would recommend them to study. In his preface to his three sermons on human nature he expresses a wish that all books could be destroyed except Just a few of the most difficult, for he was quite certain it would do the world good if they could have had more difficulty in reading, and therefore more necessity for thinking.—The motion proposed. by Mr. Pilcher having been sec- onded, was heartily accorded.—Mr. Gunton acknaw- edged the vote, and the meeting then ended.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

ENTERTAINMENT.—On Thursday evening a largely. attended miscellaneous entertainment was given in the Congregational Schools, Lymm. The programme included pianoforte solos by Mr. C. H. Wrigley. Manchester ; Lan- cashire readings and. recitations by Mr. G. H. Tarbuck, teacher of elocution at the Y.M.C.A., Manchester; violin solos by Mr. G. Crowther, Manchester; and songs by Mr. F. IL Lamb, Altrincham ; and Mr. G. Crowther. The choir also gave selections.

div.head: LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held. in the Board Room, Lymm, on Thursday evening. There were present Messrs. Cameron (chairman), Dewburst, Rogers, Woolley, Gibbon, Thomason, Appleton; Ridgway (clerk), and Dr. Fox (medical officer).

SOAP BOILING AT MERSBY BROOK. The CHAIRMAN said the following application had been received :—Meeilock Chemical Works, Knott Mill, Man- chester, Jan. 31. Sir.—ln accordance with the conditions of the Public Health Act, we beg to make application to your Board for permission to begin soap boiling at our Mersey Brook works. We may say we have a similar per- mit from the Maechester Corporation for our Medlock works, which is situated under a mile from the Manchester Royal Exchange. and although situated in a crowded part we have never had a single complaint; in fact, the most fastidious could never have any poss'.ble room to do se. We may say that our principal business at Mersey Brook will be gum, starch, Epsom salts, and tanning. Trusting to have your Board's favourable reply.—We are, dear sir, yours respectfully, John Gibson and Co.—P.S. We might just say that when we have got all our plant there, and in full working order, we shall be able to provide employ- ment for most, if not all, the surplus labour of Lvmm."-- With regard to this matter the Chairman said several letters had been received. Mr J Rylands, the Grange, Thelwall,wrote to say that having learned that Mr. Gibson was about to apply for a license to manufacture something which would probably be a nuisance, he should be obliged if he (the chairman) would, on behalf of himself ',Mr. Rylands) and others, request the Board to delay granting any license for the present, so as to give them an opportunity of opposing such license if they thought it desirable. Mr. Peter By- lands, M.P., wrote from St. George's-square, Pimlico, Lon- don, protesting against the license being granted. The works were, he reminded the Board, situated in the midst of a valuable residential property, and he trusted the Board would protect himself and other owners from the injuries the works were calculated to do. Mr. Henry Stanton wrote to say that he hoped the Local Board would not sanction the introduction of any manufacture which would become a nuisance to the neighbourhood; and Mr. W. H. Bleckly wrote to protest against granting such a license, as works of the description must be extremely detrimental to property, and a nuisance to the inhabitants. Colonel Mclver wrote as agent of the property of the late Mr. J. R. Fox to say that he felt it his duty to inform the Board that formal com- plaints had been made to him with respect to the noxious smells which had been experienced, and to ask that the Board would not countenance the carrying on of any manu- facture which would prove detrimental to an agricultural district, and a nuisance to the surrounding neighbourhood. —After a short conversation on the subject, the Board decided, on the motion of Mr. DEWHIIRST, seconded by Mr. THOMASON, to defer its further considera- tion till the next meeting. Later in the even- ing Mr. Gibson waited on the Board with regard to his application —The CHAIRMAN mentioned that several gentle- men of the neighbourhood had written to object to the grant- ing of the licence, and expressing the opinion that a nuis- ance would be caused.—Mr. GIBSON thought it a perfectly unnecessary alarm as there would be no nuisance at all.— Mr. HALL: You speak about employing workmen how many would you employ P—Mr. Gosox : We should em- ploy from 100 to 150 regularly.—Mr. HALL: Are the labouring class about here suitable for that kind of employ- ment P—Mr. Ginsort said it was only plain labour and there would be an overseer.—The CHAIRMAN said there had al- ready been complaints of the smells, especially during the night.—Mr. GIBSON : I think they must exist in the imagination.—Dr. Fox: I don't think that is fair; they have really felt the smell.—Mr. GIBSON said, to give an instance of the prejudice which existed, that before anything was on 'the premises except wheelbarrows and such-like things, a farmer came and told some of the men that if they polluted the brook any more he would take out a summons. As a matter of fact they had sent nothing into the brook but pure water from a well.—Mr. Gibson then being informed that the Board would further consider the matter at their next meeting, retired.

div.head: CHANGE OF GOVERNMENT.
div.p: THE CHANGE OF GOVERNMENT.
The following aro appointment; in addition to those given in another column :
Chancellor ot the D—uc—lay of 1. Mr. Henelrge, Lancaster Solicitor General Mr. Horace Davey, Q.O. Lord Advocate Mr. J. B. Balfour.

Secret--y to the Lot I'. Govern- 1L Mr. jease Collings. ment Bo .rd Financial Secretary to the Lea- 1. Mr. H. H. Fowler. sury Pesretary of the Admiralty Mr. Ribbed. ' Under Secretary for India Under Secce ry for the Colo- nies Mr. Wodehouse. Civil Lord of the Admiralty Lord-Lleutenant of Ireland Lord Chamberlain Postmaster General • First Commissioner of Works ' Earl of Morley. Solicitor-General fr Scotland Mr. A. Ashent Comptroller of the Household The Hon. E. Majcribanks. Junior Lords of the Trea / Mr. Cyril Flower and sury - Mr. Geo. Leveson Gnwer. Another consultation between the new Ministers took place on ay morning at Ea-A Granville's. Mr. Childe-s, Sir W. ifircriurt, and Mr. Campbell-Bannerman reached Carlton House-terrace about half-past eleven, and having first called at Mr. Gladstone's crossed to Lord Granville's, where they were joined twenty minutes later by the Prime Minister himself, the last-named looking exceedingly well. A large number of telegrams were received at Mr. Glad- stone's during the morning. • It was rumoured at Leeds on Friday that Mr. Herbert Gladstone will be appointed to a prominent office in the new Government.

The writ for the election at Derby, caused by the ap- pointment of Sir William Harcourt to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, WA2 received at Derby on Friday morning. The Mayor fixed Tuesday next for the nomination and Thurs- day for the polling. Sir William is expected to address the electors or, Mon lay next. The writ for the Brigbtside Division reached Sheffield;on Friday mornin!:, and the Mayor has fixed Monday for the nomination and Wednesday for the polling, if any. The Mayor has received a telegram from Dr. Millar, the hero of more Oar] one gam° at Sheffield elections, stating that he will come forward, but no importance attaches to this an- nouncement. •

A statement that Mr. Bryce has been appointed Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs is officially confirmed. Lord Salisbury arrived at Cowes on Friday evening en route to Osborne. He dine* with the Queen and returns to London to•day (Saturday). . _ _

Lord RoselierY has itiipointed Mr. F. Villiers and Mr. Cecil Spring Rice to be his private secretaries.—Mr. Chil- ders has appointed Mr. E. Ruggles Brise and Mr. Steptien Simeon to be his private secretaries. Mr. Parnell has selected Mr. Stephen O'Mara Mayor of Limerick to contest the Ossory Division of O'Mara, County. Mr. John Morley will address a meeting at Newcastle on Monday evening. _ _

Mr. Trevelya-U in his address to the electors of the Border Burgbs endorses Mr. Gladstone's opinion on the in- adequacy of the treatment which the late Government pro- posed to apply to the Irish question. Mr. Trevelyan adds that his recent public utterances about Ireland were care- fully and maturely considered, and in his opinion they are consistent with a policy which would be generous, just, and safe.

The Central News says :—Although as will be seen by the official list which we were enabled to circulate early on Friday evening, the Irish Viceroyalty and other important posts have been filled up. A number of appointments have yet to be made, and it is not probable that the Administra- tion will be completed before Saturday evening. Mean- while, all statements as to Mr. Gladstone's intentions in the matter of appointments may be taken as entirely con- jectural. At 9-30 this (Saturday) morning a special train will leave Victoria for Portsmouth with some of the Conservative Ministers on their way to Osborne, and at 11-30 the mem- bers of the newly-formed Cabinet will also travel by special train from Victoria, returning the same afternoon.

div.head: -T-HE PROPOSED EXPULSION OF FRENCH PRINCES.
div.p: -T-HE PROPOSED EXPULSION OF FRENCH PRINCES.
PARIS, FRIDAY.—It is stated that the extreme Left con- sider the proposal for the expulsion of all princes of former reigning families is inopportune, and it will therefore pro- bably be withdrawn.

LATCHFORD BAPTIST CHAPEL. The Rey. E. Parker, D.D., president of the Baptist College, Man- chester, preached two sermons in this chapel, on be- half of the funds of the college. Each service was well attended and the collection realised nearly £4. BUCKLEY-STREET BAND OF HOPE.—The fifth en- tertainment of the season was held on Tuesday in the schoolroom, Buckley-street. There was a very good attendance. The chair was taken by Mr. John ' Taylor, and after a short address an interesting pro- gramme was gone through, to the great satisfaction of the audience. A humorous dialogue was given entitled "Tom Wildrake's Folly,' in which Messrs. H. Halford, S. Wright, D. Leigh, J. Adams, Mrs. Adams, and Miss Alice Morrall took part. WINDOW SMASHING EXTRAORDINARY.—A few days ago, on work being resumed at Holy Trinity! Schools, it was found that 25 panes of glass had I een deliberately smashed by stones, a number of I which were strewn about the floor of the school- ! room. It is supposed that the depredation wais com- mitted by men under the influence of drink. The schools are somewhat isolated, and those who corn- I naitted the damage must have watched their oppor- tunity, and managed to do so unobserved. The matter is in the hands of the police. THE NEW GAIETY. This place of amusement has been well patronised during the week, the fare provided being of a good order. The spectacle, in four tableaux, entitled "Father come home," in which fifteen Warrington children appear, as well as members of the company, was much appreciated. The company included Mr. Harry Brown (motto and topical vocalist), Miss Dorville (serio-comic singer and dancer), Mr. Harry Collins (comic vocal- ist), Miss Amy Jukes (ballad vocalist), Kelmar (ven- triloquist), Jean Clancy (dancer), Messrs. Herbert and Kelly (negro artistes.) HOLY TRINITY CHuncx.—On Sunday morning the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton. preached in aid of the Addi- tional Curates' Society, and took for his text the words—" For what if some did not believe? Shall their unbelief make the faith of God without ef- fect?" In the evening the preacher was the Rev. ' G. E. O'Brien, M.A., of Salford, late curate of the Parish Church, Warrington, who took for his text I the words—" And unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from I evil is understanding." There was a good congre- gation at each of the services, and collections were taken in aid of the above-named society. WARRINGTON TRADES COUNCIL.—The usual meet- ing was held on Tuesday evening, at the Cocoa Rooms, Horsemarket-street, when delegates from I the following societies were present :—Wire- drawers, filesmiths, glass-cutters, bakers, brick- I layers, general union carpenters and joiners, and the Dallam lodge of ironworkers. Information was given by the wiredrawers with respect to the strike, which has unfortunately taken place in their trade, and the usual course was adopted with respect to it. Several suggestions were made and discussed with a view to make future meetings more interesting and useful, and an agreeable evening was spent. ST. MARY'S CHURCH, L ATCHFORD.—The annual tea party and ball in connection with St. Maly's Church, Latchford, was held at the Public Hall, Rylands-street, on Wednesday evening, and proved a thorough success. From 200 to 300 people sat down to tea and subsequently the Rev. Father Thompson cordially thanked those who had given trays, the ladies who had presided at the tables, and all who had contributed to make the affair a suc- cess. The ball held after tea was exceptionally well attended, refreshments were provided, and a good band was in attendance. Dancing was kept up with spirit until the early hours of next day. PADGATE WESLEYA.N MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—On Thursday evening Mr. Andrew Rath- bone read a carefully-argued paper on "Free Trade," comparing the condition of the country be- fore and after the adoption of the system, comment- ing on what he conceived to be the causes of the present universal commercial depression, and ex- pressing the opinion that the remedy for the same was certainly not to be found in Fair Trade. An instructive debate ensued, in which Messrs. A. Ben- nett, •H. Whitham, J. J. Nield, G. Mather, W. J. Bennett, and Charles Plinston took part. Next Thursday the Rev. G. E. Cutting is to lecture on "The Great Duke of Wellington." ST. ANNE'S. CHURCH.—A new font was opened at this church on Sunday evening, when there was a large congregation. The preacher was the Rev. J. Ward, M.A. ; and Mr. Percy Randall, the organist, nave a short organ recital in a manner that showed him a master of the instrument. The choir ren- dered the anthem "Call to Remembrance " in a creditable manner, Master Lowe taking the solo. The cost of the font has been defrayed by voluntary subscriptions, and is the work of Messrs. Williams and Clay. The stone is of white Caen, Gothic design, octagonal, with four panels carved with the emblems of the four Evangehsts. The basin is sup- ported by eight cherubim at the eight angles. The font is well finished, and Messrs.:Williams and Clay deserve credit for the masterly way in which the work has been accomplished. THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON.

—For week ending Saturday, Jan. 36th, 1886.—The mean temperature was 35.5 Fahr., and therefore 4.9 degrees higher than the preceding week. The • maximum temperature 41 Fahrenheit. was recorded on the 26th inst., and the minimum temperature. , 27 Fahrenheit, on the 25th inst. The rainfall/ measured I.loin. The general direction of the wind was E. During the week, which was the sth of the current year, 4-4 births and 17 death were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 19.07 per 1,000, against 28.8 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 22.9 the cori- responding week of last year. The deaths included 2 from whooping cough, 2 from tubercular diseaqe, 1 2 from old age, 4 from brain disease, 1 from heajrt disease, 3 from lung disease, and 1 from injuries fr m fall of a spout. Eleven cases of whooping cough were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament. Infectious Diseases Hospital :—No of patients in Hospital Jan. Ist, 4; admitted dui.' ng January, 1; discharged, 5; in Hospital Feb. Ist, iil. ' —JOHN H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health. I AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY'S MEETING.—A meeting ' of the Council of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society was ..held on Monday, at the Lion Hotel, Warrington, the yhair being occupied by Mr. R. Lonsdale, of Boothstown. The object of the meeting was to receive a better from the Royal Agricultural Society of England with respect to agricultural experiments, thEm dis- cussion upon which had been adjourned from a meeting held several weeks ago, and to complef :e the revision of the prize list. A deputation from Pres- ton waited upon the Council to ask them to 'grant prizes to exhibitors of cheese at the different fr iirs in Lancashire and Cheshire, and particularly at' Pres- ton. The Secretary (Mr. T. Rigby) pointed 013 it that if they gave prizes at Preston they would be ex- pected to do the same at all the cheese fairs ila Lan- cashire and Cheshire. After some discuss-on the- Council promised to give the matter their 3favour- able consideration, and the meeting ended. At the subsequent dinner the Secretary, in respon ding to the toast of the society, said he felt convince d of -the importance of their doing all they could to ;promote the better education of farmers' sons. Ha) hoped that when the time came there would be ai,' goodly number at their examination. I

THE CHARGE AGAINST A BANKRUPT.—At War- rington County Petty Sessions on Wednes4day, Mr. T. J. Ridgway, Official Receiver, mentir3ned the case of Garnett T. Longshaw, which had been ad- journed until that day. Since then a fresh i'summons had been. taken out against the defendant, a chemi- cal manufacturer of Great nkey, whicl,ll was due for hearing on the 17th inst. He asked 4he Bench that the case should stand adjourned m until that date.—Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for tele defend- ant, said that the case had been adjourned to see if the matter could be settled between t.l ie two. par- ties. Since then Longshaw had been codmmitted to prison for contempt of court, to remainl there until he had purged his contempt by filing certain accounts. The summons charged dei !endant, the tenant of a house on the Liverpool-road,. with re- moving fixtures therefrom, belonging tip Mr. Robert Garnett. He (Mr. Browne) contencl(Td that the defendant was not the tenant, but tlyiat the house was tenanted at the time by his ifse.. He asked that the summons be dismissed. There was another summons served on the defendant Nstihile in gaol, and he thought that was sufficient for - the Court to go on. Seeing that no earthly object w°ould begained by going on with the first suinmons, • he asked that it should be dismissed.—Mr: Ridgway stated that at the right time he should be prepared to go into the matter. It was on his advice tlariat the second summons was taken out. He was, quite prepared to argue that the first summons should be adjourned, but he did not think that that was I ;he proper time to open the case and to go into legal arguments.— Mr. Browne submitted that the rr magistrates could not adjourn the case until they hartd heard the evi- dence, and both parties had conse, nted to it.—The Chairman thought the proper coimrse would be to adjourn the case. It was possible that the defend- ant might be present in a fortnight.—TMr. Browne stated that it was impossible .to maim out the accounts in a fortnight, and it would 13E) a month at least before the defendant coubji appear.—After a little further discussion the case was adjourned.

TILE An -VAC —Last week P.S. Commins served distress warrants upon several anti•vaccinators who had failed to pay fines and costs imposed upon them by the ewton magistrates for failing to have their children vac- cinated. Since then the amounts claimed have been paid by the defendants, and consequently the necess:ty for hold- ing a sale of the furniture was dispensed with,

AccinENT TO A COLLIER.—Rob4rt Roberts, an employ 4 at the Wigan and Whiston Colliery, residing at 5; Wigan- street, Huyton Quarry, was on Wednesday morning injurel by the fall of a stone from the roof of the pit where he was working. It cut his head, causing a wound two inches in length, and bruised his arm and shoulder badly. His in- juries were attended to by Mrs. Tomlinson, the district nurse.

AN OLD FARMHOUSE AND ITS CHIMNEY.—Before the magistrates sitting at the Newton Town Hall en Saturday. William Longt.n, a farmer in Crow-lane, was summoned for having the chimney of his dwelling-house on fire on the 14th January. P.C. Spencer proved the case, after which Mr. H. J. Longton, solicitor, who appeared for his brother, explained that the house was an old farmhouse, and the de- fendant was about to leave; but the landlord promised to repair it and put it in good condition. Oa that account the chimney had not been recently swept, and the housekee r might have thrown some straw on the fire.—The Bench in- flicted a fine of ss, inzluding costs. I.O.G.T.—The quarterly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tempters was held on Monday* evening, under the presidency of Bro E Newman, W.C.T. After the transaction of formal business, Bro Thomas Gorse (W. Sec.) submitted his repert for the past quarter, iehich was of a vet", favoarable character. The number of Members in good standing was 62, showing an increase of 4 on the past quarter. The reports of Brothers K Maelvenzi• (W.F S.), James Barnard (W.T.), and George Warburto sour. (W.M.) were also of a satisfactory character. Bro E Newman (superintendent) reported that the juveniles in the Juvenile Temple were 19 boys and 32 girls, a slight increase over the previous quarter. All the reports were urenimously adopted, after which the nomination and election of officers for the ensuing quarter took place. The following were appeinted :—W.C.T., Bro George E W^ burton ; W.V.T., Sister E C Barnard e W.S., Bro George Clarke : W.F.S., Bro K Mackenzie ; W.T., Bro James- Barnard ; W. Chao., Bro John Taylor; W.M.,. Bee J. Flaherty; W.1.G., Bro S Wightman ; W.0.6', Bro James Walker; W.A. See, Bro Thomas Gorse; W.D.M., Sister ft Whittv ; P.W.C.T., Bro E.Nevernan ; electoral superin- tendent, Bro George Clarke; lodge deputy, Bro John Ware turton. The officers were installed by Bro John Warburtoe .D., assisted by Bro George Warburton, senr., as the sick, absentee, finance, and programme committee., were afterwards appointed. ALTERATIONS AT WARGRAVE CHURCH.—During the 'past two weeks alterations and improvemen's of an exten- sive character have been in progress at Wargrave Varish Church. The principal alteration is the removalof the old. organ and the erection of a new and more suitable instru- ment, but this work has necessitated other important work.. When the whole of the improvements have been carried out the interior of the edifice will have an entirely new, and, consequently, more pleasant appearance, to the parishioners and congregation. In addition to the fine new organ, which has cost about £5OO, and which will occu- py a similar position to the old instrument, the pulpit will be removed to the opposite side of the cleurcheand instead of one reading desk as hitherto, there will be two—one placed on either side of the centre aisle. A number of pews will also be removed from near the organ, while the mem- bers of the choir will take their seats, not in the old position, but opposite the organ, on a raised daise which is le-'ng erected for the purpose. There will also he an addition. of two pews to those in the centre of the church. New heating apparatus is also being arranged throughout the building. The whole of the interior will undergo a thorough painting and re-decoration. The new organ is being sup- plied by Messrs. Forster and Andrews, of Hull, and it is ex- pected that it will be erected in the churchon Monday next. The instrument formerly in use has been disposed cf by private treaty to the Primitive Methodist body wor- shipping in, I. egh-street, Earlestown. The heating apparatue is being supplied by Messrs. John Slee and Co., Earlestowu, the joiners' work is being done by Mr. Thomas Scott, of Market-street, and Mr. Starkie, of Market.street, will do the painting and decoration. A pleasant circum- stance is the fact that all the pl_ns and drawings for the alterations and improvements were gratuitously supplied by Mr. Charles Whitley, architect, Stratton (Cheshire), eon of the esteemed rector, the Rev. Canon Whitley. Apart from the new organ, which has cost about 5500., the altera- tions and improvements to the edifice will cost about .Cl,OOO. It is expected that the whole of the week will be completed in a few weeks.
